Author: @necronlord52
Content: Well. In my country, Montenegro, there are 3 types of meat. First you can buy in supermarkets, and it is off the commercial production. I've being on those farms - their conditions aren't so bad, but definitely not optimal. This is the cheapest meat, and it is really available to anyone. Then, there is the home-grown meat, mostly pigs, some chicken  - where uneducated people are raising pigs the way their grabd-grand parents did. Not too clean, not fed very well, but mostly organic and without torture. You cannot put a price tag on this meat, because no one sells it raw, usually. It is also processed the old way (smoking, dry-salting or whatever). Third kind is the farmer's production, like myself. It is organic in the best way, at least from those farms I know personally. Pigs, caws and chicken run free, eating all the suitable and diverse food. But this meat is something elite, and it's price is double to the regular one.

Author: @yaalpi
Content: the problem of money doesn't come from the people buying it alone in my opinion, let's say I pay 2€ for a portion of pig (unrealistic as this may be as I usually need about 5€ for an actual meal, I can only think of going to some fast food thing where you get a bun of bread and pure cooked flesh on top for about 2€) anyways, before even getting my wage, let's say 100€, in the country I live in, already 100€ have been taxed from the company paying me, then from the 100€ from which I pay 30-35% aka € for taxes and socials (insurances and stuff), so I actually get say 67€ from the work, in simple terms, from all the money that flowed to me 33% actually reached me, and this is before I have paid for my portion, if I buy my bun with flesh for to go there are 7% taxes on it and if I eat at the same place there are 19% taxes on it instead...  meaning I not only technically lost 67% in taxes to my income, but I also pay 7/19% from what I will buy to eat.. calculated the portion would cost about 5 cent (7% tax) to me earning my 67€, which doesn't sound like much until you calculate me needing at least 3 meals a day over the course of 30 days which is 90. 90x5 = 4,50€ is what I will give to survive of this food, we speak of not eating or consuming any other nourishing stuff, again 4,5€ sounds like not that much to 67€... but you pay rent for a LOT, you have a car, you need to replace stuff from times to times, a hobby, machines at home working for you, and so on, and you actually manage to survive with these 67€, but all the above were like 50€, so you are left with 17€ which I would specifically dedicate to stuff you would do in your free time and savings, if having less than 10% savings then I believe something is fundamentally wrong... even if everything costs just a few cents here and there just a little more, it's not about people beeing able to afford it, it's about people beeing allowed to afford it. It is ofcourse even more complicated, letting everybody earn just more creates inflation, which is what slowly happens in my country too, stuff gets expensive, minimum wage gets higher year to year, not by a lot, it is in controll after all, but this can't keep going forever... I do not want to say anything in the kind of "eat the rich", I am most certain, most people would act just as they do, if they were in their shoes. Money hoarding is a problem though, even worse when people are competent with money. Absolutely everything needs to make profits, directly or indirectly it does not matter. What rich can do is controll, with money, indirectly. The reason why monopols are so dangerous.. Carfour, Kaufland, Lidl, Cosco, and other are technically all the same, they usually apear as enemies but they are semi enemized, they are not really working to fight eachother, working more together, not for our good though. All the production of food is controlled even before it's started, supermarkets know how much they will sell each season, at least roughly, if no complications occur (example: corona).. If something regional comes around, or is a concurence, big supermarkets are backed up by such large sums of money, they can sell stuff with loss, so the local market collabses and they have the dominance and dictate prices. Sometimes they get stupid high, like in east european countries right now. People have little money to rely on, suddenly a cheap supermarket apears with better prices, people go and buy there, suddenly nobody goes to the local markets, they go bankrupt and fail, then supermarkets raise prices higher than they were in the regionals to get more profit. What happens is, you have a brocken local market, the people cannot go back onto relying, but they can also not afford anything the supermarket has to offer. What happens now is difficult, somebody will have to lose in such situations, and in 3th countries it's the Country itself and the people together usually. a way to go is to simply ban profiting supermarkets, they must stay profit neutral and the country must directly controll them so no 3th party inported provider takes the money and takes it away from the country as a worth. people can starve to death and it has happened before, in this situation.... However you turn it, don't get me wrong, I am not against Capitalism, as it's our best working system yet we ever, but we can't live forever in a way, in which people allways need to profit of everything. This is compareble to a game like CS:GO, people will allways need to win, but where there are winners on the one side, there are losers on the other...

Author: @protoncracker_xp
Content:
Fourth time I've seen this video. I have castrated a baby pig, and some friends of mine have grinded their teeth and clipped their tails. When I was with the tool in hand and the screaming baby pig being held in this lecture on my class, *I was told they felt not that much pain and it was mostly the being scared part.* They said the same about baby humans a while ago, unsurprisingly it was untrue. 

(Oh and sorry for this being long, just finished writing. Such a big rant, I know.)

They also told me it was for the best, since the testosterone would make them fight more in closed spaces. Never told me that this would simply make their meat go bitter. They have not applied any kind of anesthetic either. And their mothers were right beside them, clearly agitated, probably furious, in a closed cell with water and food droppers, side by side other mothers, and around 4 meters of distance to the place where they place 3 week old pigs ("maternity") to then be introduced to pig food and then be placed in their own enclosures.

The same happened to chicken. But worse, probably - I missed school that day. The laying hens we kept in small cages, roughly the size of 2.5 chickens. Clipped beaks. In the class I missed, we'd slit their throats open and put them upside down to drain. Alive. No anesthetic involved. Squirming around. All my friends and me felt weird after doing so.
At least the cows had a easier go. There, they were range free, and sent to a special slaughterhouse to be made into meat. In there, to ensure the meat is tender, they don't want to scare the animal, so they get the cow there many times to make her ease into it, and one of the times BANG. Shot right into the head. It is a decline, theirs bodies fall on the ground and they roll all the way down and bleed out a little. After that, I don't know. All I know is that I've seen the school's freezers and they had pigs cut in half hanged by hooks.

So, yea, I know *how* my meat is made and how it gets to my plate. It does disgust me. Yet, vegetables are at an all time high. Our salary is around 200-350 dollars a month. I will literally die in around 6 months if I don't buy cheaper things (such as MEAT, which is around 4 dollars a kg). And if I can barely afford vegetables, do you think I get the double-the-price meat pieces? 

Rent is around 200, food is around 100 to 175 if you live alone. Bills are around 50 to 100. It does NOT add up (350 minimum total), which is why we often have 2 jobs AND gigs, making around 400 a month and mostly living with our parents or in very bad housing. I tried the online gigs market, and still made no money. I got 1 order on f1verr in like 4 or 7 months and it was from someone trying to get me to create the code for a card cloning scheme. 

Humans are disgusting little entities. For most of us outside of USA it is not about principles, its about survival - you can be hella sure we care more about our survival than their wellbeing. And I'm half sure it is the truth for a lot of you out there as well, although Kurzgesagt showed that only chicken doubled the price it is more than likely to go higher than that since its about early investment and supply/demand. I don't even KNOW how much it costs here, I haven't found "Certified Humane" or "Certified Organic" anywhere, and honestly I'm scared to look into it.

The problem is the waste, the economic disparity, the shattering of our economic values (prices for OTHER things like the foods that the animal themselves eat is high because land prices), rent going up, etc etc. You can be sure I wouldn't be supporting this if I had been given a easier choice like "ey, pay less on streaming services and gaming to end animal cruelty!" rather than "ey, die in 6 months eating only enough to keep your body up and alive to end animal cruelty! (for you)" (and ofc I guess I'd last more than 6 months, I have fat and muscles to burn, but you know what I mean). 

My ex-vegan (5 years) fiancée is SEVERELY anemic. And their parents had their money, she can't afford the lifestyle anymore. If only certain talents were more appreciated, maybe we'd get around this concept and we'd eat only chemically made food, like them beefs scientists made using grapes. That'd be good. I'd like that. But we aren't going to pay out correctly the people we are outsourcing our work for... right America?

We ain't ending this so soon then. 

I live in Brazil. Minimum wage is BRL R$1518. That is USD $282 today. And most people here make money outside registered jobs, which is often lower than that I said. My salary is what I've seen people spend in 4 minutes in online games like Roblox, Fortnite, or skins for Ahri and battle passes. Often US or EU people, mind you. We have one of the highest taxes too, btw. Top 2 in highest tarrifs, top 1 taxes in Latin America, around 32 to 34% Tax-To-GDP. USA is 25 to 27%.

The conjoined amount of money I've spent in online games (including microtransactions and everything) comes around to 60 to 80 dollars in the last 4 years (when I started getting some money). That's all I could afford. I'm not waving a poverty card, I'm trying to speak for non-US listeners. We can't afford 1 dollar more on each serving of some foods, we barely can keep up as is. If YOUR demand increase, the prices for export/import will skyrocket for everyone else and we'll have to find other foods. It is not viable. Economy IS a great problem worldwide in the matter of wildlife care, natural life care, about improving the climate, the kids, everything. ALL of it. It kinds of fixes everything or most of it.
~protoncracker.

Author: @ShockInazuma
Content:
I eat meat and I love animals. Vegans tend to have the logic backwards when they use pets as an argument for eating meat.

First thing: Cultures are different, but pets are generally treated well and not harvested for food. At least where I'm from, that is. Using pets as an argument for eating meat is just an unfair argument to make since they’re different. Pets are our companions, not our food. (Not to mention some pets aren’t even safe to eat in the first place.)

Second thing: Humans are omnivorous. We always have been since the dawn of time. We eat meat, we eat plants, we eat eggs… We eat just about any type of food so long as it doesn’t kill us. While there’s nothing wrong with eating purely plants, the things to keep in mind are: plants are also alive, and most humans aren’t going to stop eating part of what they eat because that’s just how they’re built. Technically speaking, we’ve EVOLVED to eat meat. It’s part of our DNA. It’s how we get nutrients, too. And not just from meat, either. Stuff like eggs and milk are also rich in nutrients, namely protein for the former and calcium for the latter. A lack of one or both can lead to severe health problems.

Third and final thing: You can’t control or get mad at people for eating meat. It’s how we’re made. There’s nothing wrong with us eating meat. If you want to point the finger at someone, it’s the companies who make living conditions for _farm_ slaughterhouse animals bad, subjecting them to said slaughterhouses instead of offing them peacefully. As for farms, themselves. A lot are locally owned. While it’s true that some may off their animals, they still take care of them before it’s time. Overall, farms have better living conditions for these animals than company-owned slaughterhouses. So most of the blame should be shouldered on said slaughterhouses. It’s unethical and cruel, and there should be advancements to making sure they die peacefully and not suffer.

Overall, most of us cannot deny our nature to eat meat. It’s part of who we are. But that doesn’t mean we can’t be against these companies and how they treat animals. If I had to really choose, I'd prefer the meat on my plate came from an animal who lived a peaceful life until death than suffer a gruesome and inhumane fate.

Author: @newenso2780
Content:
Great video as always, but I think the cost section might oversimplify what a full transition to high-welfare or outdoor systems would actually involve.

When Kurzgesagt says that moving all pigs or cows to “free-range” or outdoor conditions would only raise the price at the dinner table a little, the math behind that seems to miss some major real-world costs. Looking through the linked sources, the estimates mostly come from incremental welfare upgrades (more space, straw, daylight, or removing crates) — not from converting massive industrial indoor systems to full outdoor or pasture-based farms.

Key things that don’t seem fully included:

Labor: outdoor and lower-density systems need far more staff time per animal.

Land: true free-range requires vastly more space, which means new land purchases or repurposing cropland — often the biggest cost driver.

Infrastructure: fencing, barns, water systems, and transport have to be rebuilt, which adds large capital costs.

Risk and efficiency losses: outdoor herds can have more losses from weather, disease, or predation, plus slower growth rates.

Scaling effects: small pilot studies don’t capture what happens when the entire global meat system shifts — land scarcity, higher feed prices, etc.

So while marginal welfare improvements may add only a few cents per serving, a genuine move away from industrial confinement would likely raise prices much more. It’s not really an apples-to-apples comparison between a mega-farm and a smaller organic or free-range model.

Author: @edim108
Content:
I only ever buy free range antibiotic-free chicken. I know full well that I'm paying a lot more for the same amount of meat with most of it going to the store, but at least I know the chicken had a decent life and the meat actually tastes good.
I did a small experiment. I bought two packs of chicken carcasses with wings- one was "regular" and the other was free range antibiotic-free. After weighing each on a scale both were within 10g of eachother for my test.
I made two batches of basic stock- just the chicken boiled in water. I boiled them in two identical pots with the same ammount of filtered water taken from the same jug. I boiled them side by side on the same burner setting for 6 hours.

The difference was STARK! The regular chicken tasted like greasy water, it was cloudy and had a really inpleasant aftertaste. The free range chicken was actually flavorfull, the stock had depth, it wasn't as greasy and it wasn't cloudy.
I then took these two batches of stock and made "rosół" (chicken soup) with them. I measured all the ingredients by weight to get them as close to identical as I could and simmered both pots side by side for 4 hours on the same burner settings.
The regular chicken soup tasted like oily vegetable broth with the only "chicken" flavor being that bad aftertaste. The pasture raised chicken soup was rich, it had body to it and bc the stock wasn't cloudy it had that beautiful clear amber color.
Then the final part of the experiment. I intentionally left just under two cups of soup in each pot, I put them side by side on the counter covered and waited for them to go bad. The cage chicken one went frothy and smelled sour two whole days before free range chicken soup!

I know it wasn't a perfect scientific experiment, but it was as close to that as I can manage and if nothing else the taste alone convinced me to always pay extra and get that cruelty free chicken with no antibiotics. I am willing to eat less meat and make up the difference with kidney beans and stuff if it means the chicken gets to live a decent life before being processed and I get meat that actually tastes good. I already get a lot more calories than I need daily so if anything eating less meat and more vegetables is good for my diet.efore pasture

Author: @waltercomunello121
Content:
many of us humans aren't willing to give up part of our well being to livestock, poultry or pigs. By eating less meat we can 1. live better lives, 2. give (at least partially) better lives to animals, and 3. save money. Humans feel so entitled, and this saddens me.

I'm not saying "don't eat meat". Meat is good, in some instances better than other protein sources. But I see no reason for which we *have* to eat *that much* meat as we do now. By eating less meat and paying it just a little more, we could make stables less crowded, have animals live in environments more suited to their lifestile, or give them better food. And in the end, better living animals *will* give us access to a better quality meat, improving our health in the process. It's a systemic reasoning.

By sacrificing a little bit of this or that, we can live so much better with ourselves.

Correction: 

Free range hens: allowed access to the outdoors, typically with a minimum of just 2 square feet of outdoor space per bird. The term "free-range" is regulated by the USDA, but standards are less stringent compared to pasture-raised eggs.

Pasture-Raised Eggs: have significantly more outdoor space, with a minimum of 108 square feet per bird. unlimited access to the outdoors. hens have a more diverse and natural diet, including grass, bugs, and other foraged foods, in addition to their feed. The term "pasture-raised" is not regulated by the USDA, but organizations like Certified Humane.

Author: @DePadreAHijo
Content:
The current recommendations are completely wrong and useless. The real solution is to fix the incentives.

Here’s how: we set a baseline tax on farmers, which they can avoid if they pass an annual audit. The worse their audit results, the higher the price-per-serving they’re allowed to charge. That means low-quality meat becomes more expensive, and high-quality meat (from farms that treat animals well) becomes cheaper.

In the supermarket, we’d see cheaper meat with better quality, plus visible certifications showing what standards the farmer met.

Farmers would need to renew their license every year or face taxation again. During that licensed year, they could be randomly audited. If they fail a random audit, they pay double tax for the rest of the license period—and they’re banned from renewing until that period ends. That’s the penalty.

This would guarantee better animal welfare, transparent pricing, and consumer trust.

The truth is, the solution is simple. The problem isn’t technical—it’s political. There’s no real will to change it.

Content:
From a guy who worked in a chicken plant. It’s fair to say that the current standards we have are not ok… I worked at a gorges plant for more then at least six to eight months…

Conditions inside the plant despite the FDA having staff there… we’re not ideal. For starters they treat food like it’s an assembly line. Their quick to push you back on the lines that they don’t provide mandatory or decent times to get new equipment or wash everything, including your own hands. Gunk and fat is constantly falling on your clothing, and if you pick up raw food off the floor. Instead of going to a wash bin. They made me just spray my gloves with water and get back to work. I even heard from one of my friends that worked there. That they don’t spray shipping boxes down if they fall on the floor… and it’s mostly full of immigrants that some hardly speak, or even outright refuse to speak English… unless they absolutely have to, when facing coworkers that don’t or are facing supervisors & employer’s.

The down side is Eventually kept getting sick every two to three weeks. Eventually got fired… only to find out after still getting sick. I had campylobacteriosis. A common bowel infectious bacteria that only exists when you don’t wash your hands. Or are working with raw chicken that has been exposed to it’s excrement (poop) for long periods of time… I nearly even had to do a nasty surgery to check for Colin cancer… as the symptoms were quite similar… it’s no funny buisness… I wouldn’t recommend ever working in poultry industry. Author: @EllyCatfox
Content:
This video fails to acknowledge the land use problem and how it relates to the environment, climate change, and energy costs. For every animal in captivity helped by *expanding* their land use, even more natural wildlife habitat is destroyed, creating more suffering in the wild and even for humans. The materials to build bigger barns have to come from somewhere. The land has to come from somewhere. The carbon emissions have to go somewhere.

Improving animal welfare through extensive, organic production systems creates a false dilemma between animal ethics and environmental sustainability. While these systems may provide marginal welfare improvements for individual farm animals, they consistently require more land, energy, and resources per unit of protein produced, creating greater environmental damage and habitat encroachment than intensive systems. More importantly, both intensive and extensive animal agriculture systems remain dramatically less efficient than plant-based alternatives in terms of land use, resource consumption, and environmental impact.

The most effective path forward involves transitioning agricultural land and resources away from animal production entirely, rather than attempting to optimize within existing animal agriculture paradigms. This approach could simultaneously address animal welfare concerns by reducing the total number of animals in agricultural systems, improve environmental outcomes through more efficient resource use, and create opportunities for habitat restoration and carbon sequestration on formerly agricultural lands. While this transition faces significant political and economic challenges, the scale of environmental and ethical problems created by animal agriculture suggests that incremental welfare improvements within existing systems is insufficient to address the underlying issues.

Author: @Cindercrisp
Content:
I do like the information shared, but one connotation is space... Especially in population dense areas like the EU. There are plenty of health and safety regulations that prohibit farming too close to population centres, think of it like zoning and destination plans ( different i know, but its a rough idea) also recent environmental laws severely reduce the square kilometers allotted to farms... Dealing with these regulations will result in either more 'torture camp' style farms or less production which lowers supply... Which raises the price drastically as demand is only rising with our rising population and immigration trends (think of that how you will) truth is, yes we want better lives for the animals we eat, as that also increases the quality and taste of the meat, but there are too many constraints to realistically achieve it. Both physical (space) and economical (supply and demand)
In my personal opinion, innovation can do a lot to make it better, but we sadly will always have to deal with physical constraints of reality 

On the Muscles question, yes eat them more, farm them more. Luckily most coastal counties (at least here in Europe) have a strong muscles eating tradition. The Netherlands and Belgium have a muscles eating season, Spain uses them in Paella, Italy and France in 'Fruit de mer' and in the UK you even have deep fried muscles... And plenty more examples to mention.

Author: @parkereatsplants
Content:
I really wanted to like this video. Really did. That’s because it is shedding some light on the horrific situations animals are put in, but, I believe, not offering practical solutions. Over half of all useable (not deserts or ice) land is already used for animal agriculture. Increasing the space animals have while continuing to eat as much meat is impossible. The number of animals would have to significantly decrease, and the amount of meat humans eat would as well. Good for the animals since not as many will be brought in to existence to suffer. However, I think leaving this fact out of the equation makes it a misrepresentation of reality. Also, these better conditions are not always better for the environment. Cattle grazing is a greenwashed idea that actually worsens our greenhouse gas issue as an example. And, although their lives may be of a higher quality, they still end in unnecessary, and often horrific, deaths. As long as we eat animals that will not change. With the mounting evidence that eating animal products of any kind is not necessary for humans and is often harmful, I think there is one real solution:
Stop eating animals and their products. Best for human health, planetary health, and the animals themselves.

Edit: i forgot to even mention that meat is significantly more expensive than what we pay for in markets. In the US, for every $1 spent on meat in a grocery store, there is a hidden $2 in tax money given to the industries through subsidies. I believe this example is specifically for beef. But it is all more expensive than what is shown on the shelf.

Author: @danicarovo8818
Content:
I used to be a huge meat eater. My favourite food was tartar beefsteak (raw beef) and foie gras, and I liked my steak medium rare. 
I had a crush on a pescatarian so I got interested in the topic. So I read a book called "Eating Animals" by Jonathan Safran Foer. 
It completely changed my life. 
He, also an omnivore, is a journalist who was curious about how his meat is produced. And what he found was so shocking, that by the end of the book the writer was vegan. And so was I. 

It's almost been 5 years since I went vegan, and it was the best decision of my life. 
And, very surprisingly, it was one of the easiest as well. What you like to eat is largely out of habit (your neighbor probably eats quite differently to you). After a few weeks of adjustment, I learned a couple recipes I liked. Instead of picking the one thing off the supermarket shelf I take the other. And that's it. I lost nothing. On the contrary - I discovered my love for cooking and for food through that initial phase of learning new recipes. 

I didn't get together with my pescatarian crush, but I'm thankful for him for unknowingly making me vegan:))

I’m not a vegetarian, although I have been in the past so I’m not saying this to shame anybody, but it immediately lets me know whether or not I want anything to do with somebody if I ask them a question like, “why do you eat lamb?” And their response is to immediately regress into a toddler who has no ability to rationalize or reason and say, “BECUZ IT TASTE GUUUD.”

Author: @TriangleChloros
Content:
Just want to comment on the mussels thing: Mussels often contain a bacteria called Vibrio Vulnificus. For most people, this is not particularly dangerous - the worst that will happen is some food poisoning if you don't cook your mussels enough. However, there are certain medical conditions that make Vibrio *extremely* dangerous. One of these conditions is hemochromatosis, which is a genetic condition that is often only diagnosed quite late in life. You probably know if you have liver failure, but you might not know if you have hemochromatosis.

The chances you *do* have hemochromatosis are very low (less than 0.5%, I believe), but if you're going to eat mussels it's still a good idea to be *very* sure you cooked them properly.

Author: @tophy43
Content:
I am sorry, but as a vegan, I must say this video is inappropriate to say the very least on multiple levels. Let me give you my perspective on it:

1. I don't think a topic like this is a good fit for kurzgesagt as the art style kurzgesagt employs is way too colorful and "idyllic" for such a topic, even if they try to make it look as "cruel" as possible. The problem with this is that it suggests, because of its lack of ability to depict cruelty, an absence of said cruelty. Even if you say it's really bad in the voiceover, the images are more persistent than the words; they are way more tangible. One example where one could see what I mean is where the make chicks got shredded and only feathers came out. I know this probably has to do with youth protection and stuff, but nonetheless, I truly believe that a proper tackling of the matter must involve proper imagery, something which kurzgesagt cannot supply for such a topic. Given this reason and my other criticisms, I think, that it would have been preferable if this video hadn't been made in the first place. Now, I am not saying the art-style in general is bad, it's just poor for this topic.

2. Your entry question ("What would it cost us to avoid animal torture but still have our fried chicken?") is already quite inappropriate. The problems animal rights activists and vegans have isn't really that these animals are killed or "tortured", their problem is that they are being seen as a resource, like raw iron. Seeing sentient beings as a resource creates all the issues you criticize in your video, but the actual underlying problem is not touched. Avoiding animal torture is stopping to see them as a resource, and doing so would cause us to stop industrially breeding them in the first place, making us unable to consume them or their products. That is the price we pay for actually avoiding animal torture. You classify life stock industry practices into three categories: Torture camps, prisons, and decent, when a more appropriate classification would be torture camps, slightly better torture camps, and slightly better than slightly better torture camps. While the "best" practices can create slightly better lives for the animals, the animals are still seen as a resource and treated as such, and this is the problem we have. So, in a nutshell, if you want to avoid animal torture, you can't have your fried chicken, and if you want your fried chicken, you cannot avoid animal torture. 

3. Following up with my second point of criticism, I want to mention that the standards we have for animals are very low to begin with. We call actually horrible conditions for animals "decent" because all the other "options" are much worse. This already skews the discourse from actually improving the situation to doing at most micro-adjustments, none of which are actually enough to improve anything on a substantial scale. There's also a huge double standard there, and you even mention it: You literally said "image treating dogs like this", and you are totally right! Yet you frame micro-improvements as totally game-changing for the animals when they aren't. Problem I have is that we have very high standards for how we should treat dogs and cats, etc., but not for the rest. My problem with this video in this regard is that you do pretty much nothing to fight this double standard. And by the way, if you are interested and even if you are not, look into how the dog breeding industry operates and you will see that they are treated just like pigs and cows are treated, it's just hidden from us even more.

4. The next point is less about veganism but more about the socio-economic implications you touch on. You say that improving the situation for animals will increase prices, which is true, but then you make a point that for the love of my life I cannot leave uncommented. You make it out as if an on average 50% increase in meat price isn't all that much, when it really is A TON. Fact is, most people in the Western World and pretty much everyone not in the Western World is too poor to afford "good" meat. It's so bad in fact that they have trouble filling dining plates halfway through the month. How are they supposed to choose the "good" meat if they are too poor to afford any food? Your argument is a kick in the face for anyone with class awareness. It's generally something that most people get wrong about the way our economic system functions: you cannot really freely choose what you want since what you want since you can only choose what your material situation allows, and if your material situation is bad, you can only, if at all if you are lucky, afford the worst quality and by that legitimizing the worst practices.

5. My next point extends the fourth point a bit further and generalizes it a bit more: Economic democracy is a myth in a capitalist system. As I said before it's not your "democratic right to choose whatever you want" that directs what you can choose, but it's your material situation. Your material situation determines how much buying power you have and as such how much influence you personally have with your consumption behavior. The richer you are, the more you can consume, and the higher your impact is (despite it being near zero, even if you are very wealthy.)  Since your material situation is mostly influenced by the family/environment you are born into and not really at all by your willingness to improve it, and the system is not meant to improve the material condition of the utmost percentage of people, economic democracy in this system is not "hard to achieve", it's not even "very challenging to achieve", it's outright impossible to achieve.

6. My last point is something that a bunch of other commentors have already mentioned: Since the current system is driven by nothing but the need to grow, and grow more every year, any increase in living conditions of life stock will cause a disproportional increase in price. Companies are not stupid, and enterprise advising firms are explicitly advising companies to increase prices if the situation allows for it. We could see that happen very blatantly during the COVID pandemic: politics was saying that prices were going to rise because of the crisis, and companies did that, even if their production prices were not actually influenced by the crisis. Why? Well, because everyone was expecting an increase in price, and it would be very stupid from an economic perspective to leave out on these profits. 

In conclusion, this video is very much not anti-meat-industry, but more like class-struggle from the top down. I think you cannot really decouple ways of creating market signals from the material condition of the people. Asking what we can do and not what the industry can do, thereby offloading responsibility off to the consumer is a known Neoliberal playbook strategy. To anyone who is actually interested in improving the situation: Organize yourselves. Put pressure on the industry, shift the discourse away from blaming customers to blaming those who are actually to blame, those who caused this mess and those who profit from the continuation of this mess. This has proven to be more efficient than relying on an imaginary market system whose proponents are telling you fairy tales about invisible hands and economic democracy. Anyways, I am out, GO VEGAN and take care of yourselves and everyone and everything you love, including animals!! Peace <3

Plants aren't food, plants are what food eats. Meat, especially ruminant meat is the most nutritionally dense food you can consume. Plants are full of toxins and the human digestive system is not designed to eat a plant based diet.

Increase in brain size among early hominids correlates with increased animal fat consumption.
Fossil records and stable isotope studies show humans have long relied on meat-based diets.
Evolutionarily, access to high-calorie, nutrient-dense fatty meats have enabled the energy demands of our larger brains.

Lectins irritate gut lining, especially raw
Oxalates bind calcium, to form kidney stones
Phytates inhibit mineral absorption
Goitrogens disrupt thyroid hormone production
Tannins interfere with iron absorption
Solanine	neurotoxin in high amounts

Humans have a monogastric system like carnivores, not a fermentation chamber like ruminants or even hindgut fermenters like gorillas.

Archaeologist Clark Larsen notes: “The shift to agriculture resulted in declines in oral health, increases in infectious disease, and malnutrition.”

Plants aren't food, plants are what food eats.

Author: @tom0419
Content:
I've actually raised chickens for both meat and eggs. Your calculations on the meat birds are WAY off. A Cornish Cross bird reaches butcher weight in 10 weeks. It's incredible. You can almost see them growing hour by hour. No hormones, no drugs. They're just genetic freaks. The next best meat birds take almost 3 times as long to reach butcher weight. Feed cost is the primary cost in any farming venture.

Cornish Cross have a feed conversion ratio of about 2 to 1 (2 lbs feed to 1 lb growth) which is INSANE. Other meat birds are at around 7.5 to 1. It's a huge cost difference. Your chicken would cost triple and waste far more natural resources.

Hard facts. Chicken is the most sustainable meat on the market by far. If it's any consolation, they absolutely emphatically are NOT thinking animals. They are pure instinct and no soul. I could tell stories and give specifics but I won't.

Author: @ayys-be-in-my-a-hole
Content:
20-50% increase in food costs is a MASSIVE deal when you have cheaper alternatives that are nearly identical products, with more severe impact the lower the income. Such barbaric conditions, if they significantly reduce cost for such highly elastic goods, are *actually* the best moral decision in most circumstances worldwide. Providing proper nutrition and food to the people, yourself, and family > animal suffering. Plus, even if you set standards on farmers, you'd have to somehow deal with imports from countries with low welfare standards. The profit margins for farmers is *razor-thin* and the  competition is insane. Historically, the best improvements for animal welfare have been through technological innovations; the work of Temple Grandin is one of the most famous (also known for being an autistic savant).

Cheap, plentiful food is the cornerstone of economic growth, poverty alleviation, and improved living standards globally. We see the same thing for burning fossil fuels. It's easy to think sacrificing our own convenience will nourish Gaia, but in reality most of what we do is put the poor and developing on the altar to be sacrificed.

Content:
Honestly, I feel like this idea of ,,we can spend a bit more and get animals more free" is, as mentioned clearly in the video, a gross oversimplification. I'm sure vast majority of people, if asked, would 100% wish to pay just a couple pennies more for animal products, but the companies responsible for this industrial meat production do not want this to be the case. Many of them do their best to eliminate small, regional farms which may treat the animals good, just so they can turn more profit and eliminate a potential competition. I'm sure many farmers also would want to treat their animals better, but they simply can't afford to in their specific market. It's the large, chain corporations that are an issue here - but since they turn billions of revenue to the budget, no-one really has any desire to change that.
 But my favorite recommendation in that video is to not throw away meat. The same goes for everything - it's not just a waste of animals, plants, farmland or CO2 emitted, it's also a waste of your own money and time. You spent quite decent amount of money, time and effort just to clutter your fridge and then ditch it in the garbage. Don't cook more than what you're willing to eat within 3 days or so, and if you want to 'experiment', go to the restaurant to try a certain food out before cooking it yourself. If you can, avoid buying 'fresh' fruits and vegetables if you don't have any plans for them, and try to buy only canned food for 'unplanned' ideas instead.

Author: @finalbarrage7108
Content:
i wanna debunk the "20% of meat just gets thrown away"
ive worked in retail for 12 years now, 4 of which as a store owner. Around 35% of the meat we throw away are due the package tearing, either during transport or if a customer is careless. Or if customers leave them out of the fridge without us catching it, or also commonly.. they put them in a freezer. All of these things render the meat unsellable, due to strict regulations for food safety. Some of it we can donate, and we do.. but most of it we simply cant. 
And around half of the meat we throw out, are due to spoilage. And you may think its easy to blame us for stocking too much, but the simple truth is that its far more cost effective for us to order a bit more, and keep shelves stocked and throw some out, than it is to risk running low, which is frustrating to customers. There is no solution to this, beside government incentives to lower waste. Alot of this spoilage meat, also results from producers pushing for campaigns, and overestimate how much meat customers are willing to buy at the targeted price.

A small detail here, if we price something down, say by 50%, this is still considered "50% waste" in the books for us. So even if we sell it at half price and it gets consumed, half of it is considered "wasted".

The remaining 15% of waste, are miscellaneous. Unregistered waste, theft, missed deliveries that we dont catch, etc. Its when we "correct" our stocks, and there are deviations.

Content: With some experience in the US poultry market: “cage free” here means 2000 hens crammed into a 2000 square foot room. If kept outdoors, farmers can't keep the numbers safe, so cages may seem horrible, but they are the safest option. It would be preferable for a person to have a few free-range chickens and share with the neighbours over mass produce farming.

Also, sowing crates are used to protect the piglets. Pigs are some of the WORST animals when it comes to cannibalism. Sows left in groups, even with enough space to and resources, will eat their young, or the young of each other. They have to be kept separate. The sow crate is designed as it is to sweep the piglets out of the way when the mother lays down, and to allow them to crawl around when she stands up. They are taken at three weeks because that's usually when they go back into their heat cycles anyway.

I'd also like to point out that most young animals are not anaesthetized when castrated. 

I'm not saying the treatment of animals is good overall, but you should really learn the WHY before saying some of this stuff. It's important for people to know the full truth. Also, you need to understand why it costs more to keep animals outside. Many of the farms mentioned are working on limited space as it is. Feedlots for cattle are not cages. They are normally pens that have enough space to move, but instead of cattle finding their own feed, the feed is brought to them. There is also a large number of dairy cattle that have some seriously cushy lifestyles that live indoors with some outdoor access. Cows are the most destructive animals of the mentioned, and will destroy pastures easily. It's why feedlots are cycled in each year.

Content:
thanks for the video guys.. I know you won't be reading this but anyway: 
While I really appreciate the effort and the wording used etc.. the topic is so vast it would need a series of its own..
Because one thing you didn't bring up in the video at all is the slaughter part. And all slaughter are not born equal. From slicing the throat of animals and letting them bleed out, to literal gas chambers for pigs and so on.. And while it's very difficult in some countries to even know how the animal has been killed, sometimes you can avoid it if you avoid any hallal or kasher products for the throat slicing part for instance.

Even if EVERYONE would be willing to pay more for better conditions, we simply CAN'T do it.

Another topic would be an easy one: since you show at the end what kind of meat is purchased, and it's often burgers, sausages, nuggets, milk etc.. Those things have been made without using any animal product and are just as good if not better as the original one. With 0% cruelty and better for the planet, and for decent low price (lower than organic meat etc). So if you plan on eating a burger or make fajitas or a BBQ with merguez, you can opt for a veggie alternative (that doesn't suck, there are tons, I'm not here to sell anything) and save up animals while enjoying your food. 
Yeah there is no alternative currently to a roast beef or the likes, but that would be a huge improvement already. 

Anyway already wrote too much, like I said the topic is so vast it's never ending..
Just do your best when it comes to buying your food, a little label reading and going out of your comfort zone can go a LONG way against animal cruelty (and human cruelty as well, since life in slaughter house is borderline torture as well for humans working there for minimal wage)

Content:
I think the issue isn't just the per unit price, but also the property price. See if you cram ten chickens into the space that one should have, you're paying tenth of the property value for the same profit. You're also just generally increasing production. One of the reasons why meat prices have gone more affordable in the past, and why waste is so common is that we just make more meat. If every meat producing place suddenly doubled the space per animal they could only produce half the meat, it's simple as that. Since it wasn't mentioned as a factor in the video, and the price changes displayed seem too good to be true, I have to assume this just wasn't accounted for.

Don't take me wrong, I still think this situation needs to be changed drastically, if the cost of meat skyrockets for it then so be it, but I think this limitation is an important factor that wasn't mentioned at all.

Author: @jawa6306
Content:
So I worked on a farm my teenage years. Let me share my personal experience. (Remember YMMV, the world is a big place). 

The chicken farm was the worst. If you are buying your chicken from Tyson or Pilgrims pride they are grown in 60foot wide, 300 foot long metal buildings with fans on each end. The chickens in particular were called "Broilers". We'd get a shipment in and turn them out in half the house with a curtain to keep them all on one side. Water pipes with nipples and feeders connected to augers hung from the ceiling and could be raised or lowered with a pulley system. 

At the end of the day it wasnt really the lack of space that got them, though it was bad, but the ammonia from their feces. It would become steadily worse as the chickens grew and could kill anywhere from 10-50 per day. If for some reason the fans failed you had minutes to fix it before the birds suffocated. You had to walk thorugh the houses several times a day and collect them. Sometimes the chickens would gang up on one that had a bald spot and literally peck it to death. After they were gone we had to rake all the crap out of the house and clean all the feed trays and water lines. Chicken crap would go on a spreader truck to use as nitrogen for the fields. There was this one time I forgot the shreperd's hook (to run the winches on the ceiling) in a house I'd already cleaned and I didnt feel like walking all the way back to the control room to turn the fans back on. I didn't make it 3 steps into the house before I turned back. The ammonia burned my eyes, nose, and throat even while I held my breath. It was like I'd been maced. I later learned that ammonia gas combined with water and air to make ammonium hydroxide which is extremely causitc. I quit not long after that and still dont eat chicken. 

The cattle on the other hand lived great lives while we had them. I cant speak for the feed lots, but locally We had multiple plots of land around the county anywhere between 3-20 acres that we would rotate the cattle around. Once they got big enough they'd be sold, but for a few years they were pretty much placed in a huge field and left to graze at their leisure supplemented by other crops when we had them. We'd trim their horns, spray them with medication to deter worms and biting flies, and let them go until they ate 2/3 of the foliage and then we'd load them up and move them again. 

Most of the farms in my area operated in a similar manner on both accounts. I had no experience hog farming for there were none in my area. Generally they do it out in the middle of nowhere because the urea hogs produce from their rich and fattening diet STINKS. I visited a huge one out near Vegas after I became an environmental engineer that had ammonia concentrations in the tousands of mg/L. They were fed buffet scraps from the casinos.

Author: @firestarsparkleaj8182
Content:
Me personally, I'm a vegetarian, I believe people shouldn't eat meat for my own personal reasons. 

Reasons why i believe people shouldn't eat meat: 

#1: Overconsumption of meat
The vast majority of people, especially in countries like over here in the US overindulge in the consumption of meat. This is a big  issue bc a lot of these animals in large-scale meat farms suffer immensely. The more meat that people eat, the worse it gets for the animals that are born year after year into these horrible conditions. It would be way nicer if people bought humane meat (pasture-raised, or organic meat) but they most likely won't bc they believe it's more expensive when in  reality, they just don't want to change their habits, so they continue to eat excessive amounts of factory farmed meat, which leads them to not being able to afford to buy from better sources. It's the same vicious cycle. 

#2: Respect for life 
People tend to forget that the meat that is on their plates, was once an animal that had a life, a life that meant something and had value. Since people love other animals (wild animals like elephants and lions, pets like cats and dogs) they have way more empathy for them, but they tend to have little to no empathy on what goes with farm animals in the meat industry as long as the food gets on their plates. This also leads to overconsumption of meat and is a waste of animals lives. 

#3 Animals have personalities
 Have you ever seen a happy cow, chicken pig, goat, sheep, or turkey? Just like cats and dogs, farm animals have the ability to be loving companions, they show affection and have lively personalities when their happy. When these animals aren't raised in these factory farms they're able to exhibit natural behaviors that they would show in more humane farms. 

#4 Their very smart
Farm animals are far more intelligent than people give them credit for. They have emotions, problem solving abilities, and social structures. For example, cows can recognize faces and remember people who treat them kindly or crulley. Can learn to solve simple puzzles and even open gates. They can even learn their names and respond when being called. 

And lastly #5
Connection to nature
When we recognize animals as fellow being with their own place in the world, we foster a deeper respect for nature and our role within it. It's a beautiful thing bc ever since becoming a vegetarian, I've grown to appreciate the animals and nature more. 
That being said, I believe animals are here with us, not soley for us.

Author: @INeyxI
Content:
I'm sure the comments here are going to be totally respectful and fair when it comes to the meat industry and our consumption.

My Thoughts:

I love meat. I eat a lot of it, probably too much. I barely eat vegetables, and honestly, I don’t even touch fruits. Pretty much every meal I have includes some kind of meat (though I’ve been trying to cut back... not very successfully).

That said, I’d say I’m pretty healthy and sporty. I try to offset my carbon footprint by cycling, taking public transport, and using green energy when I can. 
Funny enough, a lot of people assume I’m vegan based on my lifestyle, which always leads to some awkward conversations when I have to admit I’m basically a carnivore.

I prefer white meat (chicken) over red meat, I don’t like fish, and I’d love to try insect-based alternatives if they became a real option. I also cook most of my own meals.

But even as someone who loves meat, I realized years ago that the way we treat animals, the way meat is priced, and how the industry runs is just messed up, morally, environmentally, and even from a health perspective. 

It needs to change. Making meat more ethical and sustainable will probably make it more expensive( at first), but meat should never be a throwaway product. Honestly, no food should.

I try to make the best choices when I can, voting with my wallet and Voice. 
But let’s be real: the more ethical choices aren’t always affordable as long as the cheap and unnecessary cruel side of the industry exists (and is even subsidized), you can’t really blame people for buying what they can afford.
 
At the same time, as meat eaters, we shouldn’t freak out when the industry gets criticised, it deserves to be criticized. Fixing it benefits everyone.

On the other side, it doesn’t help when some militant vegans act like meat eaters are evil, animal-hating planet destroyers.

Life’s complicated. People’s situations, needs, and opinions are complicated. 

If you’re able to go full vegan and it works for you, that’s awesome, be proud of it!

But no one is perfectly "green" in every aspect of their life. And that’s okay, that's society we carry each other where others fail. 

At the end of the day, we should all be working towards making things better where we can. Even as someone who eats a LOT of meat, I’ll adapt to change. 
Meat isn’t disappearing anytime soon (and maybe it shouldn’t), but the way we produce it, needs to change.


🧀 
Also, as a cheese lover, I cannot wait for scientists to finally crack the code on synthetic milk or a real alternatives. Imagine being able to enjoy all the flavors of  real cheese without having to steal a calf’s 🐮 life juice🥛. That’ll be a great day for humanity and calfs.

Author: @silvano1988
Content:
I've always wanted to support Kurzgesagt, and now that I could afford it, it suddenly no longer feels like a voluntary community support - but like a multi-level subscription model aimed at pay-to-be-important.

It used to be that you could simply make a one-off donation because you valued the work. Today, on the other hand, you are categorised into ‘Trainee’, ‘Junior’, ‘Senior’ and other ranks - depending on how much you pay. This feels more like an exclusive membership than open support for educational content.

Precisely because this is about science communication and not a luxury club system, this development is disappointing. The original idea of jointly promoting knowledge seems to have given way to a financial tier model that favours people with bigger wallets.

It is understandable that sustainable funding is important - but it would be nice if there was still a way to support Kurzgesagt without this sense of ‘class society’.

Content:
The video misses a very important bit. If we accept the higher costs for more 'humane' farming, necessarily people will feel the higher costs and ask for higher wages. People don't want to lose their standard of life/purchasing power, as they shouldn't. This is kind of mentioned in the video. However, if we change farming practices and wages increase, then necessarily profits will fall; not only for farmers, but for all producers. This will certainly trigger reactionary protests from capitalists that tend to control most of political power. So, it is not a clear cut thing about just accepting higher costs for better treated animals. There is a lot of political economy behind it.

I'm of the opinion that this should be done. However, not at the cost of workers, but producers/capitalists. This is a tough political project though.

Content:
As a middleclass brazilian, I can say that food is not the cheapest it has ever been around here. Also, I think that most of the population of the world does not share the lucky of europeans and Americans to pay "the lowest ever" on food. 

Just to be clear, I do think that animal torture has to stop, but at the same time, if space is the best thing you could do to a animal, to a farmer, this is a upfront cost. It will be repaid as the meat sells, but, lets say, to give 30% more space to your animals, you will probably need to reform the building where they are imprisoned right now, to make all cells 30% bigger. Probably 30% of your animals would no longer have a place to stay after that, if you keep the same number of cells and animals per cell, so you would need to buy a new prison, probably at least 30% the size of the first one, to put the animals remaining. 

Farmers often work with not much working capital, so they can pay their expenses and get their profit, but for a new building, they will have to get access to a credit program. In brazil, that's not hard for a big farmer, because they are an elite group and have a lot of representation in the government, but is more work for zero profit, thinking that the values discussed in the video are just to cover the costs of giving the animals better lives and keeping the profit the same. 

So, I have not done any research on the topic besides my daily life, but it doesn't sound so simple like "raise the price by 3 cents". 

Great video anyway, just don't feel like it represents my reality.

Author: @geraar88
Content:
The confusing labels are the main reason I've never really bothered paying more for "ethical" products. Thanks to your video, I've checked the situation in Belgium for eggs:
- torture eggs: Did not find in store, but is apparently still used as ingredient for other products. It would be nice if there was a label to show if these eggs were not used in products.
- barn eggs: ~€0.20/egg (9 chickens per m2 in a barn, 1/3 of space is covered with hay, a minimum daylight, beak clipping allowed)
- free range: ~€0.33/egg 65% increase (4m2 outdoor space per chicken, unlimited access during the day, has to be partially plants)
- bio eggs: ~€0.40/egg double the cost (4m2 outdoor space, 6 chickens/m2 indoor space, no beak clipping, fed with biological grains)

I did not realize the labels were actually relatively decent if they are enforced well. I will reconsider buying eggs with a better label

Author: @lorenzobaldini5921
Content:
I don’t want to sound like a whataboutist, but what about land usage? Of course, we must treat animals better, but we have already exceeded the usable land. In fact, every year we consume more resources than the Earth can regenerate (as shown by the Overshoot Day), and a large part of agricultural land is used to grow crops for livestock rather than for direct human consumption. So, I think prices would rise due to lower supply. Maybe, with some anti-torture laws, we could achieve this goal and, as a result, reduce meat consumption—replacing it with more sustainable protein sources, such as mussels, edible insects, or other alternatives—which would also improve human health.

After all, meat has always been a premium product, not a cheap one. In medieval times, for example, it was much more expensive and mostly reserved for wealthy households. Its current affordability is more an anomaly of modern industrial farming than a historical norm.

There will be a difference in taste though because of the way the meat is handled. Something about the blood as I recall. But it is not necessarily bad. Although that means you can't get pork. 

It isn't cheap though. Because the demand for these products is low - since they cater typically to Jewish people keeping kosher - and the kosher certification has a price as well.

But if more people buy, it will drive the price down.

Author: @ZeroesOnes
Content: Even where labelling is accurate its not always representative of the animals conditions. Take for example the scandal involving free range poultry. Meat from chickens was labelled as free range, because the animals were freely able to access the outdoors, they were barn reared and the doors were opened daily and the animals had free access but the farmer added a contraption that simulated rain over the door to their housing. Chickens won't tend to go out in the rain so they never left the barn, which meant the chickens were being forcibly kept indoors despite being allowed access to the outdoors. The issue was barely reported on and few people were aware that was happening. I think it was regulated against following the discovery but its a sign of how complicated the labelling issue can be.

Author: @acccardone7679
Content:
I grew up on a farm, with friends who farmed, amoungst a farming community. I became a vegetarian because of what I saw and learned. 

Of course, philosophically, I would prefer the population to become vegetarians. However, I don’t bury my head in the sand. I live in the real world. 

Given this, at least 1/2 of what you are saying SOUNDS like how a better world should be. But, reality doesn’t work by our ideals. 

Did you know that mother pigs can’t tell that they have laid down on their babies until it is too late? Without the nursing cages, only about 3-5 of a litter of 24 piglets will survive to 1 month of age because their mothers will accidentally lay down on them. Baby piglets weigh in at only a few ounces. Adult pigs weigh 500-800 pounds. Don’t get me wrong, though. Pigs are EXTREMELY smart! They also nurture their young. But we’ve bred some nurturing out of them in exchange for size. Plus, having you ever stepped on something the size of a pea, or found a squished spider in your bed? That is the comparison for an adult pigs. Did you feel the pea sized spider when you squished it? Are you sure YOU squished it?

For chickens, all chickens will kill off the weakest chickens until there isn’t an overcrowding issue. Thus, you are correct about chickens needing space. 

As far as free ranging all types of chickens (having chickens in “pastures with grass and bugs and all), sadly that’s not realistic. Egg laying chickens definitely do best in a free range situation. They are very smart animals. Otoh, meat chickens are not as smart as your average fly. We’ve bred all the smarts out of them. (Same with domestic turkeys.) They will literally drown by looking up in a light rain. In addition, they are not smart enough to identify water or food unless it is in the proper serving containers. (My brother-in-law worked on a commercial poultry farm for about a decade. I no longer have a big problem with people eating meat chickens or poultry since that time. Especially after I tried to care for a meat chicken…)


One year I took in a rescue meat chicken for a friend. She was not yet fully grown, so she shouldn’t have had trouble adjusting to a new life. After two months she had irrevocably earned the name Stupid. She never did adjust to anything…

All my other rescue chickens, were of laying hen stock. They were smart. They knew their names and came when called. They knew where  I put out the chicken feed and all the places where I had water bowls for them. I also had a safe chicken house they could retreat to when they wanted. I often found them there on cold mornings, and they were usually there when they napped on rainy days.

When I got Stupid, I put her in the safe house. This house was raised about 3’ off the ground, and had perches, in addition to chicken feed and water. After about a month I opened the door to allow Stupid to join the other chickens who were free to wander wherever they wanted. Stupid never figured out, nor showed any curiosity about using the 2’x3’ door to the world. 

Stupid couldn’t conceptualize water being in any of my water containers except one that was of a commercial chicken farm style. Nor could she figure out that anything was food that wasn’t in a commercial chicken farm style feed container. I spent over 6 months trying to teach her that food and water weren’t dependent on being in the proper trays.  As an animal trainer I have never been faced with an animal that couldn’t understand food or water. But Stupid was a learning experience for me. She would try to eat or drink from the containers she expected food or water in, even when they were empty; and when I swapped out the containers with different ones with food or water, mid peck, she just stopped trying to eat or drink instead of checking out the new container in the same spot. I could shove her face into the food or water, but if it wasn’t in the proper container she couldn’t comprehend and would let it fall from her beak! I tried everything I could think of but she couldn’t comprehend anything that wasn’t as she leaned when she hatched. Even having the other chickens eating and showing her the other containers had something in them that made other chickens very happy or excited had no effect on her. 

In the end, about 9 months after she came to me, we had a day where the weather was 5 degrees F warmer than normal. I had just filled the food and water trays before heading to work. I put Stupid next to all those food and water trays, as I did every time I filled them. Sadly, when I got home from work, Stupid had passed, exactly where I had left her. All the water trays were full except for the one that was of the commercial style. That container held about half a gallon. I guess she drank the entire thing dry. It held a good twice what all the chickens, together, would have drunk. I guess her bulk contributed to her inability to cool down. It was a sad thing, but she didn’t appear to have suffered, as she never even bothered to move around. (Yes, she could still walk, as I was regularly making her move around.)

I’m not going to go into any further examples, but not all that farmers do is as bad as it may seem. Otoh, not all that farmers do is as simple as they claim, either. One really needs to learn about each situation before judging. 🤷‍♀️

Author: @mikalkrall
Content: On the whole, I completely agree with this message, but there's a considerable problem that's ignored here... wages. While it may seem like a great idea to simply spend as much on food as people did in the 1980s, for much of the US at any rate, that's going to be impossible. Real wages haven't grown in decades, while costs of goods, services, and housing increase yearly. Asking regular people to make changes is placing the onus and blame on those with the least control of the situation. Changes need to happen systemically for it to make any difference. That means passing laws that force companies to provide better conditions for animals, as well as laws that increase real wages for all. Our inability to provide living wages forces people to buy cheaper products, which forces companies to produce things more cheaply, and so on. There's a reason the $5 Costco chickens continue to sell out, regardless of news and/or rumors about their living conditions.

Author: @jamesmayfield6715
Content:
There were several comments in the video about percentages of animals kept in certain ways that don't really take into account the vast differences in practices across the globe. For example, Australia is only a relatively small country, but dairy cows here almost universally live outdoor lives, far, far better than what was described in the video. (Source: I have worked on multiple dairy farms in Australia.)
Similarly, I think it is far too simplistic to say "if it's not labelled it's torture". If I go to the butcher in Australia most meat isn't labelled, because it isn't packaged. That doesn't mean it's farmed in "torture" style farms. I have family members who run farms and I've seen the practices from end to end.

None of that is to say the underlying point of the video - we can through our consumer choices make things better for the animals we keep for food - is in any way incorrect, just a warning about global generalisations.

Consumers can do a little, but most won't, especially when they can see cheaper meat on the same shelf.  We are not gonna solve this problem with individual consumers biting the bullet, especially while labelling is still a complete wilderness.

Regulation is gonna be needed and that will need to be complimented with tariffs or other measures to manage importation of torture meat.

Actually, instead of trying to label what is good, it might be a good idea to set some kind of overall 3 teired labelling system like in the video.  Torture meat or unknown are labelled as torture meat.  Then meets domestic standards, then exceeds.  I think consumers would be quite responsive to a labelling system like that if they believed it could be trusted.

Content: The degree of tragedy we attribute to the suffering of animals should have nothing to do with the number of animals that suffer. Only each organism suffers. Content:
Even tho I work in agriculture, My comment won't make it through anyway, but I must say. While all this IS true, there's some underlaying. Small farmers with free range chickens or pigs or cows can produce only so much meat/milk/eggs. If you want to scale up, you need those cages!

Firstly, there're infectious diseases, that infect free range animals easily. You have to distribute vaccine properly, go and do that to free range animals! You have to deliver it individually to each animal, whereas in cages you can just... spray it. In the air. No risks involved. 2 hours of work for a single non-educated person versus 20 hours for a team of professionals. 

Then, you have feeding machines. You HAVE to feed all your chickens, pigs, cows EQUALLY. And how would you ensure it if they go free range? 

Finally, you have weather! Where do you keep 100 000 of free range chickens when it starts to rain heavily? Or to snow? Or if it's hot as hell? Cages allow to ensure the temperature is comfortable for animals. 

Prolly the tighter cages are definitely bad, but they're so much cheaper, I don't inow where are the numbers come from, I can show you my own numbers if you want

Caged break  movement  refers to is a form of direct action where activists destroy eggs from caged hens in stores to reduce profits for companies that support factory farming. People do this because they see caged hen farming as cruel—hens are often kept in small, overcrowded cages with little space to move. Activists believe that traditional methods of protest, like petitions or boycotts, aren’t enough to create change, so they take more extreme actions to disrupt the system directly.

Author: @kronusexodues7283
Content:
while I don't disagree with your video, there are two aspects to the animal industry that you completely ignored even though they are quite essential.
first is scale. The numbers you showed are really sketchy. Essentially you compared the price for torture meat and prison meat and then concluded how much more expensive prison meat would be, but it's not that simple. On the one hand, farms where animals live decent lives, are in many countries heavily subsidised. On the other, if we really switched from big totrute farms to lots of decent farms, this would come with a ton of logistic problems that you just skimmed over. How much more people would need to work in the industry if it was decentralised? how would the logistics of transport and slaughter change if the entire system changed? In Germany for example, a large portion of industry workers in slaughter houses and torture camps come from eastern Europe and barely speak German. This works fine in large industrial complexes, but would work a lot less fine if we switched to lots and lots of small decentralised decent farms. where should all the workers come from? where should all the land come from? How would it change the appearance of cities and rural areas? You pretend like you can just scale up the decent meat industry and scale down the torture industry and it's just not that simple.
The second is that you didn't even mention the real reason why raise animals like that. When you say it's only to make prices cheaper, that's honestly just outright wrong. A mayor mayor factor in and reason for this style of farming is disease control. A lot of really nasty deseases for humans originally come from animals. The idea being, that when you lock all the animals in a big concrete box and only expose humans in sterile security suits to them, you can prevent diseases to spread from animals to humans. At the moment we do have small farms, yes, but imagine that amount of animals was instead held in close proximity to humans. How much more likely would it be that a disesase jumps from an animal over to a human and starts the next pandemic? surely with more animal and human mixing, the chance of that happening would increase. How would the veterinary services control that amount of decentralised farms?

You can absolutely address both points and still come to the conclusion that we should strive for decent living conditions for animals. But outright ignoring those points all together is just plain awful.

Content:
I feel that meat has always been a part of human diet and necessary for maximising our development potential, but we don't need huge amounts of it. This part is clearly misinformation. 
People only say that pigs are smart, but they don't talk about their behavior. Pigs are raised on livestock farms unless there is a mud-stained pig ranch. 

Things you probably don't know 
1. Pigs are omnivores, which "like many wild animals" bully or eat their own offspring or the offspring of other pigs. 
2. Currently, domesticated pig females do not "take care" of their offspring. Berkshire Hogs, or YLD breeds, which are known for their good taste, tend to take care of their offspring more. I enjoyed watching the video. I thought about animal rights.
But you can't just make very "small" sacrifices like you did in Denmark.
Even now, organic (or eco-friendly) eggs, pork, and chicken are about 30% to 40% more expensive than the same products.
It's also difficult to place legal restrictions to address this. The only way is through absolute power.
And I don't like it, I just want to eat something cheap.

Author: @Danatar555
Content:
I'm a farmer, and I'm doing my best to make my animals' lives as good as possible, but even i have to admit that this problem is much more complicated than it seems and raising the prices is just one of the solutions.
 
One huge caveat is LAND. Say, you have 100 cows. A single cow needs 1.5-2 acres of land to roam and feed on. A 100 cows need 200 acres, probably more because you need to roam your herd as much as possible, otherwise that land will become useless in just 1 year. Cows eat a LOT of grass, they can weigh up to 600kg, this land will become barren very fast.

Second issue regarding pricing, competition. If you're a small farm with humane conditions, you have to compete against huge corporations who can pump out insane volumes of goods at superb prices. Consumers vote with their wallets, and while we would all love to go around spending just 2 dollars more to save animals from extreme cruelty, but this is a noticeable bump in price to absolute most of the customers. 

Third issue is profitability. If you're a small farm, let me tell you that there won't be some huge profit waiting for you in this business for all the time you've spent. Unless you ramp up the stock and scale up, of course.

So, here's my few tips to people who want to make a difference:
1) BUY LOCAL. Don't buy stuff from supermarkets, go to your butcher, ask them where they get their meat, go check out the farm. Take some time to learn about the food that will be on your table. 
2) Don't support major fast food corporations like McDonalds or Burger King, Vendy, etc. Their food is nasty.
3) Spread the word. Together, we can make a difference!

Content:
The topic of video is quite controversial as video itself. It might be cost a little more for more decent conditions to raise animals at farms, but consider this - larger spaces for animals demands a larger space for farms themself. For chickens that might be barely noticeable, but for any cattle bigger that would mean a double, or even a tripple increase in sizes of space, which is critical for European countries and other smaller nations, there cost of land is pretty high. That would lead to that ever-increasing demand for meat will force any larger meat industries to move somewhere else, in less densely populated areas - and thus, increasing costs for meat even higher, because of costs to transport.
Also, not so many people are so thoughtfull of the animals which they eat daily. They simply have different problems to think of, like paying ever growing bills or thinking about kids future, and they probably won't think about 'is it morally bad to support animal cruelty by buying meat from industrealised producer'. Content:

If i could flip a switch to have never had animal meat farming in our history, i would do so in a heartbeat, mostly because that would be easy. but sacrificing convenience, culinary mastery, cultural and social bonds through food and cooking is a tall order for any individual to stomach when the result of them doing so is a net zero change to the amount of animal suffering going on it wouldn't change a thing. Note that this is not an argument for why you should eat meat, simply a reason why doing so, in a western context is entirely unrelated to animal suffering in any way. though i would not blame you if you found the practice disgusting and wished to abstain on those grounds, or any other grounds of preference because on some level, by eating meat you may not bear any causal responsibility, you still deserve a portion of shared blame for engaging in an evil system.

Primarily though, I'm always disgusted by Kurzgesagt and their eternal insistence that individual action actually does anything. i find the way they allow for viewers to 'feel good' by implementing their useless measures in their daily lives instead of making hard political decisions and get out of their chairs and protest if they care enough, not just making useless decisions. (though getting your meat from better places is still better than nothing if not my much). protest through market forces is bullshit, the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house.
