Content:
The main argument here is and remains space.

It's nice to give animals 1500% more space or even more for freeroam care, but many developed countries have no free land which isn't protected nature or forest reserves or pre-drawn as XY zone of usage. You can't just build a farm in a zone classified and taxed as an economic or residence zone.

This leads to land being insanely expensive and often even if bought yearlong bureaucracy to change its classification.

Breaking it down to "give them more space" is false. To generate that space quickly you'd literally have to eat less meat since you only have mostly your current space.

Thus the realistic solution unless we invent instant-bureaucracy culling magic is literally to eat less and then you get the "envy" issue of... if you cull your consumption who says others do. As such you don't want to.

Author: @HulkTheSurgeon
Content:
As much as I love Kurzgesagt, I feel like the video drops the ball in the end here. Stating "you can change the industry by choosing to buy cruelty free meats" is a gross oversimplication, using the same logic of "You can reduce plastic waste by not using plastic bags." Modern companies arn't going to have a psychic link to every consumer, realize one person decided to not buy a product, andreduce production by a few units per person. It'd require a massive, organized pushback strike against such practices from a large chunk of the population, all done at the same time to make any company consider reorganizing practices. Even then, it could have the result of them highly upscaling their prices to offset losses or new infrastructure. 

I'm all for reducing animal cruelty, but feel like this oversimplifies things when in reality, it's a large scale issue that requires largescale problem solving. There's also the fact that paying more for food isn't really an option for some people. Two bags of groceries where I am is over 300 dollars, and I hardly even eat. The only realistic suggestion and practical suggestion I can see is Kurzgesagt's suggestion to push for legislation to ban such abhorrent practices.

Author: @rikuleinonen
Content:
I really do think we should stop fighting amongst ourselves regarding food. Because it's painfully obvious that the average person will not stop eating meat. This is for several reasons, but those are frankly not relevant -- all that matters is that it can't be done. So we should focus on what we can do instead, which is exactly what this video describes. Rather than fighting amongst ourselves and villifying each other for personal beliefs, what if we instead just take a good long look at the meat industry itself and do something about it, together? Because frankly, that's going to lead to a much bigger and more meaningful change in the amount of animal suffering, even at the global scale.

Another thing we have to do is acknowledge the real difference in price between torture meat and good meat. That is because it helps tremendously with finding vendors that are actually committed to animal welfare rather than simply capitalizing on the compassion of the consumers. A company that cares more about profit than animal welfare is almost certainly trying to trick the consumer in some way, shape or form -- it's an useful stereotype to go by.

Author: @Waladil-v5l
Content:
I think that what this video really reveals is how massive the profit gains are for the total meat process (some individual links in the chain may be unprofitable or barely profitable, but the chain in its entirety is very profitable). 

Providing 30% more space raises costs by ~15%. If we assume that space is gained simply by having less animals in a given area, that means production would drop by 25% (4 pigs per 3 square meters -> 3 pigs per 3 square meters means each individual pig goes from 0.75 to 1.0 square meters). 

So dropping production by 25% would mean raising prices by only 15%? And thats not considering extra costs to put in ventilation or lights or whatever. By this logic, it seems like less than 60% of the price of meat is the production cost. The remaining 40% is... Uh... Well, lets just call it "the capitalism tax."

Author: @MesonoxianMethuselah
Content:
People don't care about "animal" rights. They care about "VERTEBRATE" rights, and barely. When's the last time that an "animal rights activist" protested the killing or consumption of insects or crustaceans? Take the recommendation to eat bivalve molluscs near the end of the video because they don't have brains. You don't need a brain to be an animal, yet for some reason the rights of this animal are incumbent on the complexity of its nervous system.

If cockroaches, shrimp, and clams don't deserve rights, then it's not a binary question of "animal rights vs. animal cruelty," but rather a question of where to draw the line regarding which taxa/clades deserve rights. And there is barely any daylight between the positions of "all vertebrates deserve rights" and "only humans deserve rights."

I'll start listening to arguments in favor of "animal rights" when they address the issue of "invertebrate rights." Unless, of course, "animal rights" is actually really just about "vertebrate rights," but then "animal rights" activists would have to be honest about how they don't care about the vast majority of animals.

One issue is that in a country with an unstable economy, an increase of 0.85 EUR can have a significant impact on lower-income populations. This could mean going from eating rice, eggs, and beef to just rice and eggs due to rising costs.

For example, in Brazil, an egg costs approximately 1 BRL, or about 0.15 EUR.

A 0.05 EUR increase per egg represents a price hike of over 30%.

For a full carton of eggs (12 units), this would amount to an additional 0.6 EUR, or 4 BRL. Given that a carton typically costs around 20 BRL, this new price for a whole box of eggs is about 1.4% of the minimum wage.

Author: @edytaurbanska3706
Content: This video does not bring anything new, it is just repetitive formulas that are abundant on the internet. For example, releasing pigs to pasture is practically impossible in a large part of Poland due to ASF spread by wild boars. Pigs must be locked up, before entering the place where they are kept, you must disinfect your shoes, change into clothes that are only used for contact with pigs. Only designated persons are authorized to enter, EVERY entry by an outsider must be recorded in the documents. Pigs cannot have contact with any other animals, because they can transmit diseases. The place where pigs are kept must not only be closed, but the building must be surrounded on all sides by a double fence. Without meeting these conditions, you cannot sell the raised pigs. Compliance with these regulations is checked, depending on the danger zone, from 2 to 4 times a year. Cages for mother pigs that are so demonized are there so that the mother pig does not step on or sometimes attack her children, which often happens if it is her first litter of piglets. The difference in size between the mother and the child is huge. Piglets are born at a size of 1.5 kg (3.3 lbs) and their mother is 300 kg (660 lbs). It is important to remember that pigs have hooves, so stepping on a piglet causes great damage and often leads to its death. On our farm we do not use cages for mother pigs, but sometimes this results in situations where out of 13 piglets born, 3 survive and the rest are trampled by the mother when they try to drink milk from her.

Author: @andersmadsen4487
Content:
@Kurzgesagt
How in the world can you hate on organic foods and call their measures stupid?!
While animals may not care too much about their fodder being organic (although they should since organic products are richer in healthy and tasty phytochemicals) or not, organic products are better in a number of other ways, since they exclude the use of pesticides.
1. Pesticides kill different "unwanted" organisms like fungi and bugs. While we don't like our crops (whether being for human food or animal fodder) to grow molden or eaten by bugs, it is also a bad idea to just kill everything but your one crop, because we also stand in a biodiversity crisis and for example are loosing a lot of important pollinators (not so much the honey bee as other wild type bees and bugs, but also that), causing also the floral diversity to diminish and so on.
2. Pesticides ends up in our drinking water and poisons ourselves too. Just a little bit, but enough to have an impact on our overall health and reproductivity via the cocktail effect (the nasty synergy that happens within our bodies when different toxic chemicals are acting in concert on our biology).
3. When you eat animals that have eaten pesticides you get them in an upconcentrated form - especially those that are hydrophobic since they cannot readily be excreted via the urine ... and those are for the same reason also the worst ones for you.

I don't remember the sources from which I have picked all this up and I unfortunately don't have the time to find them (or others that back these claims), but please let me know if you could have an opening for a remote job (or even just an internship that might lead to employment) with you guys at Kurzgesagt. I am a fan and I love science and hold a Masters degree and two Bachelors degrees within science (and a minor in math... and know my way around Python and Pandas programming).

Author: @sausageskin
Content:
We do a lot of terrible things to other humans, but it all pales in comparison to what we do to animals. Let’s consider the scale. In the First and Second World Wars, we killed about 100 million people over roughly 10 years, which means about 10 million humans per year.

Now, if we look only at land animals (chickens, pigs, cows, sheep, etc.), we kill about 100 billion (with a B!) every year. That means the rate at which we are currently killing land animals is ten thousand times greater than the rate at which we were killing each other during the bloodiest wars in history.

And what's truly bizarre? We just ignore this fact. Given the sheer scale of suffering we are inflicting, this should be the number one issue on everyone's mind, by far. Thank you, Kurzgesagt for spreading the awareness.

Author: @bobdenalio2074
Content:
I for one am Getting real sick of these European anti-human propaganda pieces. 

These kinds of videos always seem to follow a predictable trajectory—start with a reasonable concern (animal welfare), then subtly push for lifestyle changes that conveniently align with broader agendas that always seem to involve higher costs, personal sacrifice, and less freedom for the average person.

The "just pay more" argument is incredibly detached from reality for most people. It's easy for a content creator in a European bubble to say, “Just pay 50% more,” when many families are already struggling with inflation and the rising cost of living. The idea that food has gotten "too cheap" and we should happily pay more is tone-deaf at best and is ideological at worst.

And the "just eat less meat" rhetoric? Yeah, that’s been part of the slow creep toward the “eat the bugs” push. It starts with “cut back for the animals,” then it’s “cut back for the planet,” then “cut back for equity,” and suddenly, Bill Gates is investing in cricket farms while steak is reserved for the elite.

Of course, no one is advocating for cruelty to animals, but it's always interesting how these videos never present realistic middle-ground solutions. For example:

Why not promote regenerative farming? It improves soil health and allows animals to live in natural conditions.

Why not incentivize small farms instead of propping up industrial mega-farms that are the real source of factory-farming horrors?

Why does the burden always fall on the consumer? Why not demand better regulations instead of just saying "pay more"?


At the end of the day, these narratives always seem to demand sacrifice from normal people while the wealthy continue business as usual. You don’t see the Davos crowd switching to oat milk and cricket burgers, do you?

It’s always good to watch for the bigger picture behind messages like this—especially when they start normalizing rationing and acting like it's a moral obligation to accept higher costs and lower quality of life.

Don't buy it. Fight the machine.

Hey Guys! I think a big part you‘re missing here is pest control. These systems weren’t only built like this for profits, but also for making sure pests from wild animals don‘t infect the domesticated animals and become a danger to humans when consumed. Thats also a big part in why the animals in industrial farms for meat are not getting any or a lot access to pasture to move freely. It is to reduce contact to wild animals as much as possible. Of course due to the little space the animals are crowded in, infections can spread and antibiotics are needed to keep them consumable. Still, if a bigger pest, dangerous to humans would break out, all the animals in the farm of the outbreak are killed and a spread of the pest to other farms is prevented. Of course this is morally extremely bad, but it is a valid reason economicly for farmers and gouvernments. If the animals of the infected farm could possibly have contact to wild animals, stopping a spread of a pest would be nearly impossible. 

I absolutely love your videos and would love to get an answer to this topic ☺️❤

Author: @waveydavey82
Content:
Good video, but I think it may be slightly misleading for some because the video talks about the price increases in terms of per serving instead of per pound (or kilo.) But we don't tend to think in these terms naturally. We aren't buying individual servings at the grocery store, we're buying by weight typically. The total cost of the package at the register is what means the most to us. 

For instance, if the 10 lb. bag of tortured chicken meat I buy costs me $7.50, and it would cost almost a dollar per serving more to give the chicken a better life, that 10 lb. bag is going to cost me about double or more. 

Servings are additionally misleading because, while we may standardize what we consider a serving, an actual real world serving is going to be different for each person. I'm 6 ft 160 lbs with about 15% body fat and have a decently active lifestyle. I'll eat 2-3 chicken thighs in one sitting, along with plenty of vegetables. At my literal poverty wages, I just can't afford to spend $15+ for 10 lbs of chicken. 

Of course, none of this changes the reality of  how terrible most "farm" animals' lives are, so the basic point of the video remains perfectly valid. But I think by putting it in terms of per serving rather than by weight, people will have a skewed idea of the real savings at the register. 

And then there is the further reality that it is quite simply naïve and unrealistic to think that meat producers would pass anywhere near 100% of those cost savings on to the end consumer. The markups on even slightly more ethical treatment are insane! 

I've been trying to significantly reduce my meat consumption, the idea being that if I can't afford the ethical meat, I can at least reduce the extent to which I'm part of the problem. That's all well and good, but it's difficult for me because my body is highly sensitive to carbs, and there are no inexpensive plant based proteins that don't also come with a hefty dose of carbs. And I'm not going to give myself diabetes just so that I can abstain from participating in a torture regime that will not be reduced one iota by my boycott. 

So yeah, it's a hard problem. I'm not trying to say we just shouldn't care. And while my political views tend to skew libertarian, given that we are talking about living animals, I wonder if the only workable solution is to legislate the treatment of animals and impose a cap on profit margins. I think that's a pretty abhorrent idea when applied to nonliving materials, but in the case of the quality of actual lives I think it makes sense. Of course, the best solution is to raise your own animals, which is what I'm working towards. But obviously that is not entirely practical or even feasible for many if not most of us. Which is why I begrudgingly recognize that it's likely the case that the only thing that will solve this problem is government intervention; either directly applied to the treatment of animals and the pricing of their meat/eggs/milk, or applied towards increasing the income and wealth of poor and middle class people.

Author: @shuntakeda9559
Content:
The problem is that the farmers don't dictate the price of meat, it's the slaughter houses that package the meat.  If the slaughterhouses are used to buying cattle at $4.00 and someone presented them with a free range cattle of $5.00, who in their right mind is going to pay more for the same quality beef.

Ranchers will try to take their cattle to custom slaughter houses and get their product packaged and try to sell it in retail, but now they're competing against large multi-billion dollar corporations.  Even if they do the same $4.00 cattle, your end pricing is going to be around $0.20 higher than the big corporations.  They're already at a disadvantage at this point.

So the ranchers that do get their brand and product out, they now have to sell it to distributors and grocery stores that end up marking up anywhere from 20-1000%.  When they see niche product like this, they will mark it up significantly higher due to spoilage.

Author: @basilmemories
Content:
In California, the ordinance is that chickens have to be able to spread their wings and turn around, which is sort of a bare minimum, to be honest. However chicken prices have gone from where you could get a whole chicken for 5$ in 2010, to the average cost of a whole bird being 12-18$ today in 2025. However there's other factors to consider. first is that we're talking a 15 year period and in that period, there have been even further consolidation and collusion of meat corporations, often squeezing out and making life nearly impossible for independent farmers. 

secondly, if wages didn't remain stagnant with costs (or if rent had matched the stagnation of wages instead of skyrocketing, or if public assistance had gone up instead of staying stagnant or even being CUT...), and people had the proper cost of living increase that they had 15 or even 30 years ago, this would be more than manageable to afford. 

Thirdly, a lot of the price gouging for no real benefit really started in 2020 and hasn't let up since and we seem to be... ultimately fine with that for some reason.

To really offset these potential costs, the answer isn't going to be "just eat less of this!" people are ALREADY eating less of what's healthy of them, lining their bellies with little more than space-fillers so that they don't feel the gnawing pangs of hunger. What we need is an expanded program where people can get more funding to buy what they need, and funding to local farms (and less to large corporations) to bring more ethical, healthy foods to a place where people can easily and affordably get them. That means those places need to be accessible by public transit, and that public transit needs to be accessible to someone bringing groceries home. It means those places being open after the normal working day (a lot of farmer's markets close at 1pm). it means that things like food stamps need to cover HOT meals, not just cold food or raw ingredients that an already-exhausted parent has to cook after a full day of work. 

In short, this situation, like nearly every broad social problem, is a matter of many connecting factors and equally many steps needed to solve it. However that doesn't mean we should avoid doing it, it means we also solve some other problems along the way as we do it.

Author: @zapticuno3930
Content:
I wish people raising their own animals were a viable suggestion to this problem- unfortunately even for eggs, chickens are NOT the way to save money. Besides people not always having the space or time to care for these animals properly, the cost just to set things up, obtain the animals, and raise them until you get their return is costs that aren't really good to justify raising just for saving money. What you **do** get out of it is convenience in having that meat or eggs, ease of mind that you know exactly how the animals were raised and what they ate, and more often than not some of the best meat and eggs you've ever had. As someone who has raised a couple animals (a steer and a chicken) for meat and had a plethora of fresh eggs from neighbors, that is very true.

But, also, when it comes to the meat end of things, it's also VERY hard to send that animal off to be butchered- or even do the act yourself. In the end I've been able to eat the meat just fine, even get possessive over it because that was an animal I cared about, but besides the costs and effort of raising the animal, if you get attached it may become hard to kill that animal or eat their meat. That is another problem with raising animals. Eggs are of course much easier- you just pick up eggs the chickens lay- but if you also want meat, that can be difficult to bring yourself to do.

If you have the time, money, space, raising even just chickens for their eggs is a lovely idea. They're relatively the easiest farm animal to care for. If you can handle even the butchering, whether sending them off or doing it yourself, that's even better. As the video said, I'd recommend heavy bodied breeds not bred for specifically meat- go for dual purpose breeds, not your meat birds like broilers and Cornish crosses. Meat birds are a ticking time bomb of suffering even if you raise them in the mist ideal conditions, and you HAVE to butcher them when they are of age. Plus, with their health problems and how they're bred for by hatcheries, you can't breed them to get your own. You gotta buy new birds every time. Slower growing breeds can survive much better on their own, you can butcher when you're ready, and at least according to some even have better tasting meat. I'd think so. Also, they come in much more colorful varieties, and if you're the sort of person who likes pretty birds, you have nice eye candy while they're kicking around, and maybe you can use their feathers to make pretty crafts :3

Again such an option isn't for everyone, but god I wish it was. I know hatcheries aren't the best either, but if you can get your own flock going, especially if you live in an area that allows roosters and so you can breed your own birds, then you don't need to go to hatcheries. If anything, see if you can buy from a local hatchery you can go to in person, so you can see how the birds are kept.

Apologies for the ramble, but as one of the many who loves meat and animals, felt like sharing my piece in the matter with my experience.

Content: The luxury markup is a great example of a market failure. If there was a significant market for compassionate meat, more producers would fill that need and bring prices down. Hence, the market remains niche, consumer habits don't change and the luxury markup remains. Another angle of looking at this is that the luxury markup is a way of monopoly powers protecting their market share. Ironically, keeping prices high drives out the competition.

Humans are animals. Animals survive by harming /some/ other living thing, to one degree or another.
That said, as sapient beings, we are obliged to make our surviving and thriving as harmless as possible.
We owe it to our food to not make its life hell.
Good farming practices can reduce suffering and even improve the quality of our food simultaneously.   
Many meat alternatives come with a hidden cost to our health and environment while merely changing who suffers.
Ethical farming practices and scientific advances will get us where we need to go. It's just a question of how and when.

Author: @digydigdogdead
Content:
This is a very frustrating video for me.

I love seeing my favourite educational channel make a video to highlight and expose damn-near *everybody's* cognitive dissonance on this subject. Basically everybody believes that these practices are wrong, and yet almost nobody is willing to make changes to go against them.

However, if you have to affix every suggestion you make with "this would still be a bad prison, but it would be a slightly less worse bad prison", does that not make you feel awful for *not* making the anti-meat video? At what point do you think, "maybe we *should* be making the anti-meat video"?

The changes proposed here would reduce animal suffering, absolutely, but trivially. The chickens and cows would still be allowed a *fraction* of their usual range, would still go through the trauma of an abattoir, and would still be killed a long time before the years they should've had.

This doesn't cover the very many other massive problems with animal husbandry. These changes would still allow the animal agriculture industry to be one of the (if not *the*) leading contributor towards climate change. These changes would still create crowded conditions of homogenous animals that are the leading root cause of pandemics.

Consider making the anti-meat video

Author: @the8u9
Content:
There was a time when this channel used to say smart things, but these days, I swear it's become so intellectually dishonest. Just because production has allowed for the raw resources to become the cheapest its ever been by maximizing efficiency, it doesn't mean that there isn't a reason why things are the way they are. The production chains have gotten longer and a 15% increase to the production cost of the raw material is literally that, a 15% increase to the final price as well. Just because 1 additional dollar SOUNDS small doesn't mean it isn't proportionally a 100% increase to the price for chicken.

Showing us the chicken breast price from the farm to be $3.20 by the end has nothing to do with how this ends up meaning like $10 more by the time it is handed to us in a bucket at a KFC. I know that the video disclaimed that it doesn't want to attack farmers, but every single improvement listed on the video would only affect the farmers and a video like this WILL only hurt the farmers as well. The real problem here is the increase in price caused at every stop of the chain of production and the corporation at the end of it selling the food to us.

Content:
The recent increase in egg prices caused by the bird flu is evidence that people are willing to pay more for eggs. In this case, that willingness is simply desire: to keep eating eggs because they’re a part of our regular diet.

That’s what we do: We creatures of habit are willing to pay extra for convenience. We will generally suffer the convenience fee if the trade off is truly convenient—even if the cost is absurd.

But what’s truly absurd is that the increased costs we would suffer by reducing suffering for the animals we enjoy eating are not unreasonable. They are warranted—morally justifiable, even.

Being indifferent to suffering is convenient. I wonder how many of us are willing to pay extra to do what is morally righteous. I wonder how many of us would forego eating meat temporarily if it meant sending a message that we consumers are concerned about ethical consumption.

Then again, typing this message was inconvenient. It was time consuming and tedious. I’m sure reading it was just as tiring! The extent of my activism was slapping my thumbs on my phone screen—and that is as far as I am willing to inconvenience myself.

Content: My family has been purchasing entire butches animals from a local ranch since I was little. The reason has nothing to do with the quality of life for the animal or sustainability, for us it's a fringe benefit. It's all about cost. The ranch and butcher take a way bigger cut than selling to a grocery, and we get a huge variety of cuts and a ton of ground meat. It works out to be way cheaper than grocery stores meat too. The meat is flash frozen once the butcher is done with it, and we keep it in a deep freeze. The ranch the animals come from is absolutely beautiful, the animals live great even if not perfect lives, and most importantly the meat we eat is legitimately cheaper than the grocery store. It works out to be about the same price as ground meat per lbs, including all the steaks, roasts, and stew meat. That said an entire cow can cost $3500+ and you need the freezer space to keep it. Split up between family and friends, it's actually not that bad. I would highly recommend anyone with the means to invest in a year's supply of meat, look into local ranchs. Our ranch sells cows, pigs, and chickens. The ranch I buy from sells cows and pigs by the 1/4 1/2 and whole (fully butchered unless requested otherwise). The chickens are only sold whole and are only prepared as full birds the way you would get a frozen whole chicken at the grocery store.

Author: @DanG-xl5op
Content:
I'm a bit disappointed in Kurzgesagt on this video. As someone who spent time on farms and studied Animal Sciences at University, their numbers seem to be off. At a glance, it looks like the cost of raising the animal in different conditions is relatively inexpensive, which is likely true. It bothers me they don't mention terms like "Mortality" and "Morbidity". It doesn't seem to me, the increase in Morbidity (aka rate of animal loss) is calculated in these figures when raising animals in these other farming techinques, let alone how Morbidity is factured in. When videos are regularly 20-30min, i find it concerning they spent so little time on this one and left out 2 basic terms that every Animal Science college freshman learns. This could have been a better discussion. 

Furthermore, i don't know what dairy farms you visited or talked to, but they do not sound like most mainstream dairy operations. Dairy cow stress is one of the easiest to study objectively. The main stress hormone (cortisol) blocks the receptors for oxytocin; aka a stressed dairy cow is a poor producing dairy cow. They are milked 2x (minimum/day during peak lactation), so that is a minimum of 2x/day a dairy farmer is made aware that a cow could be stressed. That would also assume they never look at their animals at all in between (spoiler, they do). I'd recommend reading up on works from Dr. Sapolsky (chronic stress and its effects), as well as reaching out to universities with very strong dairy programs (ex. Penn State) to be better acquainted with the subject matter.
Ultimately, I'm disappointed with how this was thrown together with cherry-picked data. This comes across to me as an opinion piece with very specific data used to push an opinion. This video could've been a good start into a deeper conversation about a complex topic that needs to be discussed and analyzed; why certain farming practices were adopted (the pros and cons), the cons of all the farming practices that were mentioned in this video (they do exist and it bothers me why they were left out), improvements that could be done, why they're not, the hurdles farmers have to overcome, corporate monoplies and the harm they're causing, regulations (how theyve improved and how they  eed to be better), and the genetics that have helped, hurt, and a better application of them moving forward

Author: @WORLDPEACE561
Content:
**Refutation of the Video's Analysis on Food Prices**

**1. Then vs. Now: Real Purchasing Power Has Declined**

- **1987 Comparison:**  
  In the United States during 1987, a monthly expenditure of about \$88 on chicken, pork, beef, eggs, and dairy would buy significantly more than it does today. For instance, consumers could purchase approximately 10 kg of chicken at \$1.50 per kg, 5 kg of pork at \$2 per kg, 5 kg of beef at \$2.50 per kg, 3 dozen eggs for around \$0.80, and 15 liters of milk at \$0.60 per liter. This \$88 represented roughly 4–4.5% of a typical monthly salary of \$2,000–\$2,500.

- **Today’s Reality:**  
  Today, \$88 now constitutes only about 1.8–2.2% of a monthly salary in the \$4,000–\$5,000 range. However, the quantities purchased have dropped dramatically:
  - **Chicken:** Only about 4–5 kg can be bought at \$4–\$5 per kg.
  - **Pork:** Around 2–3 kg at \$6–\$7 per kg.
  - **Beef:** Roughly 2 kg at \$8–\$10 per kg.
  - **Eggs:** 1–2 dozen for \$3–\$4.
  - **Milk:** 5–10 liters at \$1–\$1.20 per liter.

- **Adjustment for Inflation:**  
  Even after adjusting for inflation (approximately 130% in the US and 80–100% in Germany), prices for these items have risen much faster than wages. For example:
  - Chicken prices have increased by 150–233%.
  - Beef by 200–300%.
  - Eggs by 200–400%.
  
  This means that, in real terms, consumers today get significantly less for their money compared to the 1980s.

---

**2. The Impact of a 50% Price Increase Isn’t Negligible**

- **The Video's Claim:**  
  The video argues that increasing the cost of meat, eggs, and dairy by 50% would only add an extra \$43 per month (or 35 euros) to a consumer's food bill—implying this additional cost would barely be felt.

- **The Reality:**  
  If consumers already purchase less food for the same proportion of their income compared to the past, then a 50% price increase further reduces real purchasing power. In practical terms, an additional \$43 or 35 euros would mean even fewer quantities of food can be purchased, leaving families with a tighter budget than before.

- **Wage Growth vs. Price Growth:**  
  Since wages have not kept pace with the dramatic increases in food prices, the extra cost would impose a heavier burden on today's consumers than the video suggests.

---

**3. Broader Effects on Processed Foods**

- **Hidden Costs:**  
  The video narrowly focuses on primary products (meat, eggs, and dairy) while ignoring that these items are crucial inputs for processed foods like nuggets, pizzas, and ice creams.

- **Ripple Effect:**  
  In the U.S., if processed foods—which account for a significant share of the \$337 monthly food budget—experience even a 20% price increase due to higher input costs, the overall impact could raise the food bill by 20–30%. This means the actual increase in consumers' expenses would be much higher than the simple \$43 or 35 euros the video claims.

---

**Conclusion**

While the video uses certain base numbers to argue that food is "cheap" today and that a 50% price hike would be barely noticeable, a deeper analysis shows that:

- **Real purchasing power has declined.** Even though nominal salaries have increased, the real quantity of food you can buy with the same percentage of your income has fallen sharply.
- **The extra cost is significant.** For families already struggling with higher food prices, a 50% increase in basic animal products would further tighten budgets.
- **Processed foods would amplify the price impact.** Since many processed items rely on meat, eggs, and dairy, their prices would also rise, worsening the overall effect on household expenses.

In essence, the video's calculation oversimplifies a complex economic reality, and the claim that a 50% increase would be "not felt" is misleading. The data, when adjusted for inflation and wage growth, indicates that these items have indeed become more expensive in real terms, leaving consumers with less purchasing power than in previous decades.

Meat has definitely not gotten cheap recently. If anything, market trends show that meat price increases have far outpaced inflation. In comparisson, other foods have shown a less moderate increase in price. 

It is a classic example of how fake premium products drive the prices up. You get fake super-duper-bio-pasture-organic products which are more expensive, and the lower end of the market inevitably catches up, which leads the "premium" brands to raise prices again, making this a non-ending cycle.

The 50% increase in expenditure for animal raising also does not mean you only spend 50% more on meat. There is a ton of other products that use animal parts including sugar, cosmetics, medicine and clothing...even condoms and plastic use chemicals derived from animal sources. Now, while I don't advocate for animal cruelty, it's important to neither downplay the impact that animal products have in our budget. Author: @Maou3
Content:
I am glad to see this talked about. As per usual, this is the result of a classic market failure: information asymmetry. A consumer may be able to keep up to date on industry terminology and hushed information on brand practices on one of their foodstuffs, but to do so for all of them would require an unreasonable amount of time and effort. The producer has an asymmetric information advantage over the consumer, who, at point of transaction, cannot feasibly know which brands raise livestock ethically, so a race to the bottom among producers is guaranteed to occur by market pressure. There is a market demand for ethical practice, but a free market simply cannot service that demand.

Good thing the US has a president who respects her regulatory agencies and wants to enable those agencies to foster a competitive and healthy market.,.,.,.,.,.,...,,.,.,.,,.,.,.,.

Author: @xaiano794
Content:
I thought the best way to consider eating meat is from the animal's perspective - what if you were the animal?
Most vegans would claim it's a simple choice between dying and not dying, but that's a lie and it undermines most of their credibility.

The true argument is between not existing (since animals wouldn't be bred for meat if there was no demand) and existing with the inevitable outcome of being eaten later.

It becomes obvious that, provided that life was enjoyable, that you would choose living over not existing and so the argument becomes one of animal welfare standards, that they should be high enough that life, albeit an artificially short one, is worth living and that slaughtering is as painless as possible. Given that, it would be better to live and so eating meat is fine.

This would have the added benefit of decreasing meat consumption and improving meat quality whilst also improving profitability of family run farms, a win-win for all parties concerned. The only people losing out would be shareholders of mass factory farms, but as we all know, people are easily conned by propaganda campaigns of large industry players and I think that alone leads to people opposing animal welfare standards.

The biggest irony is that vegans themselves commonly stand in the way of improving animal welfare standards by insisting that the goal should be zero meat rather than simply reducing meat consumption.

Author: @mikerich32
Content:
Sadly, the problems that Americans face that prevent them from reducing their contribution to animal suffering is multifaceted and is due to  psychological, social, and monetary issues. 

Most Americans can't afford to make the changes necessary and/or don't want to give up anything. The ratio of living expenses to income is a big problem, especially lately. People want as much as possible as cheap as possible, which means not giving up animal products and not paying more. Along that point, a lot of people don't have the time to look into such issues nor have the time and mental energy to figure out how to make such changes. 

Also the marketing tactics of companies to put positive sounding labels on meat that make you feel better, but when you research what qualifies for having those labels, you'll see that they are intentionally misleading. On that note, you can't forget to mention the lobbying and propaganda that comes out of the animal agriculture industry. A lot of money is being spent to make sure people are not well-informed (and even intentionally misinformed) about what goes on in the animal agriculture industry and the effects of consuming, or not consuming, animal products has on our health and the health of the animals and the planet. 

And finally there are the social impacts of reducing the intake of animal products. There is a large counter culture in America that prevents people from making a change. Those who do make changes are mocked, ridiculed, and bashed for trying to make a positive change, even if they never get on a soap box about it. Those in that counter culture feel like they are being personally attacked just at the idea of others making a change, and this frustration comes out in the form of attacking others, and no one likes to feel attacked.

Author: @tsnevtbl
Content:
Mussels - the texture of nature’s fabric
Ethical obligations should not be based solely on cognitive ability or the capacity for pain but on the interconnectedness of all life forms.
Even if mussels do not experience pain, they may still be harmed in the broader ontological sense. Harm can be understood not only as the infliction of pain but also as the disruption of an organism’s natural state of being. In this framework, harming mussels might involve disrupting their ecological role—such as altering the balance of marine ecosystems by overharvesting them, thus indirectly harming other species that depend on them.

Author: @mal2ksc
Content:
I'm afraid there are associated costs that aren't being factored in, and can use the real life examples in California. We've had a couple rounds of bird flu that required culling entire flocks, but because of SEFS standards, we're not allowed to import eggs from states that don't follow those regulations. The first time, the outbreak was mostly out west, and the price of eggs shot from $3 a dozen to about $8 a dozen. Just as we were getting the flocks back up in numbers, we get the _wider_ bird flu waves which have the entire country in our position. Eggs are once again $8 a dozen, and I haven't had any in a couple months because of it. If the cost were to permanently rise to $5 to implement further changes to farming practices, I think a whole lot more people would be priced out of the market. A permanent 60% increase in the price of a basic food staple is going to hurt a lot of people.

During the first wave, much of the gap was taken up by prepared food products that already have eggs in them, which aren't regulated the same way as whole eggs. This allows food made outside the state to have eggs that don't comply with California's animal welfare laws. But this time, there aren't any such side channels.

Content:
Living in a developing nation, most of the people here don't have the luxury to be picky about food. We barely earn our living, and have to go for the cheapest option available to eat. Meat is a great (and major) source of protein here. We can't be picky about what type of meat we eat, what are the farming/living conditions of the animals we eat. But chickens that are breed for meat experience a horrible living condition. Yeah, I feel bad about their living/farming condition, but I have to survive. Farm chicken meat is often the cheapest source of meat. Author: @XboxSykocell
Content:
Meat is Sold by Weight, Not by Serving

The video assumes a serving of chicken breast is 3-4 ounces and estimates that switching to more humane farming methods would add about 9 cents per serving in the U.S.

However, a typical chicken breast weighs 1 to 1.5 pounds (or 4-6 servings per breast).

This means the real cost increase per breast would be 36–54 cents, and per pound, around 36 cents.

More Ethical Farming Produces Smaller Chickens, Further Raising Costs

Modern industrial chicken farming breeds chickens for rapid growth, yielding large, heavy birds.

Switching to slower-growing breeds—which is necessary for better animal welfare—would result in smaller chickens that take longer to reach market weight.

To produce the same amount of meat, farmers would need 2-3 times as many chickens, increasing total production costs far beyond what the video suggests.

Ignoring Market Realities: Monopoly Control and Profit Margins

The poultry industry is dominated by a few giant corporations that control pricing, contracts, and supply chains.

Farmers often operate under contract systems where they are locked into agreements with major processors (Tyson, Pilgrim’s, etc.).

If farmers transition to more ethical farming but don’t control pricing, they risk financial ruin, as the cost burden isn’t necessarily passed to consumers—it may just squeeze farmers’ already thin margins.

Retail Markups and Real-World Pricing Effects

The video implies that consumers would only pay a bit more, but that assumes cost increases translate directly into retail price increases.

In reality, supermarkets mark up prices significantly based on demand and branding.

Ethical meats often become premium products with inflated prices, meaning the actual consumer cost increase could be far higher than the video suggests.

What This Means

The video oversimplifies the economic impact of humane meat production. While it’s true that higher welfare farming can be achieved, the idea that we could do it with only minor cost increases is misleading. The real price increases would be much higher due to:

The need for more birds per pound of meat

Higher feed, land, and labor costs

Market forces that control farmer earnings and retail pricing

Author: @NudaStreetTriple
Content:
Kurzegesagt has a tendency to stretch the facts when it comes to veganism. I wouldn't be surprised if the writers weren't very representative of the population. But overall there is some good suggestions.

Claiming pigs specifically "are basically dogs" is a giant stretch. Show me the pigs who can help the blind, herd other animals, protect you, fight in wars (without it just being running rampant), help the police etc etc. It's a product of limited research but there just isn't sufficient evidence to make that claim. I believe they are reasonably capable animals, but there's a certain level of empathy and intelligence towards humans in dogs that allows them to understand us in a way I doubt pigs have. 

As for organic, there's also the fact that you cant give the animals any *preventative* doses, this is stupid and ultimately negatively affects the animals. Dairy is heavily dependent on the area and I'd disagree that they get it worse. In Britain and Ireland its roughly 95% have regular access to grassland however Germany may be lacking on this front, dairy cows diet is also very important for the quality of the milk so they get a more varied and interesting diet that they prefer. 

I'd agree with little needing to change for cattle although I think there is a bit of an underestimation of costs, ideally you'd want less cattle on slats during the winter as that's the real difference between "prison" and a cozy home during bad weather, pigs are more difficult as they can't really be let out on grass, they are extremely destructive and it effectively becomes a giant mud pit that is useless except for letting the pigs look at the sky, maybe that's enough, maybe there are better ways of doing it. Chickens are notably simpler less intelligent animals (walking around while headless is a pretty big clue among other things), free range is aesthetic but I'm unsure how much of a difference it makes when compared to just more space in the shed with a few elements from nature thrown in.

Author: @MrPsycomando
Content:
Unfortunately, the situation goes far beyond just the price. While price is an important metric to evaluate this issue, it's impossible to see the entire picture through this lens alone. As someone with an environmental background living in a highly agricultural and livestock-rearing country like Brazil, I can attest that managing animal resources is an incredibly complex task with significant environmental repercussions.

Free-range animal husbandry is beautiful and commendable, but it’s not scalable, just like organic farming. If everyone were to consume meat from free-range animals and organic crops, we would struggle to maintain production levels due to logistical challenges and space requirements for large-scale operations.

Currently, the Amazon rainforest is being deforested daily to make way for agriculture and livestock. If we were to avoid GMOs, pesticides, and intensive farming practices, we would only exacerbate deforestation to accommodate such vast operations. Moreover, when we consider the environmental impact of livestock, it’s significant. Controlled environments can help mitigate this impact effectively.

At the end of the day, we must weigh everything in perspective. While pesticides do contaminate groundwater, the impact of agriculture without them could be even greater due to the land area required. The same logic applies to livestock management.

Author: @marianneparent5591
Content: While I agree with the message that improving animal welfare has a small cost to the consumer, I found that the video had a few shortcomings. First, describing indoor housing as a "prison" applies very negative connotations to housing animals. Housing animals indoors was a major move for the reduction of disease in these animal populations. Second, I think the video should have addressed the definition of welfare and the complexity of defining this concept. Disease has major welfare implications. A good recent example is poultry housed outdoors (described in this video as the best option for welfare). With the presence of influenza A(H5N1) circulating in wild birds, the transmission of this virus can result in the mortality of almost the entire flock within 48 hours. One main change to the management of poultry to prevent the transmission of avian influenza is to move them to an indoor facility where contact with wild birds is reduced (and please note that here I said reduced and not removed, because there can still be transmission of the virus to poultry housed indoors).

Author: @KiwiSquawks
Content:
This video misses many of the inherent evils in animal farming. Dairy cows, for example, must have been recently pregnant to produce milk, so they're turned into baby-producing machines, get mastitis from how much milk they have to produce, and have their babies stolen from them (they are very maternal creatures and are known to cry out for their babies for weeks after the fact). "Good life" or not, all animals slaughtered for meat are slaughtered when they're basically still children, often at 5% of their full life spans.

I appreciate Kurzgesagt for bringing light to this issue that nobody seems to be talking about, but being reductionist in animal consumption almost never means anything (ie. meatless Mondays are often followed by a day in the week where you let yourself eat extra meat because you did "good" on Monday). Change doesn't start with "oh I'm going to reduce my consumption a little", it starts with boycotts and nonviolent radical action. Until then, nothing will change.

That Kurzgesagt doesn't point out the scientific fact that we can thrive without animal products (as per the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics) means they are proceeding from a premise that is fundamentally deceptive.

What the narrator calls decent is still exploitative and oppressive, and still ends in the ultimate form of degradation and violence: the dismember/ng and commodification of a sentient being. When we reconcile that with love, compassionn humanity and decency, it's not just them who are being debased.

Historians will tell you that slavery was modeled on the 'domestication' of other animals. The industrial sl@ughter of humans was inspired by the industrial sl@ughter of other animals. Even if you don't have an affinity for beings different from you, it still makes sense to care about them, as their freedom is intertwined with ours.

We can't do even what's suggested in the video (and which can't scaled up anyway) without subscribing to a belief in might making right. Ask yourself what it means to believe there can be a good kind of suprem@cy. It's not about taste. It's about a commitment to an identity of superiority.

And this is without even considering the environmental implications. Animal agriculture is the most ecologically destructive industry in the world. Less inhumane methods of production are actually worse for the environment. They take up more space, and require more inputs over a longer period of time.

Even if we stopped using fossil fuels today, emissions from animal agriculture alone would keep us from meeting any climate goals we have set (see Joseph Poore's study on the environmental impact of animal protein).

If you care - not just about other animals - but about other people, then it makes every bit of sense to stop consuming these products. It's really that simple. 

A plant-based diet can actually save you 16% on groceries, which is equivalent to 500 USD/EUR a year (per Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine).

By asking consumers to make better choices, Kurzgesagt are not only shifting blame to consumers, they are also giving the companies a free pass. Consumers have very little to no agency when making choices and food companies know this and market accordingly in a way that buying decisions are frictionless or not thought about much. Consumers need easier and cheaper access to better food. Unlike fast fashion, fast moving consumer goods are almost always unconscious snap decisions.

Author: @VultureXV
Content:
03:18
This is a misleading way to present the cost of eggs...
Yes...it doesn't look like it's a lot PER EGG but if you ran any sort of baking industry you just saw your raw material costs go up almost 30%. If you once bought 1000 eggs at $300, you're now buying the same amount of eggs for $370. If you're a large scale industry buying these raw materials the tens of thousands, this cost increase _is NOT insignificant_ even the approximately 8% increase (at 2 cents) that comes with the original. Inflation is already at critical levels and the plan here is to make food less accessible to humans with MORE inflation? Most people don't live in milquetoast sunnyside apartments making six figures a year from making animated educational cartoons on Youtube... Some people budget $300 or less in food a month to survive. Why do you want to make life harder on these people?

06:14
Incredibly misleading.
Pigs don't have social structure like dogs. I worked in preclinical research for a while and swine were a model used for medical research. Dogs have incredibly complex social structures while pigs are generally more socially independent. They may have a capacity for high intelligence, but that only translates to certain behaviors and problem-solving rather than communication and social empathy. A pig only "kinda" bonds with people, rather than a dog that sees humans as part of it's pack. Also...I'm noticing a pattern that you aren't specifically mentioning which "cut" of meat here is being used. That's also misleading.

07:56
"Just 15%"
You mention a 15% increase so incredibly casually I don't think you even understand the gravity of 15%. If my stocks went up 15% I'd be laughing my behind off to a bank. I feel like that encompasses _most_ of the arguments here. Once again, carrying the kind of "champagne socialist" viewpoint of spending "just a lil more to make things better!" WHILE being utterly inconsiderate of people who simply _cannot_ spend more on the product.

Of course, no one would want to do these kinds of practices because you can't turn a profit when you're constantly increasing prices like this. Quality goes down and supply decreases in all of these outcomes. You made no measure, nor effort, nor attempt to go over the potential pasture size increase, the potential impact on land acquisition, and the potential struggle of newer and smaller farmers trying to acquire the available land and tools necessary to get "up to par." All of these points will most certainly be forced into fruition via mandates and government intervention which is a _VERY BAD BUSINESS MODEL_ that will utterly make the meat produced in these countries with the mandates far, far, far less competitive in a global scale...thus making things even MORE expensive as the countries which pick these mandates go for importation of food rather than self-production due to sheer unaffordability of it all...

Y'all have hearts of scientists and dreamers with no rooting in human socioeconomic balance.
All of these are horrible ideas which will have long lasting ramifications on small and large farmers alike and further monopolize meat industries under government-subsidized pockets rather than having rural workers choose how they want to do business. You're going to kill competition with mandates, make a necessary food item more expensive, and cause supply chain issues.

I haven't even GOTTEN to the fact that animal products are as expansive as leather, adhesives, cosmetics, upholstery, medical research, medicine, and far, FAR more. You're not only making meat-eating that much harder *BUT THE INDUSTRIES WHICH RELY ON THESE PRODUCTS AS WELL.*

This is a horrible idea, ungrounded in any practical reason that will only cause extreme problems downstream.

I think there's an important social aspect missing in this video, around the world we're experiencing a growing disparity between the rich and the poor. This can only be countered by the governments actions.

Author: @Aranciata35
Content:
I live in the EU (Germany) and am grateful to this country for giving me the freedom to choose. I know that many don’t have this privilege—I moved from an Eastern European country and understand the reality there. In Germany , even in a small local supermarket I am able to buy free-range eggs and chicken meat and I gave up pork and beef long ago. Letting go of red meat was easy, the real challenge was creating a well-balanced diet for my family. We are healthy, active, and my husband is a triathlete.
I dream that one day we’ll be able to move within Germany to a place where I can have a small homestead—chickens, ducks, maybe goats. I would love to grow our own food and provide for my family myself.  The ethical question of eating meat was never a burning issue for me. As a child, I grew up close to my grandmothers' farm and knew how clever chickens could be—jumping onto your lap like kittens or puppies. I saw how bonded a calf is to its mother, how it would lick your hand with those huge, gentle eyes gazing at you.
Back then, life near the village didn’t seem as exciting as in the city. But now, with time, I realize it was my privilege. It shaped me into a compassionate person, helping me understand what many city dwellers might find hard to grasp or accept.

Author: @Soepstengel2000
Content:
While it is impressive and useful that someone actually did the math on all this, what I'm missing here is an acknowledgement of just how tight people's financial situations are at this point in time. For example, a price increase of 1,2 euros per serving of pork meat, or (on the simplest level) a 15% raise in prices, putting us at the level of costs that people in the late 80's paid. If taken in isolation, this doesn't sound like a steep price to pay, but these things do not exist in isolation. Households across the low and middle spectrum of income already can barely afford the cost of living if at all. The massive consumption of meat is indeed tied deeply to culture, history, convenience and a general resistance to being told what to do, but what I'm not hearing in this video is the fact that a lot of people also consume cheap meat in bulk *because it's cheap*, and they cannot functionally afford the more expensive options. Raising prices would create another division between the haves and the have-nots in an already deeply-divided society, and it also fails to address the main issue that a lot of people are facing when making choices on their lifestyle: the economy. To me, saying "if you can afford it" does not count as anything close to a real acknowledgement of our current situation, and claiming that a 15% price increase is doable and "fair because it's what our parents paid" rings on deaf ears.

Or, in a nutshell, it's not as simple as saying "just pay 15% more, like your parents did", because we don't live in the economy that our parents live in; ours is more expensive and worse.

Author: @LordpittCZ
Content:
We have our own hens. 4 of them. I realize not everyone can have egg-laying eggs, especially people in cities. But 4 hens are more than enough to provide a steady supply of eggs (so many we can't consume them all and give them to other people) and when they get old they stop laying eggs (or slow down too much), we just make a stew out of them.
Not only do we have extremely cheap torture-free eggs this way, its also a very good way to cut down on food waste. Chickens, like pigs, will eat almost anything. Just don't give them chicken meat or bones. Not necessarily because cannibalism is morally bad, but because it causes huge health risk for the chickens (or any other animal)
Maybe even your neighbors will give you leftovers they'd otherwise throw out if you give them a few eggs every know and then.

Other than that... animals that didn't suffer throughout their life tend to have better tasting meat.

Author: @ASpaceOstrich
Content:
One of the biggest issues under capitalism is that false advertising isn't illegal in any way that matters. I would absolutely pay slightly more for more ethically raised animals. I imagine most would. This would likely render the least ethical options untenable and wipe them out, which is ideal. Unfortunately, there is zero way to know what the conditions are behind anything you buy. 

You can't judge by the price, because companies are incentivised to raise the price to match and just keep being awful. You can't judge by advertising, because "we aren't doing this awful thing" does not work as an ad campaign, because it associates your product with that awful thing, and companies can just lie. And advertising the good conditions you keep your animals in is also far too easy to lie about by just claiming the ad is an unrelated thing.

This is a problem across the board. Because lies by omission are allowed, advertising makes it impossible to make an informed decision. A product cannot advertise itself on quality or ethics because unethical and poor quality competitors are allowed to advertise themselves on the exact same thing. Its not illegal to claim your tool is high quality even when its cheap garbage, which means actual high quality is uncompetitive. The only way this is solvable would be to force companies to proudly claim that their products are garbage, which is never going to happen.

Author: @X-SPONGED
Content:
Random nobody here, I'll just lay out my two cents that could've gone to the chickens here:

*1. CASH*
The main problem lies here. PROFIT. No matter how slight is profit, and in corporate culture, everything goes to profit. On a side tangent, did y'know that every nuclear disaster on earth could've been prevented? All it would've cost were a couple hundred more dollars being spent by the government or business entity of those respective crisis(es). Unfortunately profit comes above all, morals and safety be damned.

*2. WASTING FOOD*
A problem I don't see tackled often is how eager people (both 1st and 3rd world) are to throw away food. As a child, I was taught that food wasn't only money but a resource we took from another. That chicken on my table diced so my mother could spend her hardwork to buy us some food while some poor guy went hungry in the streets. 

If everyone in my city decided to only throw away ten maybe twenty grains of rice everytime they had a meal, in a week, that's about 10 sacks of rice being thrown away like dirt. Yet, my aunt's kids would gladly throw away up to half of my grandma's homecooked meals if they were "full enough" or even outright deny it and eat instant noodles instead. It's saddening to see a sacrifice from at least three different parties be casted aside like so. I'm not poor or anything but even I won't take my food for granted.

*3. LAZINESS*
Another thing that's closely related to money is energy. As in, the effort you put in. What's the use of putting in more effort to yield less profit? Logically it doesn't make sense does it? More resources to make less money, net negative on both ends. So, why spend the effort? By taking the time to take care of the animals, they're not only wasting money but lowering productivity that could've gone to doing more work. The time needed to anesthesize 20 pigs could've been used to castrate 10 without or something along those lines. New regulations. New laws. New protocol. A complete overhaul of all the bad factory farms. That's a lotta work and all for a deficit? Nobody's gonna do that and nobody will. That's the saddest part. Even if we get through all the money, those responsible will still have to put in more effort than *_"oh okay take away this microscopically slim sliver of my earnings"_* and that is much MUCH more than what they were ever willing to do.

Author: @nickkreuzen6312
Content:
Like many in the comments, I am skeptical of this approach. As long as there is no actual legislation enforcing better living conditions, I don’t see companies changing their practices. Even now, it is nearly impossible for consumers to understand which labels truly ensure less cruel farming practices. The amount of pseudo-scientific practices and greenwashing creates an overwhelmingly confusing forest for the average consumer.

It also makes me angry that we live in a world where the goodwill of consumers is exploited just to generate even more profit. I really appreciate everyone who takes action by trying to buy "cruelty-free" products, but as things stand, it is simply not possible. Even if you buy from a local farmer, you are still responsible for a sentient being being taken from its mother, forced into pregnancy, and facing an early death in its teenage years.

*Opinion part* There are plant-based alternatives that taste just as good, are often healthier, and bypass this ridiculously cruel industry. Moreover, beyond boycotting animal products altogether, adopting a plant-based diet significantly reduces the two main causes of species decline: habitat loss and pesticide use. Our ancestors relied on animal products - we do not.

Author: @X-SPONGED
Content:
5:08 It's also kinda misleading to say "free range costs extra" because a smart farmer using free range hens would actually make a profit by using mobile coops.

It's a really renewable and green way of keeping chickens. Instead of keeping the coop stationary, they'd put it in the back of a tractor and move it somewhere on the field everyday. They'd let the hens graze and till the soil with their feet. This doesn't do much but keep the chickens happy, what they do though is make the soil much more nutrient rich because of their poop. It's a slow process but in the end, it's actually cheaper than using chemical fertilizer and as a plus, you can even call your hens "free range, wild fed"

Author: @swaminathanbalakrishnan1399
Content:
In India the situation is complex.
Dairy is not a problem; most organizations are cooperatives that keep profit caps and so individual farmers take care of cows on pastures. There are unfortunate exceptions though. The beef part is avoided entirely since Hindu.
Pigs - depends. When free-ranging pigs are slaughtered it is fine. But in urban areas there is an increasing demand that leads to situations like the one you depicted.
Chicken is widespread, with all the same conditions as in the West.
Labelling issues are much more complicated. The only labels that exist (for dairy products, I'm vegetarian so can't comment on meat) are "no GMOs" and "organic", which like you said are rather insufficient... but generally, a reliable organic label indicates decent farm conditions.
The good thing is, there is a strong cultural tradition of venerating cows and being interested in their welfare. So any trends of mistreatment get wide press; the only trouble is that counterculture takes delight in making cows un-venerated...

Author: @Yonkage-ik5qb
Content:
The crux of this issue is that there is almost zero correlation between cost to the producer, and price for the consumer, because there's about 5 layers of middlemen between the farm and the grocery store and the added cost at every step is often obfuscated or deliberately covered up. We're all paying more for eggs right now, supposedly because of bird flu culling. But a few years ago there was another spike in egg prices and it was proven that egg distributors were literally price gouging, and had to pay fines after Congress investigated this (something that is very unlikely to happen in this current administration, of course).

Regardless of what is done to the animals, the final cost is more a matter of which grocery you shop at compared to anything else. Around here, for example, you'll pay about a 25% markup to the exact same name-brands of foods, for shopping at grocery stores that aren't WalMart; basically you're paying extra for the privilege of NOT shopping at WalMart. The only difference is the very last step in the chain.

Content:
Kurzgesagt, you made quite a big mistake, just spreading more misinformation.

I don't know anything about the other animals, but I can guarantee you that you are completely wrong about dairy cows. The main reason is quite simple - a cow's mental and/or physical suffering is directly related to milk production. If the cow is in pain or stressed - it will produce less milk, i.e. less money for the farm. Therefor, it's in the farm's interest to keep the cows in top physical/mental condition. Dairy cows are literally in heaven. Now here are the most widespread misconceptions:

- You think that a cow suffers by being always indoors, but this is completely wrong. We tend to put ourselves in the place of the cow, and indeed it will be torture for most humans, but here is the thing: cows are one of the dumbest animals you can think of...literally...To suffer from being indoors, you basically have to realize you are indoors in the first place, which is just too complex for cows (and great for us ofcourse). They don't have any social system, hierarchy, any connections whatsoever. They never fight and absolutely don't care about their newborns. If a cow  "kicks the bucket" in the middle of the barn, other cows would simply go around it like it's a big rock, even using it as a pillow or a scratcher.

This video was so poorly researched that I’m starting to lose trust in your work on other topics.

	•	Antibiotic use and carcinogens in animal products
	•	The reality of slaughterhouses—panic, blood, and failed stunning
	•	How factory farming cuts most animals’ lifespans by 75–99%

Worst of all, in your “best possible actions” list, you didn’t even mention veganism—the only way to be 100% sure you didn’t contribute to avoidable animal suffering. Author: @Gilamath.
Content:
I'm a practicing Muslim living in the US who eats zabihah halal meat. The chicken from my local zabihah butcher is from a slower-growing breed, and is raised free-range. The cows slaughtered for beef don't undergo "finishing" and spend most of their lives outdoors. Of course, my butcher doesn't carry pork

Muslims like myself are often told that our meat is "barbaric" because of our slaughter practices. In the US, our animals are stunned and then hand-slaughtered. I'm told that in other countries, it's different. I can only talk about my experience with halal meat, and it has been uniformly excellent

I investigated the farms from which my meat comes from, ready to face the worst. I was pleasantly surprised that every halal vendor I investigated was specifically sourcing meat from farms that didn't sell modified or overfed animals, didn't utilize cages, and let animals roam free. Additionally, ever since moving to Texas, my family has been getting our meat from a local zabihah halal farm where the living standards are even better, and the animals seem to be living genuinely good lives

The meat is certainly expensive, I can't deny that. Our family eats less meat as a result, though as immigrants, we're also simply used to eating less meat because we weren't immersed in America's astoundingly meat-heavy consumer culture. And to be blunt, the quality of our meat seems better, as well. The chicken especially, it just doesn't look very appetizing in the supermarket compared to what we get from the farm. The chicken breasts and thighs are astonishingly large and bulbous, but the meat color and texture look... off

Author: @Quouar
Content:
I find it deeply interesting to think about the thought process that went into this video. It acknowledges from the start that animal-based industries are horrific for the animals within them. It explains some of that through talking about debeaking, living conditions, and such. However, it steps past some of the basic cruelty that's inherent to the industry, handwaving away the idea that this is cruelty with the assumption that there is no way around it. Things like the culling of male chicks and cows, the impact of breeding on the quality of life of these chickens, and the absurdity of not recognising that being sent to a slaughterhouse is a horrific thing on its own. 

Also, the idea that pigs have it the worst because they're the most intelligent is bizarre. All these creatures feel pain. All of them feel the horror of the hell they were born into. Playing horror olympics based on intelligence is a deeply perverse thing to do. 

When I went vegetarian - and eventually vegan - it was because I became aware of the horror of the system and the actual cost of what I was eating. It was through recognising that there was fundamentally no difference between my dogs whom I loved and that cow in the field over there - both were equally deserving of my love and care. I went vegan because I learned more about what's actually involved in animal industries and the absolute suffering inherent in them, and didn't want that suffering on my hands. What I find interesting is that this video is taking the instruments that I used to become vegan, saying "no one is vegan and don't bother becoming vegan because it's expensive and awful," and twisting those instruments into a weirdly pro-meat agenda. It's bizarre and kind of sickening.

On a less ideological note and a more practical one, saying "Oh, we can just increase the price of meat-based groceries 50% and that's still perfectly affordable" is a gross misunderstanding of domestic economics. When you have 12.6% of the US population on SNAP and roughly 50 million food insecure Americans as a whole, you can't just jack up a price 50% and say it's fine. The entire premise of the video - that you can absorb the cost and make a difference through paying more - is based on a fundamental lack of understanding of any element of this debate. Studies show that, if people can buy more ethical animal products, they generally do. Those that don't don't do it because they're unaware monsters. We're all aware of the horrific suffering inherent in animal industries. They do it because there's not another option that is accessible to them. This video is a rich man telling a poor man wealth inequality is on him because he just hasn't hustled well enough. 

And as an aside, criticising the structures of the meat industry and meat pricing without at least acknowledging how capitalism works? Again, a gross misrepresentation of the problem here. 

Finally, I don't see how you can reasonably and ethically talk about the harm of the meat industry without also talking about its incredible impact on climate change. The meat industry is one of the leading drivers of climate change, and no amount of ethical cattle farming practices will change that absolute reality. Saying "just look for the right labels and your involvement in unethical practices is resolved" is the most garbage Boomer neoliberal take I have seen in a long, long time.

TL;DR: This is a bizarre, awful video, and I'm not surprised they had to get Ground News instead of one of their more legitimate sponsors to sponsor it.

Content:
I've been watching this channel for 10 years, maybe even 11 at this point, and I even wore a kurzgesagt merch shirt to school today.

The majority of people are cutting costs anywhere they can just to keep up anyway. And the ones that have excess money who have the power to help very often got that money through unethical practices themselves, so they won't. 
You can't make a video so deeply related to the economy as this one and not even comment on the cost of living, corporate greed, corporate lies, or even just anything to do with the economy really.

But, I still eat meat, and frankly I don't feel right to go vegan (though due to what I'm about to discuss I contemplate it every now and again), because you aren't going to get things (in sufficient amounts) like B12 or anything solely found in meat from natural sources. It will come from manufactured and chemically-produced sources. We are quite literally hardwired to be omnivores due to all the resources we need at certain amounts.
...If I had a say in everything I ate, I would buy all organic meat and never anything less. I can see myself comfortably doing this in the future when I'm more financially stable.

But that's just the thing, isn't it...being more financially stable. What average person in the world right now is or _feels_ financially stable enough to keep buying more expensive alternatives _all the time?_ And how often are you going to find a high-high class or top 1% individual who cares as much about all of this as the average person?

I hate the economy. I hate inflation. I hate money and greed, so much. Cheap removes the quality and gives the corporations more money. Expensive raises the quality but makes the average corporation AND person feeling strapped for cash unhappy. This all goes without mentioning how other products that are directly connected to the quality of meat are changed, such as the price and demand of more space and anesthetics.


It's all a nasty, greedy, fear-induced cheapness cycle. I want out of it. How the fuck do we get out of it without feeling like we are spending too much?
