Author: @Bunny-ch2ul
Content:
I feel like you can't talk about this issue and not talk about climate. Pork and beef are extremely carbon intensive, and should generally be considered "luxuries" anyway. (I'm not saying don't eat them. I'm saying, consume consciously. Don't make beef into garbage gray cheeseburgers or Hamburger Helper. By all means, treat yourself occasionally.) Chickens are a significantly better choice for the environment, regardless of how they're farmed. 

It's also worth mentioning that making the right choice isn't super easy in the US. You can't really rely on price alone, and the labels are purposefully vague to disguise that most meat is produced under poor conditions. What we should be doing is asking for more accurate labeling. 

As far as eating less meat, vegetarian and vegan foods are more or less universally more palatable when they're not plant based versions of meat based dishes. If you want to try to eat more plant-based foods, look for foods that have historically been plant based. (I'd start with Indian food, but that's just a matter of preference.) Substituting a portabella mushroom for a steak or burger is pretty depressing. Meatless Mexican beans and rice dishes are great. Substitutions are always going to feel like a compromise. (And probably won't have the right amino acid balance, so you'll be hungry sooner. Like, there aren't a ton of nutrients in a portabella burger, even if it is "plant based.") Traditionally meatless dishes are appealing, and more nutritionally balanced.

Author: @MEWOVER9000
Content:
I think it is a genuinely ethical discussion to have, but talking about bumping the cost of meat by 50%... There are higher priorities. Priorities that affect human health. Sedentary Americans in particular are already critically under-muscled across the board. Passing legislation that would bump the cost of the most satiating, highest protein foods in people's diet would almost certainly have negative health consequences.

Framing the issue as "a few extra cents per serving" is disingenuous. Really, you're talking about a few extra dollars per pound of meat when adding everything up. You can only pass so much legislation before costs get too high and people simply start ignoring the law in order for society to function. Legislation can make things more ethical, safe, and healthy, but always at a cost. People only have so much money they can spend on food. If you're going to pass legislation that would drives the cost of food up, you need to see some return on investment. Hypothetical example, legislation reducing the amount of pesticides that can be sprayed on crops might drive up costs, but there may be a reduction in spending on healthcare that could balance the equation.

Author: @akanay22
Content:
I'm not sure how solid your argument is.

Firstly, increasing the price according to the costs of the services you're giving to the animals, assumes that you can give those in the first place. So it is based on current conditions. But making all farm animals free range and every step pain-free might end up being costlier because of the increased demand vs the fixed supply. 

Also I'm not sure if labor is counted towards the price increase. Free roaming animals require more maintenance and so does sedating etc. Even though those extra steps might not be that expensive by themselves, they might be with the labor expenses added. 

And a price increase in dairy, eggs and meat means a price increase in basically every other food too. Because they're also common ingredients. So its not about just 20 cents but realistically a much bigger increase in overall food spendings. Its not just paying a few extra dollars when you think about it like that.

Lastly, all this is data is for first world countries. There are many other countries in the world where meat is a lot less accessible and those countries have much larger populations then the west. So even if you solve the problem in the west, you can't just tell these people who can barely afford eating meat to start paying more for it. Therefore the majority of the problem will remain unsolved.

Author: @menzlo
Content: This video leaves a lot out, for example, land use. Cow pasture is already the leading cause of deforestation, which is one of the largest contributors to climate change in the agriculture sector. As the global population rises and becomes richer, demand for meat will keep going up, and we're going to need much more land (the size of multiple Indias) for agriculture using current (torturous) methods for raising meat. And ethically raised meat uses vastly more land and causes more emissions. One of the problems with meat is that animals are not efficient at converting plant calories to meat calories (9 to 1), and ethical breeds and methods are even less efficient which requires more land and energy to grow their feed. Even if you don't want to be vegan, we should all think about eating less meat and more plants, especially in countries like the US where meat consumption is really high and fiber consumption is really low.

Author: @ThatRedHead717
Content:
Honestly, I find this video disappointing. In the reporting data section, they use "cost per serving" which shifts the blame (and the responsibility) onto the consumer when it almost entirely lies in the hands of greedy ceos squeezing every cent out of their animals and forcing the competition (good intentions or not) into using the same bad practices. Then, once that price would actually get noticeably higher (>10%) they switch to percentage increase in price instead of cost per serving. It's common practice in science to report all of your data in the same units so that the reader can actually make sense of your argument. Switching halfway through like this only inhibits our understanding of the truth. 

Then, once you talk about what we, the viewers and consumers of meat, can actually do to help, the only actionable thing you say is "go for the label" which is so broad and unusable as advice that it basically could've just been left out entirely. 

The only good advice in this video is when you tell us to push for better legislation around farming practices but even that basically means nothing because right now, we are fighting for our own survival and can't spare the political effort to help animals when our democracy is crumbling around us. 

Kurzgesagt, I appreciate the awareness you are trying to spread here. This is a horrific industry that uses the worst practices imaginable to gain every cent at the cost of animal suffering. However, using units such as "cost per serving" but only until that cost is too high; shifting the blame onto the consumer; and giving basically no actionable advice makes watching this video an exercise in futility, frustration, and cruelty porn. I expect better from you.

Author: @albertnewtonify
Content:
Animal Agriculture is responsible for -

Deforestation
Approximately 90% of Amazon deforestation is linked to cattle ranching, with additional land cleared for growing animal feed crops like soy.

Biodiversity Loss
Livestock production contributes to 60% of global biodiversity loss through habitat destruction and ecosystem disruption.

Ocean Dead Zones
Runoff from animal farms and fertilizers used for feed crops creates nitrogen and phosphorus pollution, leading to over 400 ocean dead zones worldwide.

Pollution of Fresh Water
Manure and farm waste contaminate rivers and lakes, making animal agriculture the largest contributor to water pollution globally.

Loss of Fresh Water
Producing 1 kg of beef requires 15,400 liters of water, compared to 250 liters for 1 kg of potatoes.

World Hunger
Over 77% of global agricultural land is used for livestock and feed production, yet it provides only 18% of global calorie intake.

Zoonotic Diseases
Animal farming has been linked to outbreaks of zoonotic diseases like avian flu, swine flu, and COVID-19, which originate in animal-human interfaces.

Lifestyle Illnesses
Diets high in animal products increase the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers, which are leading causes of mortality.

Mass Extinction
Current extinction rates are 1,000 times higher than natural background rates, largely driven by habitat destruction and climate change caused by animal agriculture.

Global Warming
Animal agriculture is responsible for 18-20% of global greenhouse gas emissions, more than all forms of transportation combined. It also releases methane and nitrous oxide, which have 84 and 300 times the warming potential of CO₂, respectively.

Climate Change
Animal farming is the single largest driver of climate change, contributing to land degradation, deforestation, and methane emissions, which accelerate global temperature rise and disrupt ecosystems on a catastrophic scale.

Author: @supashadow100
Content:
Incredibly narrow scope of a video, disappointing to see from this channel.
The reason meat production shifts towards factory farming is not simply due to financial factors. As the video explains, the financial incentive is practically non-existent. The unfortunate reality is factory farming is the best option for environmental impact and land use. This is something that welfare arguments cannot overcome.
If you were to shift animal agriculture to pastures and open access to the outdoors, how much land would that take up if the goal was to maintain the same meat production the world is producing now? It's an unsustainable system.
Pig farming alone barely exists in a free-range environment for this reason. And the waste produced by animal agriculture is incredibly damaging to the environment. Factory farms contain that waste to a much more compact area. Unfortunately, the welfarist policies would take up and damage far more land than is sustainable for the current meat output. You shouldn't avoid that discussion when you're talking about the "cost of meat production".

And I know the video didn't want to "go there" in terms of animal welfare, but if you're going to include an 'opinion' section, how can you not address the fact that - at the end of the day - these animals all end up in slaughterhouses. They are an irredeemable evil that is necessary for animal agriculture. All the welfare implementations in the world do not justify the flawed "one bad day" argument. "Torture-free" farms don't exist, because farms don't exist without slaughterhouses.

Do better.

Author: @rebelrider3361
Content:
Rancher here. I've raised chickens, ducks, goats, and our main income comes from beef cattle. 
Eggs: The trouble with ethical free range, where the chickens have enough space to actually forage on green pastures, is that one needs to do A LOT of work to keep predators away so it can't be true free range, fences are needed for predators. (Or that and guard dogs. Some predators would still need shot because chicken tractors (movable barns for the chickens) are less predator safe than a warehouse. As for chick culling, I am skeptical of the egg testing method. It involves puncturing the egg, which could introduce bacteria and kill chicks in development, which could lead to the unhatched chicks suffering more than the quick death by culling the males. 
Pigs: Not my area of expertise, but anesthesia is a much more complicated subject than what is mentioned here. Putting an animal under is risky, so you'd have piglets die if you put them under. Most pain drugs are regulated so you need a vet to do it when the farmer normally does it.  This raises the price massively. It's also worth noting that by needing a vet, it might delay the castration or other surgeries so instead of having them at birth, they might get them done later, causing more pain overall. 
Cattle: I don't know where you got your info, but a lot is wrong. In the US, most beef cattle NEVER see the inside of a building until they go into the slaughter house. Feedlots are outdoors, not indoors. (I'm guessing the statistics were from dairy cattle.) Beef cattle basically live like wild cattle but without ever worrying about predators or where the next meal or drink will come from. I think if a cow could pick between being wild or domestic, she'd choose domestic. 
On to laws: Many of the laws are made by people outside the industry who don't understand why things are done the way they are. For example, castration of ranch animals is done without painkillers. This is because speed is more important than lack of pain. Let's say we had to give calves painkillers before doing the operations. This means first separating the calves from their mothers, then giving them shots, waiting something like 15 minutes for it to take effect (and there are 150 calves so keeping track of who is ready to be castrated is hard) and then doing the surgery that takes two minutes. During this time, the calves are stressed because they're separated from their moms and being handled by humans. The amount of extra time is going to add way more stress than just getting the surgery over with. 
Without painkillers, we separate the calves, rope them, do the surgery, and release them to their moms. They don't have to deal with the side effects of drugs and they aren't being handled as much, thus giving them less stress. Also, painkillers are not pain free. I had a goat who broke his leg. He stood still while the leg was splinted, even though that looked VERY painful. I felt bad for him so I gave him a shot of painkiller. Only then did he show distress. The shot bothered him more than someone handling a BROKEN leg. Animals can't tell us if they're experiencing side effects, they can't tell us if they'd rather we just get the scary situation over with fast. Also, full sedation for operations is risky for cattle, because if they lay wrong, they can die. 
I heard that in Europe, they banned castration of goats/sheep after one week unless a vet does it. The trouble is, their urinary tract isn't developed enough in the first week so if they get stones after castration, they're likely to die a very painful death.

Author: @bevoace-trainer968
Content:
Everyone would agree that a small increase in price is a no brainier but I think you're focusing too much on "care" increasing the price. I live in Australia and have experience with sheep an cattle farming. We have the space, so most conditions fall into the "decent" category. What we're seeing though is a movement towards a lot less families owning farms and more companies owning them. This means usually means the workers are less invested and the owners have a responsibility to care for staff. It's a movement based off the idea that basically the new generation isn't interested in being farmers. Now let's take castration as an example of a practice that could be improved upon. Castration on my families "decent" categorised property takes many long dirty days of hard work each year. I don't think it's fair that it hurts them, the real answer I think would be keeping them separate, but that's not what I'm trying to argue. Extending that process by making your workers medicate the animals first is going to make this miserable time of year even harder. It's hard to imagine it making much of a difference but it takes less than 30 seconds to castrate an lamb, double this (it'd likely slow you down more) by medication and you're making a week long activity two weeks. Not to mention you have to trust farmers with huge shipments of medication people are surely going to misuse. People don't seem to want to do this work anymore to begin with. Now lets say you keep animals in a prison condition and adjust your conditions to decent. The workers are likely going to quit, the level of effort is exceptionally higher. Not to mention cattle and pigs can be dangerous and you're not a family owned property, you have to take more expensive measures to care for your workers. Something a a "decent" catagorised property probably wouldn't have to worry about as they're family owned, the workers have a life of experience and aren't going to sue their family if a cow puts them in a wheelchair. Can you imagine how scary that'd be to an issuance company.
So keeping animals in caged or prison categories keeps your staff and financial security for your business. In countries with less space also converting to corporate owned farms, I can see prison and caged being the most viable option. 
My point is, care isn't the issue that's going to raise the price by anything significant. It's the way the business needs to operate and the struggle to employ staff. Comparing these businesses to what in my experience are primarily family owned properties isn't fair.

Content:
About solutions - it has to be both ways:
1. If you buy a pack without any reference to animal welfare - you are guilty. Don't buy it. They should of course also mean either stop imports completely, or have physical control on the foreign sites and through the supply chain (anything else and you'll get Chinese official to lie on the document). Drawback of this is political fights, and in democracy this means compromises, so probably years of slowly pushing the regs, each time getting unsatisfactory rules that are not quite what animal welfare side wants.

No squabbling against 1 o 2, but deploy 1 + 2 consistenly.

Author: @EleftheriosVenizelos-z2l
Content:
Claims like "chickens can feel empathy" rest on the most precarious heterophenomenological grounds imaginable—akin to asserting that rocks "desire" to fall and settle. Call me a sociopath, but any argument for animal rights that appeals to animal experiences is emotivist, grounded in pretheoretical intuitions, and largely driven by anthropomorphism. This is evident to anyone capable of rationalizing their affection for living beings—human or otherwise—and shaking off his cognitive dissonance.

Rights are not entitlements based on the capacity for suffering; they are constructs we afford individuals within political communities because cooperation is generally preferable to conflict. Rights are not painkillers. To recognize them, we must have both reason and means to do so. This is not merely my philosophical stance; it is quite literally how humanity has operated throughout history and, more importantly, the only rational way it can function. Once you acknowledge that, to the best of our knowledge, only humans can conceive ends and formulate rational plans to achieve them, that only humans possess the abstract conceptual framework necessary for sentiments to transcend mere physiological responses, that animals lack minds with narrative depth and exist as automata without a unified sense of self, and that, as Dennett observed, "the more we learn about their actual competences and internal structures, the less it seems that there is 'someone home' in there," it becomes clear that such emotivist appeals fail to persuade.

If you wish to argue against industrialized meat production, appeal to my self-interest. That argument has already been made, which is precisely why those who can afford it and who prioritize their well-being choose healthier meat from animals raised in better conditions. The market has already addressed this—hence the variety in the supermarket meat aisle.

Author: @Beryllahawk
Content:
Great video, and I very much appreciate once again the citations and details that allow me to go hunt up more information. I live in an area that has MANY chicken farms (mostly, laying operations, that is to say they produce eggs) and all of them have been hit really hard by the bird flu recently. Eggs where I live are now almost eight dollars US, per dozen. I have a large family, we go through 36 eggs EVERY WEEK. We're about to be not doing that because we just can't afford it, and this is without any changes to the living conditions of the birds of course. Sad to say, most of the people in this area don't see any part of chicken farming as cruelty - not even the culling. And the corporations? They don't even want to make sure the FARMERS have decent lives, much less the chickens. It's horrifying, and it's literally needless suffering. Not only because improvements in the living conditions for the animals AND paying workers a little more wouldn't have that huge an impact on prices (on average)... but because those improvements make the animals healthier, they yield higher quality meat and eggs and milk, AND that means the humans get more out of any given ounce of animal product, because healthier animals just plain result in better food.
You do mention not to throw away meat - I would add to that, also learning ways to use up every speck of a given purchase of meat. Compost egg shells for a tiny garden: you might only get a little basil and mint out of that but it's still getting more value from each egg. You can make some amazing broth and stock from animal bones, and yeah it takes time, but you can freeze that - meaning you can make up some when you HAVE time, then not have to fuss with it when you're busy later. Humans have managed their food sources for MOST of our history on a schedule that looks to seasons, YEARS, at a time - fattening your cattle for two years means you gotta make any single slaughter LAST until the next generation is actually ready for consumption. There is still much value in pre-industrial techniques for cooking and saving meat, bones, and everything but the squeal. No, you don't have to do ALL the same things a person 300 years ago might've done when they had killed a cow. BUT, you can learn what ways they had and use the methods that will do the most for you and your family's life - and make the best use of the animal whose life was given to feed you.

Author: @just_jack3309
Content:
I’m going to school to be a vet so I can work to make sure the animals we eat live quality life’s. there are certain things in this video that I don’t agree with and it paints a bad picture for farmers and the industry. Claims like not having straw and bedding for pigs being far from what they need is a claim that has been shown to be false, there are studies done that show pigs prefer concrete floors over straw because of how cool the concrete is. Sows are kept in cages when nursing their piglets so that they don’t roll onto the piglet and kill them, there was a law in the us put into place to mandate these cages.  The graphics in this video are very extreme and I don’t feel they properly represent the reality of the industry. I’m sure that there are situations with bad conditions like shown but to claim things like all of the industry being like this is not right. I love the idea of the video because there are things wrong In the industry and things that need to change but calling them “torture camps and prisons” doesn’t sit right with me. 

I’m typing a lot so I want to add this last part, this video greatly personifies animals in a way that’s not true. This video is designed to make you feel as if these animals feel human emotions and have that level of intelligence which is not true as we have no way of knowing what the animal is thinking or feeling. I hold a great love for animals and I’m dedicating my life to taking care of the livestock animals that are talked about in this video, there are problems in the industry but this doesn’t feel right how this was presented. I’m a huge fan of this channel and I know they do research but I don’t feel the research here was done correctly. Most of my information here was taught to me by a professor of mine who has specialized in swine for her whole life and is very passionate about animal welfare. Please do more research into these animals if you truly care about them and want change.

Author: @everfree_
Content:
The main criticism I have of this video is that it doesn't tackle the problem of people with low income. I myself make very little each month and spend more than half of what I make on rent alone. Whenever I go shopping each week or so, I tend to spend around 70 USD on food, with half of that being meat. I get making the lives of the animals better, and I do hope conditions improve, but I'm not about to pay nearly 12 USD on four chicken breasts when I can get six of them for 6 USD. It doesn't make sense for someone with such little income to have to pay double the amount and end up suffering financially because of it.

This isn't me saying that this video is dumb or pointless; I very much enjoyed what you guys talked about and I agree that changes have to be made. But changes shouldn't have be on us, the consumer. I can't be asked to pay an artificially increased price just to have these changes take place while draining my bank account. It's the government's responsibility to add and improve new food industry regulations and trade standards to make things better for the consumer and the animals while keeping costs low. Just wanted to add my own opinion on the matter.

P.S. Mussels are great.

Author: @Lurker37
Content:
This video seems to ignore that most farmers do not have the money to make these sorts of changes, are often in debt just trying to keep their current operation going, and have nowhere to move their livestock to while they did. The only people who could afford to make these sorts of changes would be those not currently depending on their animals for their living expenses. Furthermore, if you honestly believe that any significant amount of any price increase makes it back to the farmer, then you need to do more research. It is important to realise that in many countries where farming is not subsidised, farmers barely make a living. It is simply not possible for them to invest in new infrastructure, especially if their income would be reduced (or eliminated entirely) during the building. 

To give an idea of how bad this can get: Dairy farmers went on strike here once, pouring their milk into the gutter in a desperate effort to get paid enough to live on from their milk. Milk prices in the supermarket went up by 4c per litre. Of that, dairy farmers got half a cent per litre.

Tldr: This video is full of nonsense. Chicken, steak, and pork cost way more than what’s shown, and the real issue with animal welfare isn’t just farming practices, it’s wages. People are struggling to make ends meet, and you can’t expect them to pay more for ethically-raised meat when they can barely afford the basics. If wages don’t keep up with inflation, consumers simply can’t afford to prioritize better food, no matter how much they care about animal welfare. It’s time for real policy changes. Living wage laws are a must. No one should be working full-time and still living paycheck to paycheck. If we want people to buy better quality food, they need to have the money to do it. Progressive tax reforms could help redistribute wealth and lift up the working class, making it possible for people to spend more on ethical food. Until wages rise, it’s an impossible expectation to ask consumers to pay higher prices for humane farming practices.

The solution isn’t just about raising wages, though. We need to invest in education and job training programs so people can move into better-paying jobs. The current system keeps too many stuck in low-wage work, and it’s only contributing to the problem. If we want to build a society where people can afford to make the right choices for animals, we need to start giving them the tools to earn more. More financial stability equals more money for ethical food choices. simple as that.

Until the price is addressed, the entire conversation about animal welfare is pointless. People can’t afford to do the right thing, and producers have no incentive to change. The problem is bigger than just farm practices, it’s about a system that doesn’t give workers and consumers the financial means to make choices that align with their values. Raising wages isn’t optional. it’s essential if we ever hope to see a world where animals are treated with the respect they deserve.

there’s no way to meet global demand for meat through free-range farming. Very few countries, have the space for it. In countries like Argentina, most cows are free-range, wintering on river islands and natural pastures. The U.S. isn’t even the second largest meat consumer, Argentina and Uruguay are. Your research is lacking. European regulations don’t focus on animal welfare. they’re trade barriers that protect inefficient local farming, inflating prices and limiting access to cheaper, better-quality meat from countries like mine. Author: @Antik13671
Content:
So a bit of info for those interested. I grew up (11+, dairy cows before) and worked on and off for a few years on a small/medium free range chicken farm (UK, pre brexit). We had 12,000 chickens (laying hens). I'd guesstimate a good 50-60% didn't go outside regularly if ever. Does that mean it was pointless being free range? No. But barns need to be smaller (less hens, equal or slightly more space per hen, this should in my mind get more hens out whilst also reducing fighting issues.  Most farms do not hatch their own hens, that's a separate business. 

Interesting note on fighting issues, in general, white hens fight less then red or brown hens, I don't know why. If you can, buy white eggs, the colour of the egg often matches the colour of the hen. 

Barn hens can have it pretty good, it does protect them from bird flu and a lot of bugs they can get from the outside world. But they need a lot of enrichment to keep them happy and occupied. If I remember correctly barn hens have more internal space then free range (UK, dunno about elsewhere, and might have changed post brexit).

I will admit we did some borderline illegal things, but all for welfare. For example  RSPCA (RSPB are not involved in farmed animals (UK at least maybe elsewhere they are)) state that if a hen does not recover from a sickness or disease within 48 hours it should be culled. However depending on the time of year they were hatched a flock may have a high number of blind hens (poor ventilation due to cold temperatures, leading to high ammonia levels in their hatchery barn (yes this should be addressed it was a discrase, but the percentage of the worst flick was probably around 0.2% blind)). Other issues can also arise ( corkscrew necks as we called them, neurological condition that caused a spasm when stressed/startled made the hen turn their heads upside down). We had one hen who lost half a leg in a tractor accident (we had fencing issues with the first few flocks). We should have killed all of those hens. They couldn't survive in the barn, they all took too long to get to food and were pushed around too much. We put them in sick chick pens, away from the main flock in barn buildings, normally less than 20 hens per pen. There they could thrive. But we would have been in a lot of trouble if caught. But it was so that they could have a life. We sold off what we could after the main flock left (you only keep them for 10-12 months, I can't remember, think you buy them in at about 1-2 months old) to people who wanted a few hens in their back garden, we'd pick out the prettiest and least disabled for that (some healthy greens would always evade the catchers so they got sold off too). The rest had to be culled unfortunately.

Cows... Cows are awesome, they may not be as smart as pigs, but dairy cows at least (they are more used to people than beef cows) are really sweet (the violent ones go to slaughter early, they can do a lot of damage if they want to).

While I fully agree and respect your push for this greatly, I do believe this misses a huge financial factor.  Land. While in a vacuum these numbers add up, I unfortunately do not thing the majority of at least western countries could handle doing this. The amount of land required grows rapidly, for example expending a 10 square acre plot of land in each direction by 30% (to move up to prisons), you must purchase an additional 69 acres of land, as well ad that you have the cost of additional buildings and inefficiencies that come with larger distances. Free range would require significantly more land than that. 
In a small scale I believe this works in the way suggested in the video, but to feed everyone, I do not thing the amount of additional land required would lead to this being sustainable.
That being said, regardless of the cost I fully believe these improvements should take effect, and be incentivized by governments to do that - no matter how unlikely that is to happen. I just believe these numbers are HIGHLY optimisitic and the real cost is likely not even calculable due to how unpredictabley all of these farms suddenly expanding in size would be.

Author: @JustSomeGuy1177
Content:
As someone who is vegan (in large part due to Kurzgesagt videos on animals actually) I really appreciate this channel's ability to have a respectful, well researched discussion on this issue. I think a large part why being vegan or vegetarian is viewed as so negative is because a lot of discussion around the topic isn't about how to make reasonable changes in your own life to better the situation for animals, it's about being disrespectful to those who do eat meat and painting them as "immoral" (Peta and that vegan teacher comes to mind) instead of having respectful discussions around the topic and accepting that the world we live in is complicated and eating or not eating meat doesn't make you morally better or worse than someone. 

Plus it frustrates me that the people who eat meat are always painted as immoral, when in reality it's most certainly greedy corporations who hyper-inflate ethical or plant based products and make them inaccessible to the general public, and will then cut every ethical measure possible- even if it's cheap- to make a couple extra cents. If they don't cut ethical measures, then they put labels that will heavily exaggerate the measures they actually took to ensure the wellbeing of their animals just so they can bump the price tag. It makes it impossible for local farmers who do actually take good care of their animals to even compete with that, or market themselves when there's so many "ethically produced" labels that cried wolf over the years. I have no doubt in my mind that the general population would be very supportive of mandatory measures to better the lives of the animals we use, but unfortunately in a world of corporate greed and legal loopholes it's hard and expensive to make the better choice, especially when all the media surrounding animal wellbeing is just disrespecting and screaming at people who can't give up animal products even for completely valid reasons such as physical and mental wellbeing or price concerns.

Anyway, thanks for coming to my Ted Talk and great video as always Kurzgesagt :D

Author: @WolfVidya
Content:
I think a lot of these studies have a flaw in common: They calculate costs and leave it at that, besides having obvious blind spots such as not taking into account how to increase available space, how much farms would grow and or have to move to increase those spaces and worse, the space required to grow the extra natural food. Also important is what happens to actually doing all that and getting a product to market to compete when the change in the product's quality is negligible. 

Let's take Brazil as an egregious example, let's give pigs 300% more space per animal... How much Amazon forest do we need to kill for the pigs themselves. Now let's give them organic feed, how much more Amazon do we need to chop down to farm that feed?

Edit: No, I'm not advocating for veganism, I'm saying this grandstanding for animal morality might work in theoretical worlds of infinite space and costless land, thus sourcing them as guidance for how to act in the real world might be bogus.

Author: @Argentvs
Content:
This is a very simplistic, misleading and feels dishonest video.
First of all, the problem is SPACE, you cannot supply the global demand with free ranging animals. Very few countries like mine can do that.
Free ranging does inflate the price, because it is very EXPENSIVE in manpower time. But the most, most farmers do not have the space for so much cattle. The space demand would displace crops, which are used to feed the animals, so in the end you rise up land prices, renting and feed.
Those industrial practices are done mostly in Europe and Asia, we don't do that for the most part in Argentina for example. Most cows go free range, winter in river islands, natural and crop pastures feed with rations to speed up, winter feeding and final weight.

The US is not even the 2nd meat consumer. First and 2nd are Argentina and Uruguay, your research here was lacking hard.

And regulations only increase the prices. The European union regulations for food are nothing about animal welfare, they are market barriers for countries that outproduce and outcompete the inefficient european farming production. Those regulations are to ensure the european consumers cannot buy cheap produce from other countries so their farmers and goverments can have customers and tax payers in a fish tank. In the end you end up with old animals hard meat sold as premium under the quotas the EU allows to import and pay 15 times what I pay for better meat here. And I live in a farming area, so the animals are all locals, most cows are in open fields, only finish feed lots, pigs, sheep, etc is all traditional farming, we buy whole animals directly or you can buy at the butcher or supermarket.
Just chech the never ending EU-Mercosur free trade deal, Europe wants that we buy their industrial goods, pharma, cosmetics, cars no barriers whatsoever, but the don't want to include the agro in the deal. France directly says they won't do it because they cannot compete, and we tax heavily our farmers while in europe the state pay them subsidies.

Furthermore, the free ranging of animals with european regulations would multiply the prices, because small farms will have to pay a lot of things to keep up with them, turning unsustainable. Already is like that, the reason small farmers worlwide sell or rent to big farmers or corporations is because they cannot comply with regulations, they cannot access modern technology and constantly modernize and they don't have economy of escale. Is an unsolvable issue, here all small farmers just rent the lots and big farmers specialize in one or two parts of the process and act as contractors for others, when not making working pools or directly they are landless companies with equipment doing all the jobs as contractors.

Also free ranching chicken meat is hard, very hard compared to big indoors production.

You can improve the life of animals by eliminating bureaucracy, unnecessary regulations, nonsensical demands for farmers, tax reforms for producers, better access to financing for equipment and open markets for technology and produce with the world. Then the consumers will have lower cost options and farmers could find their niches.

Author: @VictorJD
Content:
This is the right conversation to have. I am skeptical of a consumer led movement for change though, because it runs into the same problem as opt-in organ donation, the inertia of making a change is too strong. It also runs into problems already mentioned in the comments and in this video: mislabelling with irrelevant inputs (e.g. GMO), overcharging for those extra labels (beyond the cost of any welfare improvement), and general misallocation of any price increase. I would add that multiculturalism also means that not all cultures share the same degree of western emphathy towards animals, and this sort of emotional appeal to consumer conscience will run into cultural differences.

A better solution is to lobby for regulations on the production side. Regulations should be sensitive to affordability at the point of retail and pragmatic at the farm level. Ideally, the labelling system should be standardized and the minimum level of animal welfare should be raised (e.g. not grinding male chicklets, minimum space requirements, etc...).

Author: @DwellerOfTheEarth
Content:
Additional points: 

1. If everyone made the decision to choose to eat the dead animals in what this video calls "decent" conditions, everyone would absolutely have to eat less meat. This video did not discuss the land usage required by factory farming and farming where animals roam more freely outdoors. It's not sustainable as is, and it simply could not work to take up even more space with animals in decent conditions, so just know that this means everyone would absolutely have to reduce their meat, dairy and egg consumption (as they should anyway for the animals and for the planet). Time is also important which is why factory farming is as horrible as it is, so changing the conditions would mean it takes longer. So basically, eat less meat and if you can then please just stop eating animals. It's awful for them and for the environment.

2. Cows: no matter what the farming conditions are like, artificial semination is necessary to impregnate the cows. If you want to see something absolutely disgusting, go look up what that process is like. Then, when the female cow gives birth, her calf is taken away from her so that the farmer can take the milk. They can't have a calf hanging around taking the milk they need to profit from, can they? This is standard practice. Time is important to be able to sell, so yes having a calf there doesn't help the farmer profit. When the dairy cow is "spent" and can't produce milk anymore, she goes to the slaughterhouse anyway. 

3. All slaughterhouses, where all animals end up, are inhumane. They end the life of an animal that would have preferred to be alive. If you don't believe me, go and actually look it up yourself, do some extra research and see it with your own eyes. If you look at it thinking that you'd like to be treated the way these animals have been treated, then fine. But the chances are, if you look at it and you think you wouldn't want that done to you, that's your indication you're looking at something unethical and inhumane. If you don't want to use yourself as an example, imagine a dog, cat or some other pet in the position of that farm animal being slaughtered and ask yourself if you'd want the same done to them. 

4. Animal farming is unsustainable. Again, just go and look this up, do some research please. This video isn't anti-meat but maybe it should be. More research should inform you of how unsustainable it is for people to keep eating animal products at the rate we are. 

While eating meat and animal products less is "less bad", it is not decent and not good enough for animals or the planet. More of us need to stop because there will always be those who will want to indulge and just don't care about animals or the planet. There will always be those who don't believe or understand the damage they're doing, so more of us need to make the choice to stop all together.

Author: @Sir-Sticky
Content:
Hey Kurzgesagt, while I agree with the intent of the video I must strongly disagree on one point: Seafood is not a safe alternative for humans at the moment due to Oestrogenic compounds in seawater.

I spent my degree & Masters looking into this in-part, but the general summary (and I strongly recommend reading some papers by my ex-professor Alex Ford, Portsmouth, UK) is that oestrogenic compounds (the pill, microplastics etc.) and most hormones are not actually filtered by modern chemical waste treatment plants efficiently (up to 90% survives into effluent water) and makes it into the waterways. They have a WILD effect on many molluscs who use oestrogen to influence behaviour, spawning rates, and (in)famously sexual organ expression which causes infrasex, intersex, and sterility.
This has an impact on both the biodiversity of shorelines and rivers, but it also has the added risk to humans: Bioaccumulation. If one small fish has 1g, and 100 small fish get eaten by a salmon, when you eat the salmon you get 100g of oestrogen (wildly overblown, but same principle).

The concern is that often molluscs hold oestrogen when they are biologically effected and become good transmission vectors to humans (since hormones are typically hard to biologically break-down). There are major concerns that human sperm count in predominantly fish diet countries has been decreasing aggressively for decades.

There is also a lot of evidence to suggest that microplastics interact as oestrogenic when ingested by animals, and filter-feeding molluscs could have significantly higher concentrations of microplastics than are reported (since there are no regulations on fish meat quality or chemical content in any country, anywhere in the world).

I'd strongly recommend any other form of meat to humans than molluscs or fish, simply because it is unregulated and often (quite literally) swimming in faeces.

Author: @Coffee_Enjoyer-z1o
Content:
used to taunt vegans with dismissive labels and not actually hearing them. I had been mired in my own tradition with my eyes closed and my own heart numb to convenience. After delving into Nietzsche, Kant, and Schopenhauer, however, my assumptions and the values that never really came home with myself came into dispute. Nietzsche's call to construct my own values, Kant's regard each and every life that may be capable of pain, and the appeal of Schopenhauer to compassion redirected the manner in which that I thought. Veganism wasn't political—it had been about existing in harmony with my own morals. I heard, I thought, and traveled a different course of direction, a course of direction that proceeded my own ethical compass and not the directions that had been instilled within myself. Man is claimed to be an animal of custom, ensnared in bondage by the weight of acquired tradition and the fetters of conformity. Yet free of the fetters—yet free—remains the course of higher will, the will beyond lower passions, blind custom, and the herd. I ended the use of animals not with a sensation of guilt, but with a deeper realization of my own power and duty. I ended because I knew that to partake of the pain of the world, even in the interest of tradition or pleasure, is to diminish my own power and my own dignity.

But hear this: I did not take this course with leave of it, nor did I take it so that you may be made culpable. The reason that I've made this choice is that I seek to construct a higher self—a self that does not yield to the will of the masses. To scoff at the choice of the individuals who've embraced compassion at the cost of ease of use, who've torn the shroud of deceptions that seek to rationalise violence, is to demonstrate a shortness of sight—a myopia that betrays herd mentality. We're not the weak that crave a life of compassion and cognizance, but the individuals who stay in ignorance and complacency and live in a yester that they've never questioned.

Let me be frank with you: Veganism has never been a political cause; it has been an awakening of conscience. Politicized—brought into the muck of surface argument and made a disunity device—why has the easy act of not harming when not required been a battle field? Because we fear confronting the truth? That it is easier to brand an item an "extreme" rather than confronting the extremity of violence that we construct comfort at the expense of? This is the deception that we need to move beyond.

And yes, there are a few that shriek loud and clear, that disturb with the unsubtle blow of an unrefined will. Those are the individuals who muddle the ground that they tread—who equate the force of the will with the force of the truth. Do not set the whole journey against the backdrop of the corruptors of the tools of transformation. The shrieking, the shaming protesters are children that know not how to use the force of reason, and yet you use them as the poster child of all vegans. The true vegan does not shriek; they just live the truth in quietude, in deed.

The taunting, the scorn, the sneering—it comes from a place of fear of facing the unsaid truth that gnaws at the fringes of us all: that we've placed tradition and comfort above a higher responsibility. The family will try and keep us trapped within the web of old traditions, and culture will try and instruct the deceptions of the way it has been done, but what does the word family truly stand if it kills the call of a higher good of the heart? What does culture truly stand if it celebrates wound as tradition? To free us of such bondage is not a betrayal, but a honoring of life itself.

Gaze toward the future—not the future of cold old-time attitudes, but the future of a larger conception of the self. The future in which we take power and will not yield it to the yokes of consumption and violence. To live with no fear of the guillotine does not make us a wimp, but derive strength of our own. To stand beyond the herd does not equate with loneliness, but blaze a new trail for the masses to follow.

If the vegan lifestyle irks you, it might be that it will force you toward an honest confrontation with that of which you do not want to admit—the unseen violence of your own life. There is no power stronger, however, no power finer, than facing that of which the rest of the world cannot face. Do not be intimidated with the truth; love it. Let the old-school notions of power and strength dissolve and realize that true strength lies in existing within harmony with compassion and intelligence. This is not politics. This is the emergence of a new consciousness—a new consciousness that will not be beholden, that will not be ruled yet goes beyond the herd mentality, the tradition, the culture and the artificial values that ensnared us in servility. Let us journey this course not in revolt, yet in the soft power of the righteous who realize that they march in the righteous cause.

Author: @Kapisketo
Content:
As someone who comes from a farmer family all that says this video is true but also false. I shouldn't say false but it's a very complex market that we could talk for weeks about it's troubles. For example in Spain due to tracking systems you can know in the supermarket from exactly what farm you meat comes. It's really hard to receive less than 1€ per kg of net meat and watching how they are selling it at 20€ as a gourmet meat. As my father says, for that price it's cheaper to use the cows and just killing them and throw the meat to the dogs instead of buy kibble for the dogs he also raises. Also it's interesting how you need to fight in prices with another country that permits using hormones without any control so their's animals grow faster and you even have troubles to use antibiotics in a sick animal because of local laws. But they expect you to match their pricing. Also as a small farm that only has 40 adult cows you can't afford to do direct selling to customers so you need to sell it to the dealers at the price they say (or sometime sell it to friends that know how you cows live and have a freezer big enough to keep a whole cow inside).
I'm really a meat lover and I know that I should it more vegetables but also ecologic farming of vegetables require more land that the ones that use fertilizers or pesticides and using more lands also means less space for wild animals of even having "attacks" from will boards that ruin you whole season because you started farming in the same place where they lived before.

So... It's complicated, even being part of the producing chain is hard to know what is better to do. Also the pricing that you said that would increase in using more ethical meat is for each person, just imagine a 4 member family, that is a ton of money for some people.

Content:
love the channel but some of this is incorrect, especially the claim that using heritage breeds vs cornish cross will only make a breast cost 9c more, which is insanely dishonest and a flat-out lie.

Cornish crosses are crosses and yes they do have issues, but many can raise em just fine. the problems happen when they aren't cared for properly and are overfed, as they are a lazy breed and will happily sit there and eat as much as they can, they also have a far more efficient feed conversion ratio of 2:1 or 3.5:1 (lbs of feed : lbs of weight) depending on conditions. meanwhile, heritage birds take way longer and more feed, going up to 6.2:1 or even higher taking months.
This is triple the amount of feed bare minimum for the same pound of meat, not to mention more time and the fact cornish crosses have a lot of meat compared to bones, vs heritage breeds which have less meat. At best this would literally triple the cost of your chicken, but at worst, well... more time to grow = more money regardless, more chances for stuff to go wrong as well etc.

seriously, it would cost way more. not to mention how much people will view this vid and not look any of this up themselves

Author: @yeldarBkereD
Content:
I agree with the video’s message, it’s very impractical from a business perspective.

While Ive spent half of my life working on a farm, I do have two problems with this video:

1) The price difference seems great per individual, but at scale, the cost is an enormous difference for producers.

2) These prices are not taking losses into consideration. A 10% price increase on sales is a 10% increase on losses as well. 

3) These changes will only make you less competitive compared to the producers who don’t make these changes. Companies that buy eggs in bulk buy exponentially more eggs than regular consumers, and those increases in costs will send them elsewhere.

We need more videos like this shining the light on cruel practices. We need innovations to make ethical treatment more economically viable. We need more companies buying in bulk to promote ethically sourced meat.

Author: @LegendOfMoonDragons
Content:
As a note on organic, which I agree is the *better* option, my aunt runs a cow, duck & lamb farm and uses organic practices but isn't certified. That's because if she wanted to be, she wouldn't be able to use antibiotics on her animals if they got sick, period. What she does instead is not slaughter any animal that needed antibiotics at any point. Her farm's not massive, but she's got at least 500 head cattle and maybe 300 sheep (50ish ducks??), so she's not small either. They all live outside and are slaughtered the same or next day they're taken to the slaughterhouse, meaning they don't have to get to a certain weight in a feeding lot. Again, if you can afford it and there's one nearby, farmers markets are probably the best places to get meat and eggs.

I'm vegetarian myself, but for a long time the only meat I would eat was from her farm, because I knew how the animals were treated. What you say about reducing meat is how I tend to approach people; if you're at a resturant and there's a veggie option of your regular noodle soup, give it a go. If you're buying ravioli and see there's a pumpkin and cheese one, try that. Going veggie actually expanded my tastes a lot, and I'm more interested in good food now. I don't recommend having a 'vegetarian day', I personally couldn't stick to that because it felt like I was missing out. The trick is finding vegetarian things you genuinely like just as much or better than meat, and gradually eating more of them. You need to find things with protein in them too: I eat a lot of legumes (lentils & chickpeas) and eggs. A lot of people turn their noses up at legumes but you can replace things like mince for spagetti really easily with lentils, partially mashing them, and it's honestly just as good. Anything covered in a strong tasting sauce or tomato or soy is a good start, because so long as you're getting that protein you don't miss meat at all.

The thing that makes me upset is the slaughtering of male chicks. I just spent some time doing research and I can't find any local companies in Australia that do egg sexing. I eat a lot of eggs which I get through my aunt from another farm near her, but I haven't visited that bloke's farm myself and have no idea if he participates in killing male chicks. I imagine he does. I desperately need that protein though, and even more importantly, the B12 in eggs, because I can't get it from meat. I don't know if there's anything I can do about that :(

Author: @CharlesBosse
Content:
TL;dr 👏 Eat 👏 less 👏 meat 👏

Here's the thing: government policies, trade agreements, and tax dollars in most countries pretty aggressively subsidize the meat industry and it's major inputs (food used in feed lots, commercial transportation of cattle, etc.) Sadly, you can't "buy organic" to solve this. You can buy direct from a farm or small catch hunter/fisher but that's both a pretty extreme luxury for most and also something that doesn't solve the fundamental problems of commercial/industrial animal product production. 

Perhaps at the core of the issue in is the aimple fact that we don't have enough land to support anywhere near current populations of humans eating current amounts of meat in anything close to humane ways. In fact, we don't have enough land to do it in inhumane ways: cattle farming is a HUGE contributor to the burning of rainforests, and of course to habitat distruction elsewhere and the release of an absurd amount of methane. We simply can't put all the cattle, much less food animals overall, currently in torture conditions, much less all the ones in either torture or "prison", into substantively better conditions. Sure, we could move perhaps 10% into better conditions for just a small markup, but then the costs start to increase in a feedback loop. 

As someone who has spent the last decade endeavoring to buy and consilume no animal products except for our obligat carnivores (house cats), I absolutely understand how hard that can be (and I freely acknowledge that have the benefits of privilege allowing me to do so). I also understand that meat can possibly be raised in a fundamentally less harmful way, just not in the quantities or ways we consume it. So, first and fundamentally, humans need to eat less meat. Around a century ago we jumped from meat being less than 15% of our diets to more than 30% in the USA. If we once again agreed culturally that meat was a bit of a luxury and not an essential daily meal, we could go a long way toward better health, better treatment of animals, and less environmental damage without actually "giving up" anything (though I have frankly eaten better and more interesting food as a vegan than I ever did as an omnivore, so I honestly find it hard to say I "gave up" meat). With the understanding that people who can and want to go fully vegan deserve support and not the bullying our society pushes, I also want to say that simply eating LESS meat and animal products STILL makes a difference. If meat tastes too good to give up, only eat it when it's something special. If vegan alternatives are too expensive or unavailable, then center your meals around healthy produce and legume or grain protien as much as possible and leave the animal ingredients for the sauces that have been ways to strech animal ingredients back when those were priced to reflect their real, rather high, cost. And every time you buy meat, from a small farm or local butcher, or from the market or supermarket, remember that everyone is paying extra for that and even the most "ethical" meat is taking money away from other things our economy (and government) should be supporting.

Author: @paulvanginkel4720
Content:
This video is not an accurate representation of the pork industry.

With pigs, a massive part of why they are kept indoors is disease prevention.  Birds and pigs carry similar diseases and allowing pigs to be outside would significantly increase disease amongst them as they are likely coming into proximity of wild birds.  This would lower pig life quality and increase deaths.  If there are a lot of pig farms in one area, such as north Iowa, allowing pigs to be outside would significantly increase disease rates, as wild birds can interact with many different pig farms and spread disease.  Another part of keeping pigs indoors is temperature control.  A lot of places with pigs can get cold winters, and having them outdoors in the cold would not be good.  

As for the crates for sows, calling them straitjackets is inaccurate.  While they do restrict movement, they are not as tight as the video makes then seem.  They also decrease the amount of piglets that get killed when a sow lays down, as a sow is ~500 pounds while a piglet weighs next to nothing.  A sow laying down on a piglet can easily lead to the death of the piglet.  If the sow could lay down anywhere, piglets would be more likely to end up under her.  The crate allows for space that the sow can't access for the piglets to run to when she lays down.  For the farm I grew up on, piglets are not separated by metal bars, but by plastic slats.

Piglets being separated from their mothers at 3 weeks is a lie, at least on the farm that I grew up on.  The farm I grew up on, piglets were separated from their mothers at 6 or 7 weeks, after they were weaned off milk.  After the piglets are weaned, the sows are kept in loose housing, where they are able to walk freely with the rest of the sows.  For castration, anesthesia is used.

The fighting that happens amongst older pigs has to do with a pecking order, and keeping pigs from interacting with new pigs prevents fighting.   The pens that older pigs are kept in generally are quite spacious, and not as cramped as this video makes it seem.  

Calling pig farms torture chambers is not accurate.  I cannot speak for the chicken or beef industries, but I'd wager that this video doesn't do them justice either, as pig farms were very misrepresented.

Author: @mtoboekid11mouse88
Content: Theres one good label to look out for besides organic I've seen cropping up - look up certified humane. Its a set of reasonable guidelines with the goal of giving the animals good lives while also not having a bunch of pseudoscience nonsense (for example, 'no antibiotics ever' labelling incentivizes farmers not to treat animals when they're actually sick, and instead they suffer more because of the profit loss in treating them as once treated they can't be sold as no antibiotics anymore.) I've asked my dad who is a veterinarian in primarily large agricultural animals to look it over, and he agrees its actually fairly solid. I believe that as of now, its not an official or regulated label, but they're trying to make it so, and currently its something people opt into and enforce among the organization itself rather than the government, but still - I think its one of the better starting places and is objectively better than organic in terms of actually addressing animal wellfare.

Content:
I keep chickens on a quarter-acre suburban block, and when I first got them, I used to lock them up at night. Every morning, they would cry until I let them out, so now they free range in the garden every day. Sure, it’s some work to clean up after them, but I’m not going to lock them up 24/7 just because they dig up a few plants or make a mess on the lawn. The way some people treat chickens is shocking—locking them in tiny, cramped pens for their entire lives just to avoid minor inconveniences. There needs to be a higher standard for backyard chicken-keeping, ensuring they get proper free-ranging time. Keeping animals comes with responsibility, and it’s cruel to deny them even the most basic freedoms.

This goes for cats too—don’t get one if you’re just going to keep it locked in a tiny apartment for its entire life. Animals deserve space, enrichment, and a life worth living.

Author: @carcharhinus_555
Content:
Haven't watched the video too far, and know I'm all for better standards. But even if there are government mandates, laws etc that try to enforce otherwise, the assumption that (consumer) surcharge would be based on base price, i.e. not apply to the upcharge for better livestock standards is honestly absurd. That's just not how supply chains and markets work. It's even worse, they *cannot* work that way because surcharge mostly isn't plain margins, but usually comes from hedging. If the current price to buy is x and the "upcharge" for better standards is y, a lost shipment is always $(x+y), something being overdue always loses $(x+y), there's barely *any* situation x and y can be separated so sales margins could only apply to x. And I'm sorry to say, but you *know* this. I think it's still not just a small price to pay, but our darn duty to pay it, because it's just not OK to be cruel to animals to gain a 30% discount on meat.
But the same (i.e. we should be fine to pay a premium to not enforce suffering on others, incl. human beings) can be said about lots of other things, from asylum seekers/migration, climate crisis, the Ukraine war to cheap but environment destructive small goods. Yet, not only do we choose the cheap way out, but recently we even elect governments most people know very well don't have a solution, but are simply fine to exploit others for seemingly minor benefits. So... good luck I guess, maybe the next generation cares more (if they get the chance)?

Author: @Pieguy527
Content:
I personally have been trying to buy more expensive meat which indicates free range or similar, "non-torture" conditions. But I still had an issue with spoilage at times - even knowing I had spent more and was trying to use every last piece to get my money's worth. 

If you're trying to do the same, I highly recommend purchasing a vacuum sealer and a sous vide, as my meat waste is practically 0 now. I trim, season, and vacuum seal the meat, then freeze it which can last for much longer than chucking it in the freezer. I've taken meat out after months without any of the typical freezer burn or weird textures I've experienced when freezing straight in the package. Plus, you get all of the raw meat handing out of the way in one day after shopping - no need to contaminate a bunch of utensils, cutting boards, and yourself with raw meat every time you cook.

When I get home from work I will throw in some chicken breast for 4 hours, and then take it out and place it into the fridge overnight. The next day for dinner, I either chop it up and eat it cold over a salad, or I'll sear it on the pan for some browning and to re-heat. Perfect every time. And don't even get me started on the 36 hour beef roasts!

Author: @snowthemegaabsol6819
Content:
It's not fair to compare the percentage increase of meat prices to what they used to cost 40 years ago. It's not that simple. And it's not that simple because the average person had more buying power with the wages they made back then.
This should be immediately obvious if you take one look at the consumer price index. Since 1985, it has basically tripled, meaning you need 3x the amount of money to buy the same amount of stuff. Both goods and services. Average wage relative to the CPIs of these respective years shows that the effective wage has actually gone down since then, by almost 13%. And even that's not entirely fair because there are huge disparities in the cost of living depending on where you live and wage gaps that still haven't shrunk in the past 50 years. As most people are necessarily in the lower majority, the decrease is even steeper.

Factoring in the increased cost of literally everything else, people simply have less money overall to spend on meats. So if you look at it in terms of cost relative to the budget people actually have, they would be significantly more expensive now compared to back then if the prices were increased.

Content:
I'll preface this by saying I agree with you on buying the highest welfare (and so usually the most expensive) meat you can afford. I've had to decrease my meat consumption massively over the last decade to do this but its worth it to ensure I'm not contributing as much to the bad actors who use these destructive and cruel methods.

Public transport costs have increased by 20%.
Private transport costs have increased by 65%.
Higher Education costs have increased by 120% (most didn't even charge for access).
Healthcare costs (basically prescriptions and procedures not covered by the NHS) have increased by 30%.
Hell, fruits and vegetable expenditures have gone up 300%!
Reminder this is compared to one of the worst economic decades the UK has ever seen...
The fact it used to take the average worker 3 years to save for a house, while now you're looking at 8+ years? Your argument about a small increase in price meaning a big hike in welfare of our meat is great and one I whole heartedly agree with. But trying to compare it to expenditure in the past like you did is so disingenuous in my opinion.

Author: @lmelior
Content:
Tofu at my local Aldi is $1.55 for 1 lb, and a can of chickpeas is $0.79.  Crumble or cube up the tofu, toss it or the chickpeas with a bit of oil and whatever seasonings match the rest of your meal, air fry them, and add them to your plate.  They taste good, provide some nice variation in texture, and they're cheaper than the extra animal protein you'd otherwise add to your plate.

Speaking of cheaper, you don't really need eggs, either.  They only became a breakfast staple because they were cheap, and now they're not, so you might as well just stop eating them.  Just make a breakfast scramble without them, or you can use tofu with some seasonings including black salt/kala namak and turmeric powder to get it fairly close to mimicking the look, smell, feel, and taste of scrambled eggs.  And most recipes calling for eggs have perfectly serviceable substitutes as well.  My homemade pancakes have been turning out just as good using unsweetened applesauce and a bit of extra baking powder.  My daughter made an amazing batch of chocolate chip cookies by using chia seeds soaked in water instead of eggs.  And no joke, my French toast is genuinely better and more uniform using cornstarch instead of egg (unless you're one of those weirdos that eats "French toast" [i.e. eggy bread] with ketchup instead of the proper cinnamon-y sweet real stuff, in which case just stop 🤣).

Like the video says, you don't have to cut out meat entirely to have a positive effect on reducing animal suffering...and if you don't care about that, your wallet.  And probably your health, too.  I'm not vegan, but I eat mostly vegan food anyway for all those reasons.

Author: @germanespionage6593
Content:
Philosophically, I suppose the question is: how does the value we attribute to an animal's life balance with the value of our own lives?

For sake of argument, lets say we can assign a number, that number being the value of an animal's life. This value is a function of both the quality and length of the animal's life--I think most people would agree that a long life is not inherently one of value if the quality of that life is terrible, and that the inverse would be true. Anything that increases the quality and length of its life can be said to be good, and anything which reduces those two things can be said to be bad. 

Important to note that the only thing that matters is our perception of quality, length, and how the two balance against each other, since the value we assign to them is inherently subjective. 

Assuming infinite choices, people would choose meat according to this formula:
(Positive value of consuming the meat [influenced by cost, comfort, diet, etc]) - (Negative value of consuming the meat [discomfort, health, etc]) = x (net value)
Where their choice is the meat which provides the highest net value to them.

Diving into personal opinion here...

The only reason the value of an animal's life matters to (most of) us humans is because we perceive it as impactful on the value of our own lives. The **impact to us** (whether it be emotional discomfort or something else) is what most people care about, not the actual value of the animal's life. If we wanted to get even more specific, it's not the impact of the value of an animal's life on our own life that we care about, but actually the impact that the KNOWLEDGE of the value of the animal's life has on us. 

^ (If we did not know the animals we were eating were suffering, it would not be a source of negative value. This, however, ignores that some factors like the health of the meat impact the value of our lives regardless of whether we know about it or not.)

If we genuinely cared about the lives of the animals, we would give them blissful and long lives and only consume them after they die naturally. But very few people actually suggest this. In reality, most people are willing to accept that the animals they eat will go through some level of "unnecessary" (to the animal) suffering, whether it be from a premature/unnatural death, crowded conditions, etc, because cheap access to food is perceived as increasing the value of our lives. 

So I argue, then, that the animal living a life of value only matters insofar as it results in an increase in the value of the consumer's life in measurable ways like health. As long as the consumer does not know the animal suffered, it does not create negative value to the consumer. When knowledge is 0, the only thing that matters is delivering the cheapest and healthiest meat to the consumer. And a chicken that is dead certainly does not care about whatever value its life had.

Author: @stefanvanacht7524
Content:
I don’t fully agree with your point about chickens. A broiler chick is actually a very healthy chick because it can digest its food very efficiently. A chick that isn’t healthy wouldn’t be able to do that. The claim that these chickens can’t stand on their legs is also incorrect—if that were true, they wouldn’t be able to walk to get water and feed. So in little worlds, if a chick isn't healthy, a farmer could never make any profit on it.

Another important point is that we often judge animal welfare based on what we think is best, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the chick perceives it the same way. Data shows that mortality actually increases when chickens are allowed outside due to higher exposure to diseases and disruptions in ventilation inside the house.

If we truly want to improve welfare for chicks, maybe we should focus on what welfare means for the chick itself rather than how humans interpret it.

Author: @fredhawken1112
Content:
Good video but unfortunately it is not that easy. And talking about cents as if its not that much money is misleading, we need to talk percentages to have a correct understanding.

The issues mentioned here are MOSTLY (but not exclusively) due to having to feed roughly 8 billion people efficiently.
Usually food production is spoken of in calories per m2. If you were to expand the mentioned living spaces to those mentioned in the video for the whole global meat production, there would be not enough space to house all the animals. And the calories per m2 would go down, so efficiency would go down and prices will rise A LOT more than those cents mentioned in the video because all that land needs to be maintained, watered, distances would become bigger and more people are needed to do the labour, bigger lands require more costs and are taxed heavier.
Feeding all those animals with grass and or grain would take A lot more space for the feed crops to grow and there would be no more room left for human food crops. Today already a massive part of our agriculture is solely to feed our meat industry. Again, calories per m2 would go down and prices would rise even more.

So eat less meat you say? Yeah there are some problems with that too. Meat is way more energy dense than vegetables. Because of the lower energy density the calories per m2 for vegetables are way lower than for meat production so we would need almost ten times as much room to feed 8 billion people. And this is not taking into account that it is often more profitable for farmers to grow crops for bio fuels instead of foodcrops, so it makes land surface used even more of an issue, with the whole (forced) greenification of our transport systems. Knowing that only a small percentage of earths surface is able to be used as agricultural land leaves us with not enough room for everybody to "go vegan".

Meat also provides us with important proteins and other fats and animal products that we are not able to produce artificially. We are evolved over millions of years to eat animal products, we need those molecules. There would be a lot more malnutrition in the world if people would be forced to eat less animal products (NOT ONLY MEAT)
Our cows, for example, not only provide us with meat, but also with milk, cheese, leather, gelatin, tallow, insulin, collagen, cartilage, hairs,... The list is very long and we would need to change or give up a lot of our modern society and products if we were to "consume" less animals. Most animals we consume are not only used as meat, people seem to forget this a lot.

And a lot of those things could be said for our agricultural industry too. Agriculture is also responsible for a big chunk of CO2 emissions, not all agriculture is good for the environment. Pesticides, chemical deterrents, growth stimulators,... Agriculture is responsible for a lot of water pollution and land that is un usable for decades. And to be really semantic, isnt plant life also life? Is it not also cruel to grow those plants so close to each other and then farm them with heavy industrial machinery?

Why am i saying this? Nature is cruel, nature does not give a f* about animals feelings. We are part of nature, or are we not? Problem is we humans can think about it and feel bad about things and we will let our emotions come in the way of logical and practical thinking. How far do we want to go to remove a subjective feeling of cruelty? Or do we want to feed our ever growing population with high energy food for everyone? Efficiency does not need to be equal to cruelty, but it IS a very delicate balance.

Just playing devils advocate here, again, good video and awareness about our food industries need to grow and i totally agree that we need to be more "humane" in our food consumption and have a good look at our industrial scale food production, be it meat or agriculture. But the whole global food/meat production has way more nuance than this video shows and i feel a lot is left out to make people feel guilty about eating their daily meat.

Content:
Well its not going to happen because capitalism.
Capitalism seeks infinite growth. And once the majority of cheap and decent land has been taken, once all the major competitors have settled into their roles, and once the supply chain is basically sorted, the only thing left to do is cut corners for further growth. Food deserts harshly limit the quality, price, and convenient food options. If Wal-mart is 40 minutes in any direction, theres atleast 5 Dollar Generals eating up that space to justify not building anything more meaningful.

Nothing short of concerted government effort, informative campaigns, and general increase in the quality of living and wages for the poorest 30% of citizens can curb cruelty. Without a government cracking down, farms will just be more secretive (Ag-gag laws that strictly prohibit slaughterhouse filming, because it hurts meats reputation), without information campaigns peoples ignorance will allow them to consume meat from farms and industries peddling cruelty for its convenience, and without increase in wages, the largest markets of meats wont be able to afford anything less cruel to begin with.
