Author: @tennistaekwondopiano
Content:
I'll caveat what I'm about to say with this: I have always loved Kurzgesagt, this topic is incredibly important as these animals are just as emotionally and intellectually intelligent as the pets we keep (as was said), and I understand the harm minimisation approach. BUT I can't help but feel that this approach and video is so harmful on three fronts. First, during a time of insane inequality, advocating that the poorest members of communities pay more is WILD when meat production companies take incredible profits.
Second, it is simply not good enough to claim that 100% of people paying for a shift to practices that encompass <1% of farming would even be possible from a land use, climate change and ecological impact perspective.
Third, during one segment, the words Kurzgesagt said were that we don't know if these practices are even good enough to be called welfare, just maybe slightly better, but the animations showed a happy pig sleeping calmly in cuddly hay. For pigs, having 60% of your life in the torture that was shown here instead of 100% with the same intelligence as a dog is still barbaric. For cows, having 10% of your life in torture and then watching your fellow cows die in the slaughter house before meeting the same grizzly end is barbaric. Ultimately these animals are still bred to be killed young in barbaric ways that sometimes fail leading to torture, tortured for the time they are alive as shown, and all with the emotional and intelligence faculties to experience unbelievable suffering.
Kurzgesagt, you have shed light on a truly barbaric thing that we all contribute to with this video, but then advocated in a harmful direction. Please do better and make a video on the economic possibility of taking governmental meat-subsidies and other funding away to instead support farmers transitioning away from slaughter and into plant-based protein sources

Author: @davestrider9535
Content: So I’m a dairy farmer in Canada, and a lot of what the video says is absolutely true. Now I can’t speak much for the meat production, but when it comes to milk the main issue is just the logistics of milking a large herd. Farms here tend to be smaller than those in the states because of supply management (won’t go too deep into that not the point right now), but even so we’re talking about farms that are milking 80+ animals twice a day. There’s very few ways to move that many animals in and out of a barn on a regular basis without putting a bullet in your brain. Some newer barns are free stall barns where cows are not chained up in place, and there’s a lot of innovative technology like milking carousels or robots, but these are very expensive. There are farmers in my area that spent actual millions to build these new high tech barns, but the problem is that this is generational debt because milk doesn’t make THAT much money, at least not enough to pay off a 5 million dollar barn in a reasonable time. And then all it takes is an interest rate hike and all of a sudden these people are screwed. Cheaper barns are the old standing stall barns where cows are chained and don’t move. This is definitely in no way a decent life for the animal. But they are more affordable and while they don’t get built as much any more, many farms use it because it’s a legacy design that was built say 30 years ago and is still being used. But the alternative is incredibly expensive. Sure at the end of the day the consumer may only pay a few more cents per litre of milk from a pasture raised dairy, but how much did the farmer pay? Even if they get a better price (BIG IF btw), it’s not enough to offset the debt they have put themselves in. Add on the ever increasing price of land and it can get pretty hopeless pretty quickly unfortunately

Author: @Silverhorse777
Content:
*sighs* I used to like Kurzgesagt's videos, but with this level of blatant lies and manipulation - sorry, I can't anymore...

All of this applies only to small-scale communities and small farms that own a lot of land, and magically don't make additional expences from that. All of those ideas simply cannot be scaled up when you're talking about feeding millions of people. I worked at a relatively medium-sized poultry farm/plant in Russia and I can say that almost everything in this video is literally a nonexistent utopian dream when you're starting to consider real conditions. You could say "oh, Russia is a giant country, they own insane amounts of land, what's the problem"? This is the problem. On an industrial farm just one aviary could house up to 100000 birds. Just think about this. 100000 BIRDS. And there could be a dozen of those aviaries at just one site - you need one or two for hatchlings, several for growing birds (Birds don't grow up instantly, you know? It takes up to 70 days), several for egg-laying birds, some for reserve, some for quarantine, etc. Okay, that's a lot, it's usually about 30-50k birds in one building, but you got the scale. That's how much you need to feed a relatively small city, every single day. Let's say we decide to let those birds roam free. Can you even imagine how big the field for those birds should be and how you will control this amount of birds on this field?

Then, environmental issues. You think poultry farms are all greeny-green, let the birds roam free, this will all be natural? WRONG. If we talk about 100, maybe even 1000 birds - yes. If we talk about 100k birds - hell no. Birds are living creatures. They eat. They poop. They poop a lot. The waste those birds produce is a very, very big problem. Try to drive near the processing division of those farms that work on recycling all this waste and not choke on the insane smell. If you let all those birds roam free even in relatively enclosed grassland areas, how do you intend to collect the waste? Let it rot on the field? Congratulations, you're open to an unprecedented ecological disaster. Poultry waste in these amounts, unprocessed, is toxic to the environment. It attracts bugs. A lot of bugs. It poisons water sources, which was a big issue on my worksite -  they had to construct a whole separate water-cleaning plant on site. And you seriously think this is all free and could add just a few cents on one egg?

Then, biological issues. Ever heard of bird flu? Or other infections? You can pump those poor birds with vaccines and antibiotics to the brim, those are not 100% protective. Even if birds are kept in closed aviaries, vaccinated and everything, even if you found ONE dead wild bird on site, presumably infectuous, the whole aviary has to be exterminated. No exceptions. Any viral infection is deadly dangerous on this scale. Now, imagine this amount of birds in open spaces, contacting freely with wld birds, elements and everything else. Are you ready for your business to be turned into a no-trespassing zone of biological hazard within a week? Are you ready for the new pandemic?

Okay, let's say we switched from large plants to a lot of small private farms. I'm not sure even Russia have this amount of free space for all those farms on this scale, but whatever. For a small farm, it's easier to provide those "good" conditions for the birds, and it makes almost no difference in expences, no difference in logistics, no difference in vet control, no difference in supporting ethics we are caring about, it's just a few $$$ more, right? Right? Let's just stop here and think about it, without juggling all those fancy numbers of "cents per egg". It works for a small community, a small city, a small country. It DOESN'T work in any way when you need to provide food for 100kk+ people in your country. Need for efficiency in every single aspect will eradicate all those ideas on root level instantly. And I don't even talk about the money issues for people who will (or won't) buy this meat.

Author: @Zoltri
Content:
For anyone curious on ways to eat less meat, but not feel like you're having a less satisfying eating experience, try looking outside of the normal Meat, Veg, Potato structure of most North American & Western European meal structures. 

Meal options like Curries, Burritos, Steam Buns, Noodle bowls, etc can use 1/4th or 1/2 of a normal portion of meat, but it really doesn't feel like you're missing out on anything.
Think of it like a pizza, If you get something like Pepperoni, Bacon on a pizza, It doesn't leave you with a feeling that you missed out on meat in the experience, right? But how much meat was actually on your pizza? If you have 4 slices, you probably at like, 15% of the meat you would've eaten if you had a full chicken breast as the protein for a meal. 

I'm not trying to demonize meat, but I think its just a helpful perspective to have. Something like Bao buns(Steambuns) are extremely cheap to make, and when you can get 3 portions of dinner out of what would normally be a single meal, it does help with both budgeting and having a positive impact on the global demand on meat, without compromising on your eating experience at all.

Author: @aureusphoenix
Content:
Dear Kurzgesagt-Team,
thank you for the excellent video as always.

If there will ever be a next Iteration, I would like to suggest some additional aspects to touch upon:

- The fact that many dairy cows are slaughtered while still pregnant
- The fact the PMSG is sourced from so-called horse blood farms where mare miscarriages are a fundamental part of how the farms operate
- The fact that dead laying hens and other forms of slaughterhouse waste are exported to developing countries because that is cheaper than proper waste management. This in turn causes the spread of disease, the loss of jobs, and the increase of food prices in those countries.
- The fact that male chicken offspring no longer killed on Day 1 (e.g. in Germany) is now also being sent abroad because producers are not able/willing to price their meat competitively. Again, they are typically sent to Africa without an uninterrupted cold chain.
- The fact that the import of feed from developing countries with strong currencies such as the euro and dollar causes the skyrocketing of food prices in those countries
- The fact that even without economic pressure (e.g. in small German villages like the one I grew up in) animals are typically raised somewhere between Prison and Torture Camp. Once people are long enough "in the business" (i.e. seeing animal slaughter regularly) they stop being empathic, they start objectifying animals and they will not respectfully treat them until they are forced by law. I know what I am talking about. I was on "their" side until I was in my 30s.


Thanks again for your great work!

Author: @Abyssinian121
Content: I live in Colorado, and a law passed four years ago regarding cage-free and pasture-raised eggs JUST went into effect. Retailers in CO can no longer offer eggs from producers who raise birds in battery cages or inhumane conditions. Our climate does not allow for year-round pasture-raised birds, as is the practice in the Sun Belt, so eggs are pretty expensive here. However, in-state producers had four years to convert their operations, and keeping their birds indoors, with enough room to roam around, turns out to be a pretty good way to keep flocks from contracting avian influenza (provided the workers are using proper hygiene practices (changes of boots and clothing, decontamination between inside and outside of barns, etc. I have been purchasing pasture-raised eggs for a very long time, partly for ethics and partly because pasture-raised eggs have a superior color and taste. I want these laws to stay in place, so I make a point of purchasing cage-free and pasture-raised eggs when I get the chance, and throwing nothing away. If the egg is coming up to its 'best by' date, I'll scramble it with salt or a bit of sugar, and freeze that until I need to bake. As for meat, nothing does to waste, including the bones, which I turn into bone broth, when I purchase an ethically-raised chicken or cut of pork. This lowers the cost of the meat per meal, by allowing me to get more meals out of the animal. I can get at least eight meals out of one whole roasted chicken (four with the meat, and at least four with a broth made from the carcass). We have to be kinder, smarter and lest wasteful with animal-based food. Our ancestors certainly were.

Author: @ralphiegouch110
Content:
Kansas farmer and educator here (it's actually my job to teach adults about farming and have degrees in farming). 
-One, there would undoubtedly be a much higher price increase than what it mentioned here to go pure "free-range" on our livestock. The 75 to 100% more expensive would probably be more inline with reality. It's a matter the scale of the livestock industry is truly huge and the land and labor cost increases would be huge as well. 
-Two, there are lots of industry regulations that specifically keep pigs and chickens in the conditions that they live in. It's mostly about disease control but it honestly goes far beyond reasonable. 
-Three, as a cattle producer, I know most about this industry. Cattle spend the last 60 to 90 days in a feed lot. It's not great, but it's also not the 1/3rd of their lives mentioned. Our cattle are nearly a year old when we sell them and they go to Flint Hills for another 4 to 5 months, then the go to the feedlots of western Kansas for 60 to 90 days. 
-Four, Organic label means different things for different industries. In cattle it might not mean a better life for animals than non-organic. To get the best CHANCE of actual free-range for entire life, I'd look for stuff with all the labels. Organic, certified grass-fed, ect. Both are regulated labels. 
-Five, I'm a Kansan farm boy and even I disagree with the level of cruelty in the meat industry. While my family's and I beef and eggs come from our own livestock, that's not possible for nearly anyone.
-Six, Farmers and ranchers grow the meat and this is who be most affected by any change, but we mostly certainly aren't the ones making the profit in the industry. 
To change all this would be FAR greater than a regulation overhaul. It would be a real understanding that from now on all meat would be twice as expensive, had to be produced here in the U.S., and would require a complete industry rebuild. Oddly enough, some of this is happening very slowly.

Author: @xanzon5084
Content:
Okay, this might be a bit longer:

1. The Problem of Sufficient Space for Animals
When it comes to giving animals more space to live (to reduce their suffering and increase their quality of life), larger farms or corporations can often manage these costs more easily than small family-run farms.
Small family businesses already operate on very tight margins and struggle to stay competitive, even under current conditions.
Acquiring more land is expensive, and the increased costs (land, housing, feed) can push small farmers into bankruptcy, especially if they can’t raise prices enough to cover these expenses.
While more humane meat might be more appealing for animal welfare reasons, in many markets it doesn’t necessarily sell in high enough volumes or at premium prices that make it profitable for smaller farms.

2. Inflation and Recession Concerns
Speaking from a German perspective, the recent years have been tough financially: Germany is dealing with recession and high inflation.
We are already paying more for basic goods whose quality hasn’t improved, so adding yet another price increase for more humanely produced products can be unmanageable for many.
For example, if a 10-pack of eggs costs around 3 euros (and sometimes 3.60 euros), raising that price to 5.05 euros is significant. That extra 2 euros or so adds up, especially when you multiply it across various grocery items.
This also affects restaurants: if you used to pay around 10–15 euros for a schnitzel, you might now pay 20–30 euros because of inflation. With an additional price hike to ensure better animal welfare, the cost could rise to 25–35 (or even 30–40) euros for a single meal.
For many consumers, such increases are simply unaffordable.

3. The Question of “Bio” (Organic) Products
There is a common belief that “bio” automatically means “better,” but many studies suggest that the difference between standard and organic products is not always as significant as people think.
For instance, you might pay 5 euros for a smaller portion of organic chicken compared to 2 euros for a larger portion of conventional chicken, with no obvious difference in taste or clear evidence of substantially better animal welfare.
Labels can be misleading, and higher prices do not always guarantee truly humane or ecologically beneficial farming practices.

4. Time Constraints for Consumers
Many people have busy lives filled with work, family responsibilities, and personal hobbies. They often don’t have the time to research the best sources of ethically produced meat.
While some may assume “organic = good,” that isn’t always true, and thorough research is time-consuming.
Additionally, the higher cost of “ethical” or “bio” meat might not be feasible for families on tight budgets who also have to pay rent, bills, and try to save for the occasional vacation.

5. Nutritional Aspect of Meat and the Role of Livestock
Eating less meat can be beneficial for health and the environment, but eliminating it entirely (i.e., going fully vegan) can be challenging and may not be the best choice for everyone.
Meat is a good source of protein, iron, vitamin B12, and other essential nutrients (especially in diets where these might be lacking).
Moreover, certain types of land aren’t suited to growing crops; they can, however, support grazing animals (e.g., land that can produce hay for cows). Livestock can therefore be an important part of using available land efficiently.
Many vegans also avoid dairy, opting for alternatives like almond milk, which can have its own environmental impacts. For example, almond production requires a lot of water, sometimes in drought-prone areas, raising human welfare concerns (e.g., water shortages) alongside animal welfare concerns.
It’s understandable to feel more concern for one’s human neighbors than animals when we see how resources are used.

Conclusions and Broader Social Issues
Certainly, buying better-quality meat that ensures higher welfare standards is a good goal in principle.
However, consumers are often left to figure out which labels or certifications truly guarantee better practices, and the responsibility is placed heavily on them.
Additionally, there is the social question: if someone can’t afford high-priced “ethical” meat, does that make them a bad person? Many would say no. Not everyone can handle the extra cost, especially in times of economic hardship.
There’s no perfect solution yet. Animal welfare is important, but so is human welfare—particularly the welfare of small farmers who might struggle to implement costly changes, as well as low-income consumers who can’t afford premium prices.

Author: @lavener100
Content:
Not using these animals as part of the entire system of farming is egregious too. Pigs for example are incredible composters and fallow-land-clearers. I worked on a small farm that would let a piece of land go fallow (grow wild) for a while to restore the soil, then let the pigs loose on it. Within a few days all the plants would be gone and the soil would be nicely trampled, churned up, and fertilized, ready for planting! 
And that's just pigs, cows and chickens have their own benefits in the context of a farm ecosystem. We should be taking advantage of the way plants, animals, and humans work together, instead of relying on monocultures for profit.
I'm wondering if we would be able to grow enough food for the world if we got rid of factory farms and had more small farms that use the land more efficiently and sustainably. They would probably need government subsidies, or be franchises to work in our system, but maybe it's possible? 
Going smaller is an appealing solution for lots of problems these days. I hope we'll get there eventually.

Author: @john2001plus
Content:
I don't have a strong opinion on this matter. I believe animals should be treated humanely but without excessive costs.

We often attribute human characteristics to animals. However, humans have 86 billion neurons in their brains, while a chicken has only 200 million. Their thought processes are not like ours and are largely instinctual.

I've heard that dogs’ brains are designed to remember what is good and bad, but they react primarily based on instinct and learned associations. Dogs have approximately 2.25 billion neurons, while cats have around 750 million.

Cows have about 3 billion neurons, and pigs have nearly the same as dogs.

This doesn’t mean that animals can’t suffer or shouldn’t be treated humanely.

BTW, according to Google, ants have around 250,000 neurons, though I previously read that they have only 7,000. Their brains are so simple that they don’t sleep. An ant cannot function outside of its group, as it depends on chemical signals from other ants to guide its behavior. If isolated, an ant will die. This is also true for other hive insects.

Author: @nickccutter3613
Content:
Hi guys, 
Organic dairy farmer from Germany here. 
Great video, i had a good chucke at you side swipe at biodynamic farming. 
As a farmer i agree eith everything you said in the video. The standard that most animals are beeing held at is not high enough. However i personaly lay the blame for that less at the farmer then at the industry that pays and steers them, the discounters and the processors. 
Often farmers are just given a price and eigther they can work with that price or they have to make it so they can, which impacts feed, health and management of the animals. For dairy farming farmers are payed for a month on the 15th of the following month and they do not get told the price they where producing for untill 1,5 months after they have delivered the milk. I think guaranteeing a price which allows us to calculate beforehand could go a long way. 
Also a thing not mentoned in the Video, but keeping animals outside requires more work, more so now that the wolf is comming back to out pastures. But as less and less people want to work in manual jobs the Labour pool to swap a lot of farms to pasture fed is just not there at the moment. So the prices also have to rise for us to pay people to help us do the extra work.
To the organic criticism i agree, some standards of organic production are not up to date when it comes to current possibilitys. While i personaly dont want to rely on GMO feed or animals it is a great posibility to deal with the changing climate. 
However as in the video i think that organic produce has the highest standards that are currently on the (german) marked, so if you want to buy the best current Standard organic is the way to go. Also organisations like Bioland and Naturland rise above to normal organic Standard and for example require calves to have more space and sunlight then the normal EG-Bio lable.
But if you realy want to make shure, there are farms all across Germany, which produce local Eggs, dairy and meat. Most of them will tell and show you how they produce if you ask nicely. 
If you got this far, have a nice day and i am open for questions.

Author: @austinvegan8350
Content:
This video completely sidesteps the core ethical issue: animals are not objects, and their exploitation is never ethical. Buying “organic” or “bio” meat does not change the fact that these animals are bred, used, and slaughtered as commodities. If killing a human in a “humane” way for food is still murder, why should it be different for non-human animals? The problem isn’t how they are raised or killed; it is that they are treated as resources in the first place.

Mussels, as suggested in the video, are still living beings exploited for human consumption. Even if they lack complex nervous systems, the argument remains: if the absence of certain cognitive traits justified exploitation, then humans with cognitive disabilities would be fair game too. We reject that logic when it applies to humans, so why accept it when it applies to animals?

The real question is this: What morally relevant difference justifies treating animals as objects while protecting humans from the same fate? If you cannot name one, then there is no ethical way to eat meat, only ways to make exploitation appear more palatable.

Author: @GaudiFanYAY
Content:
The biggest and first step is indeed to avoid wasting food. No food waste will do the world a lot of good, especially the animals suffering from it.

However, there is an issue with the solutions presented, that I wish would have been brought up: Space.

There is not infinite area where we can magically put farm animals. In some places, space is heavily regulated and not something that is just there for the taking. Like EU, and many parts of Asia. In USA there may still be "virgin soil" for the taking, but even then there are challenges with just setting it all up.

And then if we are to give animals more space, we will need to either reduce production (and increase prices to make up for costs), or sacrifice other precious farmland or nature reserves for this. And giving up farmland for plants to animals IS THE WORST food production trade-off deal in the world. It takes multiple fields to support animals to feed a given amount of humans, where just one field would do.

Chicken meat, is the least troublesome meat there is to deal with. The least carbon footprint, and with a bit of engineering, you can combine them with either certain crop fields (chickens eat leafy greens too, so not all crop fields can be used here) where they can act as pesticide control by feeding on bugs, or some other natural areas where they cannot do harm, like tree farms (where trees are grown from bush size to full size. Anything smaller will be eaten/trampled by chickens).

But you cannot combine farm lands for pigs or cows with crop fields like chickens. So Chickens offer the greatest amount of flexibility on this part. And it is a bit of a shame that was not mentioned either.

And for people who are gonna ask "how do you even control the chickens if they are in a crop fields or in a forest area? Chickens can be trained to respond to sounds. Train them a "food signal" sound, and they will all come running from the wilderness. Only exception is if they are too hurt to come, or stuck. But a bit of simple patrolling can deal with this, but the problem with free range chickesn is that there will always be some sort of loss. Whether to predators, sickness, injury or just random deaths.

Author: @jaredobrienlee
Content:
Unlike some of my vegan friends, I do think animal products can ethically remain a part of human diets, in moderation. But if, and only if, the animals are treated with dignity and respect during their life and in their death. This is the reciprocal duty we create when we bring thinking, feeling, sentient life into the world, for the purpose of being consumed: that it should be treated with honour and dignity. A bare-minimum quid pro quo for what we will ultimately take from it.

This is the exact opposite of the horrific, industrial-scale torture and suffering that is sadly still the norm in most industrial agriculture. The extreme commodification of intelligent life to eek out marginal commercial gains is nothing short of evil, and I think / hope public sentiment will continue to shift in this direction. Consumer choice matters, but ultimately we need a strictly monitored and enforced regulatory framework for minimum standards of care, that reflects values society can be proud of.

Content:
A full fillet of salmon (about 3 pounds) costs $40.  For one dinner.
A single steak costs $15-30, and not even the top quality cuts.  Requires additional food to be a dinner.
Eggs?  $10 a dozen now.  4-6 in scrambled eggs, one meal.

US pricing.  It's almost impossible to buy meat or fish, or even eggs nowadays.  The "carnivore diet" is literally impossible for a large amount of people.  It'd be at least $1,000 a month, on just meat.

I would eat meat and fish every day if it was affordable, but animal farming is not viable anymore.

Author: @jannepeltonen2036
Content:
A couple things I'd like to add.

Egg-laying chicken breeds are also bred to be sick. They lay so many eggs so quickly that the calcium supplies in their bodies is constantly too low. Basically, they have been engineered to have constant osteoporosis - in plain English, their skeletons are fragile. So if you want eggs with less cruelty, then you need to pay attention to the breeds used there, too.

Also - if meat consumption was to stay at the current level and people started eating less-cruelly produced meat, especially beef, the carbon emissions of the agricultural sector would explode. They are already unsustainably high.

If you want to be ecological *and* ethical, there's just no way you can justify eating meat. The biosphere cannot handle it.

Author: @Pokellectibles94
Content:
Just wanted to put these tips out there for anyone interested in animal product alternatives but are worries about price or eating out.

I've been vegan for about 6 years now and one of the main arguments I see against veganism is that it's "classist" because vegan food is too expensive. Yes, the processed meat alternatives can be expensive (normally just the novelty ones), but they have come down significantly in price and increased in quality over the last 5 years since it gained much more popularity. A 4 pack of Morning Star or Gardein vegan burgers is a little less than $5 after tax at my local Walmart, around the same price as beef hamburgers. Walmart has also released their own line of vegan foods that are around $1 cheaper than the name brands. Almond and soy milk have also decreased in price and are similar in cost to dairy milk now. If you have a Publix local to you, they almost always have a dairy milk alternative BOGO free making them even cheaper than dairy milk and they often place the processed meat alternatives like Morning Star, Gardein, Dr Praegers, Beyond, and Impossible on BOGO as well making them the same price or cheaper than their meat counterparts. If you don't mind some more in depth cooking, vegan foods are the cheapest in the store. Veggies, beans, legumes, rice, grains, pasta, tofu etc. you can make a TON of really nice vegan dishes that are just as affordable as any other home cooked meal, you just have to learn a little bit more. Also, if you live in a more rural area like me, check those discount grocery stores! I just recently bought 15 packs of Earth Balance vegan butter for $1 each and 15 bags of Forks over knives frozen skillet meals for $2 each. A lot of times you can find extremely good deals on vegan products at those stores since they are less popular in rural areas and if it's something you can freeze for later, you can stock up and save a ton of money!

One of the other main points I see people struggle with is cheese. I've tried all of the vegan cheese in every fashion possible and trust me when I say, Violife is the best cold cheese, Miyoko's is best for melting, and Chao is the best balanced for both melting and cold. Daiya is garbage, follow your heart is meh (their parmesan is good for pasta dishes), and the better goods walmart brand is just awful. 

Eating out is the main struggle and largely depends on the area you live. Burger King has the Impossible whopper which is vegan if you take off the mayo and their fries and onion rings are vegan. Any item on the taco bell menu can be made vegan for free by asking for fresco style (removes all dairy and adds pico de gallo) and substituting any meat for beans, rice or black beans. Asian restaurants almost always have a good variety of vegan dishes, they just typically aren't advertised as vegan but the thai and japanese restaurants I've been to have always been the most helpful and accommodating. Most chain restaurants like applebees have either impossible or beyond burgers. Chipotle is great, Falafel is pretty common, and don't look over veggie fajitas at your small local mexican restaurant. It requires digging for more knowledge but once you have it, you always know where you can and can't find options.

Author: @Dorgpoop
Content:
The trouble with the comparison to food prices in 1987, is that although food was moderately more expensive back then, the cost of living was much much lower, mainly because of housing costs. On paper it sounds like a small ask for people to pay 20-100% more for animal products given that they're already cheap, but a lot of people have become reliant on those cheap prices because their other costs take up most of their disposable income. 

The idea that providing animals with more access to open pasture is a solution is also complicated by the fact that farming taking more land massively increases the carbon footprint. Cattle or sheep on open pasture may have a better quality of life than conventionally farmed chickens or pigs, but they are also massively more polluting.

I think we should all try to experiment with our diet to try and replace some amount of animal products with cheap and healthy protein rich vegetable produce, like beans, lentils, mushrooms etc. I also think people need to start being a bit more open minded about consuming sources of protein that seem unconventional, like mussels, insects, GMO and lab grown meat, because if the climate crisis disrupts our food supply then we might end up needing to rely on them.

Ultimately, changing people's diet takes a long time. People don't just eat meat eggs and dairy because it's cheap and tasty, it's also nutritious and easy to prepare. Learning to make plant based foods that are competitive in cost, nutrition, taste and ease of cooking is a skill that takes a long time to develop, realistically it will take a generational shift.

Content:
If anyone here is wondering, tofu is extremely cheap and easy to cook. 

Here is a simple recipe: 

Place tofu into the freezer. Yes, the entire container. After its frozen, let it thaw out in the fridge. Once, thawed, put it back in the freezer. Yes, you read that right, BACK into the freezer. After its second freeze its ready to be cooked.

Author: @DavidRichardson153
Content:
Just so you know, while it is cheaper for farmers to essentially torture the animals, it is not so that they can provide more food for potential customers. No, it is because they usually get paid so little per animal that they need to maximize the number of animals they need to sell in order to get by. In many ways, treating the animals more ethically is cheaper, both in money and especially in resources used, but because of how economic systems are typically geared, it usually ends up being more expensive for farmers to do. This is by no means a justification for torture meat, just a reminder that torture meat was incentivized.

As for the price increases for more ethical treatment, that is largely just markup from meat companies, which was made even worse by how much they have consolidated over the years. Remember, prices tends to go up whenever competition goes down, and if, for some reason, you believe that letting the (last I checked) 6 biggest meat companies merge and consolidate down to even fewer is going to somehow bring prices down, well, there is a lot that could be said about you that is hardly flattering, so let's just say that you absolutely deserve to pay higher prices.

Unfortunately, buying what is labeled as ethically treated meat is not going to do anything to change this. Setting aside just how confusing (and largely useless) the labels are, deciding with your wallet does not affect it as much as you believe it does, especially not after how so much has consolidated under the control of so few. When all you have is "awful vs nothing," "awful" is going to win far more often than not, and unfortunately, simply cutting out meat and related products entirely is not an option for some parts of the world (and not just the "less-than-well-off" parts). If you want to end the practice of torturing for meat, paying more for a (supposedly) different end product is not going to do it; enacting price controls, market regulations, and basically going after the middlemen more than anyone else (because the middlemen really are where the bulk of the increased costs lie - not just in price hikes, but in driving down what farmers get paid) with do far more than you could ever do with your wallet.

This is an attitude commonly found in wider Thai business culture which is one of the reasons why a lot of our businesses are dying.  I expect there'll be a lot of pushback. A carrot and stick solution is possibe by adding incentives to increase animal welfare such as subsidies and tax relaxations which will help with the price rise for the consumer end, and punitive measures such as contract ineligibility or higher taxes for ones that do not comply. 

On the consumer end, are facing a looming cost of living and demographic crisis, with power being rather expensive, and food price rising as well. We had a temporary pork price increase due to various coinciding factors some time ago. My upper middle class family did noticed, but did not mind buying the same amount of pork for the higher price until things stabilized, but the less afluent side of society was in an uproar (except the muslims). Needless to say, the consumer side of the economy would not take well to price increases on meat, as it would feed into the already rising cost of living. With an aging population, household purchasing power will be reduced too. Cost of meat is already rising due to other factors like the fertilizer shortage without these proposed animal welfare policies. 

Knowing Thailand, in the end, I suspect it'll just be a political mudfight with some result coming out, and lacking much enforcement or effort past the third month unless the media picks it up.  People will be against it because hey, it makes life more expensive and more complicated for results that can be distracted away! The political capital gained from this will be....negligable at best, overcome by the costs and complications I mentioned. So in reality, I doubt 'reduced cruelty farms' will go anywhere on any meaningful scale here in Thailand.

Author: @guss77
Content: I have worked in an egg laying farm and a dairy farm. The chicken farm was barn style with 600 to 800 chickens in a 50m long barn. It was pretty wide and there are 2 heights of raised platforms for the laying coups and birds can also roam on the ground, so there's ample room, still we received chickens with clipped beaks - either because the "training barns" (where chickens live before they're mature enough to lay eggs) are kept very crowded, or because the hatchery does this as standard - these are both independent businesses we have no control over. The dairy farm I worked in was initially an open yard affair - cows live in large enclosures where the roofed area is supplied with fresh hay weekly and there's enough room for all cowes to comfortably lay down with ample room (and still on cold days there'd be a heap of cows in the middle of an otherwise mostly empty shed) and there's about twice as much open yard space to run around in. Then the farm transitioned to a robotic milking system, which necessitated the whole thing to be rebuilt - the new setup is much more compact: each cow has an individual stall that is just wide enough for the cow to easily move in and out, and lay comfortably (which is still pretty wide - cows are big), and there's only about 50% of open yard (as laying area), but cows are free to move around, feed when they want to and go to be milked when they want to - and according to the statistics I've seen, they appear much happier: there are almost no stress incidents, less sickness and a lot more milk. The upgrade was expensive but paid for itself so quickly that they built two more automated sheds.

Author: @9999cheeta
Content: Fantastic video as always, but I wanted to provide some clarification (licensed vet tech with farm animal experience here).  The crates that you're referencing at @5:56 are called Farrowing Cages.  These cages are often used after the sow (female pig) gives birth to her piglets because it allows for the piglets to suckle without accidentally being crushed by mom when she rolls over or stands up, which unfortunately is a common problem due to how big mom can get.  Also, there is a risk of sows cannibalizing their piglets after birth due to high stress levels, aggression issues, and other factors; so the farrowing cages protect the piglets in that aspect as well.  HOWEVER, I will say that some farms/companies have been known to keep their sows in farrowing cages for days on end, which I (and most of the veterinary field) heavily disagree with and are working to fix.  Thank you for the amazing video!

Author: @suicune2001
Content:
I will at least give you props for being honest about the conditions of the animals. Cows in the US are tortured and their children taken away immediately after birth and placed in solitary confinement. Their udders are too big and too heavy and can even break their legs. They're guaranteed to get mastitis which is very painful. If antibiotics don't work on them then they are sent to slaughter and you eat their infected bodies in your milk and burgers. 

Basically, all USDA labels regarding animals are BS. Free range means they could have a 1 foot space of outdoors. (no grass required) "Grass fed" means the  cow could be fed nothing but soy and alfalfa and get the grass fed label. "Organic" means they're not allowed to feed the animal plastic. (but since Trump wants to get rid of the USDA, who is going to stop them?) "Pasture raised" means the cows only need to spend 30% of their entire life outside and can spend the other 70% indoors eating whatever. If you see a chicken product with "no growth hormones" then that's misleading because chickens are not allowed to be fed growth hormones. Cows and pigs are, though. "Humanely raised" literally means nothing. The  company puts on their website what "humanely raised" means and no one checks to make sure they're even doing it.

USDA labels are just feel good labels that don't mean the animal wasn't horrifically tortured.

Author: @strati5phere
Content:
I’ve been thinking about how idealism seems to be bubbling up lately—like we’re on the cusp of evolving into something better, something perfect. And in many ways, we are. We’ve built incredible things, dreamed big dreams. But when it comes to basics like food and energy, we’re still wrestling with limits—maybe even with ourselves. I wonder if it’s because we carry this emotional weight, a tug-of-war between who we are and who we want to be.

Take a lion in the wild. When it hunts, it doesn’t pause to make it pretty or painless—it digs into its meal, raw and real, while the zebra’s still kicking. That’s nature, not cruelty. And here’s the thing: we’re part of that same messy, beautiful world. As much as we reach for the stars, we’re still animals—hungry, flawed, alive. I don’t say that to drag us down, but to ground us. We’re not above the lion; we’re alongside it, doing our best with what we’ve got.

Maybe that’s where the purpose lies—not in escaping the circle of life, but in embracing our place in it. We’re human, sure, but we’re also part of something bigger. And that’s not a failure—it’s a strength.

Author: @LoneIrbis
Content:
Well it's often far from that simple. Some farmers have their channels, it's easy to see how they work. And in a lot of cases it doesn't look remotely as bad. Take for example Sandi Brock and her sheep - yes, they live in a barn, but not in a tiny cages. They have plenty of space to run, they are handled well, fed to keep them healthy and are treated if they get sick. Sure, labs get sold for meat, but they get a few weeks of decent life, and it's often more than they get in the wild. 

And how exactly is it suggested to account in price for the quality of their life if they just sell it to them market on whatever price it's currently bought for? If the market is willing to pay $X for kg of meat, and you bring it a sheep that is worth $X*50% to grow, you won't sell it for more - you'll just get less profit or, more likely no profit at all, only loss. Sure, you can ignore the market and do everything yourself, but then you'll just end up with a bunch of expensive meat that no one wants to buy because there's cheaper alternatives of same quality. 

It probably can be regulated, but I'm afraid it has to be done not on personal level, but by lawmakers. If there's a heavy fine for bad farm conditions and a risk to get closed, it might force farmers to provide better conditions for their animals. And of course that would rise the prices because we will be the ones who pays for it anyway. Also it will increas improt meat from countries where no such laws exists, so the meat is cheaper. That would lead to local farmers no longer farming due to being unable to compete with the market. Hence no good conditions for any animals again - the ones that were raised in good conditions would just end up sold for whatever possible and the farmer would find other job (or not).

Author: @DevonThornton
Content:
I was the caretaker of a factory hog farm here in Ohio for a while. Heimerl Farms was the ultimate owner of it, even though the land was owned by a local farmer that I worked for. Here are the things I can confirm and deny:

1. The pigs do not get frustrated and attack each other under normal circumstances. Only if one jumps from their home pen to a neighboring one, and then they're "othered" and the hogs in that pen will try to hurt them. If you catch it within the first day and move them to a sick pen, they'll be fine, if a bit beat up.

2. They indeed live their lives on concrete floors under a roof. No bedding. There are slots in the floor so their waste can be collected underneath the barn, which is just one giant manure pit. The smell is unforgettable 

3. They do dock their tails, but not the whole thing. Tail bites do happen still, but again, the agression is *usually* a territorial issue from a jumper

4. The piglets indeed come in at 3 week. They then live for about 3 months until theyre full sized, then they get loaded out and sent to market

5. Theyre NOT kept in crates. The farms I worked at had 2500 hogs per building, split into pens that are roughtly 10'×10' (estimating from memory here) and have 20-30 hogs per pen. All of the hogs can lay down and there's room to walk between them and thats about it.

6. They get sunlight. All of the outside walls are windows that can be raised to let fresh air and sunlight in, weather permitting 

7. Something not mentioned here: their diet. They get feed from automatic feeders and whey from automatic dispensers. The whey is liquid form, and unless the Whey shipments get behind, the hogs never get water to drink, just whey. If they run out, it automatically switches to water, but otherwise they only get whey and feed so they're constantly gaining weight

I can't comment on the conditions for the mothers, as I didnt work at a breeding farm. I will say that one of the reasons I quit was the mental tax it took. It's heartbreaking to live it first hand and see that these animals essentially live in jail their whole 4 month life. 

That said, I did everything in my power while I was there to genuinely make their short lives as pleasant as I could. I got the farmers to stop shouting at them, smacking them to get em to move, and especially to stop using cattle prods to make em move. I found that if you walk the pens and get them used to people, then remain calm and quiet during loadout, not only is the whole process MUCH easier and smoother, but it stresses the hogs out MUCH less. I can't say for sure if my methods stuck after I left, but I tried

If anyone wants to know more, AMA

Author: @tinker_gearsmith
Content:
This is NOT a pro meat comment.

I am pretty sure that absolutely no decent human being would object to better treatment of animals.    The main issue seems to be that Kurzgesagt is arguing from a point of view of meat being what is essentially a luxury item.  It is not.  Meat is nutrient and calorie dense, freezable for long term storage, and generally affordable for lower income families.

Fruit and veggies are more expensive per calorie and generally don't react well to freezing.  Try freezing a tomato and then letting it thaw ( pro-tip: great for making tomato soup! ).  Grocery store pricing reflects this.  Couple that with the fact that most people don't have to space to grow their own food since they live in apartment.

Restricting meat through raised pricing would essentially punish low income families, have the desired effect on mid income families, and the rich wouldn't even notice it.  Essentially, we need to fix food availability first - without support mechanisms in place raising any food pricing will have a terrible outcome.

Author: @Allthecrazythings87
Content:
Theres quite a bit of context missing from the section about chickens. At least i know that because i own them. 

For context on meat birds, they are slaughtered at 6-10 weeks old. Idk where he’s getting his numbers but the difference between farming a meat bird that grows fast and only takes 6 or so weeks before its ready to be slaughtered would be wildly cheaper than raising a heritage hen that would take much much longer to mature… would need a A LOT more feed… and of course thats not accounting for all the other things we’re trying to accomplish here which is more space and maybe even smaller flocks. 

Im not saying it isnt very sad how it all is… but economically its not possible for chicken to continue to be the cheapest meat while getting rid of the meat bird. They are exclusively the reason why. 

And as far as culling, it would be worse with traditional farming practices as opposed to using meat birds… i believe they will raise both pullets and cockerels for meat… but that would be impossible to achieve with traditional farming. Roosters do not make good meat unless they are castrated… turning them into capons. But doing that adds to the cost and questionable in terms of ethics as well. Usually roosters are very mean and cannot be raised well in a flock. They’re like the fighting fish of the bird world. Ive heard of people figuring out a way to get cocks to get along (they arent roosters unless they are bringing hens home to roost), but it usually at least involves separating the cocks from the hens because the hens bring out their roosting instincts… and you still have to deal with the occasional rooster that just wont cooperate and you HAVE to cull them. 

Same is true for hens. Hens have a pecking order. And they WILL bully other hens even to death. The larger the flock the more of this happens. This is why, even in free range chickens, they might still clip their beaks. Occasionally you can even get a hen that takes on the rooster role without a rooster in the flock, and she will even grow spurs. 

Im telling you roosters are mean af. I got a couple of them unintentionally when buying some chickens for my small flock, and i tried and tried to keep them. They mostly got along… but i did have one hen die from being chased into a tree, her wings got stuck and she just died there. And when i mean being chased… i mean from being mated… with three roosters in my flock my hens were getting over mated… their feathers destroyed from constant mounting… plus they werent letting me near my flock to take care of them. So they HAD to go… all but the nicest one. 

Im saying all this because people who have never owned these animals often have no clue about how hard it really is to take care of them they way YOU want to… theyre not humans… and people attribute human qualities on them, and that actually can hurt then more than help. Like some people keep a hen or rooster in an apartment, putting chicken diapers on them to keep them in the house. Cute but thats not really natural to them. In either case the reasons why mass farming has the practices they do is because theres only so much people can do to feed the population and keep up with that demand while at the same time treating them the best. 

And ive seen people who raise their chickens in battery cages who still genuinely love their flock. So its not fair to automatically attribute malice to these practices. Theyre often used to make sure they could feed their communities. Because not every farm is feeding western society. Theres a whole world out here. 

The one thing this guy got right in this video for sure is saying how complicated farming is. That is 100% true.

Author: @UIairi
Content:
The end of the video is my primary issue -- I'm all for paying more if I KNOW that I'm actually improving the quality of life for the animal I'm consuming, but that's enormously hard to verify in the current market. When "organic" doesn't actually have any regulated meaning, and a lot of store brands are so disconnected for their source you can't even track the animal back, there's little reason to go for it. A lot of the companies that claim they're improving the quality of life of animals here in the US have been caught doing the opposite, and I'm not willing to pay a multi billion dollar conglomerate twice as much to lie to me about where they source their animals. If there was any real accountability, I'd be more then happy to do it.

I've been looking for local butchers for a while, but the cost for the only one in my area isn't pennies more but 3-6x more. A cut of beef at the supermarket that goes for $6/lb is $22/lb, and one which goes for $12/lb can be as high as $60/lb. Chicken is only about three times as much, but I still don't know where it's sourced from either. An hour away from me there's a better butcher, with fair prices, and good quality meat, but I don't actually KNOW their animals are treated any better either. I can hope, buy in bulk there, and vacuum seal and freeze it, but it still rings kind of hollow. Moreover, I consume a lot more cheese and dairy then meat, and there's absolutely no accountability there. The entire situation is just frustrating, and why we need real regulation in the industry. Words like "organic," and "free range," should actually have real quality standards and inspections behind them.

Author: @belthesheep
Content:
I just want to drop my two cents here, I know basically no one cares.

1) Meat is not wasteful, it's extremely useful breeding and feeding animals because they can eat things we humans cannot digest. Plus, they help increase soil quality when properly managed so that the land animals are kept in can also be later used for farming instead.

2) I will never understand people who like the milder taste of young, castrated pigs. Best porkchops I ever ate came from an old pig we slaughtered when he was like, 6 years old already (Which is not *super* old but like, pigs get slaughtered before they're 1 year old). He was never castrated, we kept him for breeding since he was part wild boar and it showed. That meat was red like beef and the fat tasted amazing, mostly because of the age of the pig and not being castrated though.

Edit: 

3) Where I live (Argentina) meat consumption is at its lowest level in a century. Meat is nowadays more expensive than it used to be, and conditions for cattle are worse than ever, because of government regulation. It used to be that argentine beef was grass fed, grass finished, and lived in the wide open pastures of our country with very little indoor time if any. Then, because of government regulation trying to push the price of meat down and increasing taxes on farmers simultaneously, feedlots became commonplace even though our land is so plentiful we truly do not need them for high production volume. My dad, who was born in the 80s, still laments how beef has gotten worse and more expensive.

Author: @stevendesu
Content:
The numbers in the video sounds a bit suspect (is it REALLY only a few more cents for animals to live cage-free?) so I've been digging through the sources... There seems to be a huge disconnect between Kurzgesagt's audience and what they're discussing. The video seems to imply that viewers in their target countries (western Europe and America) are eating tortured animals. But he data tells a different story. Here are the countries with a near 100% rate of caging chickens and a very high chicken population:

China (1.21 billion caged out of 1.25 billion total)
India (403 million caged out of 403 million total)
Bangladesh (301 million caged out of 301 million total),
Mexico (211 million caged out of 212 million total)
Russia (197 million caged out of 197 million total)
Indonesia (166 million caged out of 166 million total)
Brazil (158 million caged out of 166 million total)
Pakistan (148 million caged out of 148 million total)
Turkey (124 million caged out of 141 million total)
Malaysia (109 million caged out of 109 million total)
Thailand (93 million caged out of 93 million total)
Ukraine (91 million caged out of 91 million total)
Iran (66 million caged out of 66 million total)
Vietnam (63 million caged out of 63 million total)

That's a 98.2% rate of caging for over 3.6 billion chickens in countries that likely don't watch these videos. Meanwhile when we look at the "westernized" countries who likely make up Kurzgesagt's audience:

US (256 million caged out of 336 million total)
Poland (37 million caged out of 43 million total)
Spain (36 million caged out of 43 million total)
France (29 million caged out of 48 million total)
Italy (21 million caged out of 39 million total)
Australia (12 million caged out of 21 million total)
Netherlands (3 million caged out of 32 million total)
Germany (3 million caged out of 47 million total)
Sweden (1 million caged out of 8 million total)
Denmark (1 million caged out of 4 million total)
Norway (0 million caged out of 4 million total)
Austria (0 million caged out of 7 million total)
Switzerland (0 million caged out of 4 million total)

That's a 62.7% rate of caging over 636 million chickens. It seems to me like if we want to end animal cruelty the answer isn't "we, personally, need to spend more on meat". It's "we need to impose sanctions on China to get them to change their ways".

Making your audience feel guilty when they aren't the responsible party doesn't actually advance your goals. If the goal is less total animal cruelty, we need to make changes where the cruelty is actually taking place.

Author: @BingBongWasheeWashee
Content:
Paying more for so-called “ethical” animal products like organic or free-range meat does not eliminate exploitation—it simply funds a different form of it. The core issue is not the conditions in which animals are raised, but the fact that they are treated as commodities at all. Whether an animal is raised in a factory farm or on a small-scale organic farm, they are still bred, controlled, used, and ultimately killed for human consumption.

People claim they want to minimize suffering, but suffering is not the only problem—exploitation itself is the injustice. If a human were bred, used for labor, then killed “humanely,” we would still call it slavery and murder. No amount of extra space or slightly less violent methods would make it acceptable. Why should it be any different for animals?

Additionally, so-called humane labels are often misleading. Free-range chickens are often crammed into crowded barns with minimal access to the outdoors. Grass-fed cattle still end up in slaughterhouses. Organic standards do nothing to change the fundamental reality that these animals are property, their bodies bought and sold for profit.

If the goal is to minimize suffering, the logical step is to stop funding industries that exploit animals entirely. Why continue to pay for their breeding and slaughter at all when the alternative—veganism—removes support for their exploitation altogether? What morally relevant difference justifies treating animals as property in the first place?

Content:
On chickens: A lot of "free range" farms are designed in a way that discourage their hens to actually wander outside and get the stimuli they need.

Which "has to be disabled" during day time, but it costs time and money to make sure all chicks get back inside at the end of the day.  
So if you buy "free range" to feel better about your consumption, chances are that they are coming from the same horrible torture camps. Just with a nice lawn around it.

Wonderful video. Unfortunately here in the US, all these businesses are profit-driven. If we were willing to pay more for a dozen eggs, they would just pad their bottom line.

I am fortunate enough to have a cousin who we buy our eggs from and his chickens are half-free range (lives in upstate NY so half the year theyre indoors). We pay about the same as we would pay at the grocery store for healthy eggs (we pay the same as his other customers).
Though I do demand my eggs contain at least 22% unicorn!

Author: @swigytown
Content: pigs do not have access to sunlight because most domestic pig varieties are susceptible to sunburn and heat stress, and all pigs lack sweat glands and cannot cool themselves. Pigs have a limited tolerance to high temperatures and heat stress can lead to death. Maintaining a more specific temperature within the pig-tolerance range also maximizes growth and growth-to-feed ratio. And, indoor piggeries have allowed pig farming to be undertaken in countries or areas with unsuitable climate or soil for outdoor pig raising.
